recurrence_model__state_partition.explanation: Common decompositions remove the first tile, last symbol, or final operation. Prove that removal reaches the specified state and that every smaller object has a unique reconstruction. For incremental models, also show that new objects do not duplicate existing ones.
notation: The state definition must specify the practical meaning of index n.
Whether the empty state counts as 1 depends on whether the empty construction is unique.
recurrence_model__state_partition.example: A length-n strip splits into two classes according to whether its first tile has length 1 or 2, each bijective with tilings of the remaining length.
common_mistakes: Defining the state too vaguely to decide whether two constructions are the same object.
Relying only on matching early sequence terms without a correspondence between sets.

recurrence_model__memory_states.title: State recurrences with memory constraints
recurrence_model__memory_states.summary: If later choices depend on local history, include the necessary part of that history in the state and build linked recurrences.
recurrence_model__memory_states.definition: If extension legality depends on the last symbol or a suffix of bounded length, count separately by suffix type. Each state retains enough memory to determine whether the next step is legal, and transitions map classes at one stage into classes at the next.
recurrence_model__memory_states.explanation: Memory must suffice but need not retain the entire history. First write each state transition and then obtain the total; eliminating auxiliary states sometimes gives a higher-order single-sequence recurrence. Specify the state assigned to the empty string so that the first transition works.
notation: u_n and v_n may count different ending types.
$a_n=u_n+v_n$ holds only if the two classes are disjoint and exhaustive.
recurrence_model__memory_states.example: For ternary strings avoiding 22, distinguish strings ending in 2 from those not ending in 2; only the latter may be extended by 2.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the total by a fixed number of choices when different endings allow different choices.
Using overlapping states, or assigning the empty string to a state without its corresponding initial value.

recurrence_model__divide_conquer.title: Size recurrences for divide-and-conquer algorithms
recurrence_model__divide_conquer.summary: Include the size of every subproblem, whether each is executed, and the extra cost of splitting and merging.
recurrence_model__divide_conquer.definition: If a size-n problem executes several smaller subproblems with additional cost g(n), its total cost is the sum of the subproblem costs plus g(n). The recursion must have reachable base cases, with sizes on every call branch eventually decreasing to a base case.
recurrence_model__divide_conquer.explanation: Odd sizes require rounding. If only one subproblem executes, do not add the costs of two. Solve by summing costs over recursion-tree levels or using induction for special sizes such as powers of 2, then specify the applicable range.
notation: $T_n=T_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}+T_{\lceil n/2\rceil}+g(n)$ is a common structure.
recurrence_model__divide_conquer.example: For powers of two, if each equal split costs 1 to merge, T_1=0 and T_n=2T_(n/2)+1, giving T_n=n−1.
common_mistakes: Recursing to size 1 again when n=1, preventing termination.
Multiplying subproblem costs or omitting the additional cost.

recurrence_homogeneous.title: Linear homogeneous recurrences
recurrence_homogeneous.summary: A linear homogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients forms each term as a fixed linear combination of earlier terms; its characteristic equation determines the general solution.
recurrence_homogeneous.definition: A kth-order linear homogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients has the form $a_n=c_1a_{n-1}+\cdots+c_ka_{n-k}$ (n≥k), where the coefficients are constant and the coefficient of the longest lag satisfies $c_k\ne0$. Its characteristic polynomial is $p(r)=r^k-c_1r^{k-1}-\cdots-c_k$. Homogeneous means there is no additional nonzero term depending only on n; linear means the sequence terms occur only in a first-degree linear combination.
recurrence_homogeneous.explanation: Trying a_n=r^n gives p(r)=0. Each distinct root produces an exponential solution. A root r of multiplicity m gives r^n,nr^n,…,n^(m−1)r^n. Linearly combine these solutions and use k independent initial conditions to determine the constants. For real coefficients, conjugate complex roots combine into real sine and cosine terms. Verify the formula against both the recurrence and all initial values, rather than fitting only the first few terms.
notation: For distinct roots $r_1,\ldots,r_k$: $a_n=\sum_{j=1}^k C_jr_j^n$.
For a double root r: $a_n=(C+Dn)r^n$.
Initial values determine the constants in the linear combination; they do not change the characteristic polynomial.
recurrence_homogeneous.example: The characteristic equation of $a_n=3a_{n-1}-2a_{n-2}$ is $(r-1)(r-2)=0$, so the general solution is $C+D2^n$. If a_0=2 and a_1=3, then C=D=1.
common_mistakes: Making sign errors when rearranging the characteristic polynomial.
Keeping only one exponential for a repeated root, omitting powers of n.
Guessing a formula from a few terms without substituting into the recurrence and initial conditions.

recurrence_homogeneous__distinct_roots.title: Distinct characteristic roots and determining constants
recurrence_homogeneous__distinct_roots.summary: For distinct characteristic roots, use their exponential sequences as basic solutions and solve a linear system from the initial conditions.
recurrence_homogeneous__distinct_roots.definition: If the characteristic polynomial of a kth-order linear homogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients has k distinct roots $r_1,\ldots,r_k$, its general solution is $\sum_j C_jr_j^n$; the corresponding initial conditions determine C_j.
recurrence_homogeneous__distinct_roots.explanation: Rearrange correctly to obtain the characteristic polynomial, then factor it to find roots. A negative root produces sign changes in its powers and cannot be replaced by its absolute value. After solving for constants, check all initial values and the recurrence rather than only the growth rate of one term.
notation: Second order: $r^2-c_1r-c_2=0$.
recurrence_homogeneous__distinct_roots.example: Roots 1 and −2 give $C+D(-2)^n$; the negative root produces alternating signs by parity.
common_mistakes: Writing −2^n instead of (−2)^n.
Using only one initial value to determine two unknown constants in a second-order solution.

recurrence_homogeneous__repeated_roots.title: Repeated characteristic roots and polynomial factors
recurrence_homogeneous__repeated_roots.summary: For repeated characteristic roots, multiply exponential sequences by different powers of n to obtain enough independent solutions.
recurrence_homogeneous__repeated_roots.definition: If a nonzero root r has multiplicity m in the characteristic polynomial, its solution family is $P(n)r^n$, where P has degree at most m−1. Add the contributions of distinct roots to obtain the general solution.
recurrence_homogeneous__repeated_roots.explanation: A double root needs C+Dn, and a triple root needs C+Dn+En². The number of initial values corresponds to the recurrence order, not the number of distinct roots. Multiplicity of root 1 is closely related to finite differences; for example, a sequence with zero third difference is polynomial of degree at most two.
notation: A root of multiplicity m contributes $r^n,nr^n,\ldots,n^{m-1}r^n$.
recurrence_homogeneous__repeated_roots.example: For characteristic polynomial (r−1)³, the general solution is C+Dn+En², rather than just a constant.
common_mistakes: Allowing only one free constant for a repeated root.
Making the maximum degree in n one too high or too low.

recurrence_homogeneous__complex_roots.title: Complex conjugate roots and real periodic solutions
recurrence_homogeneous__complex_roots.summary: Complex conjugate roots of a real recurrence combine into real sine and cosine terms; periodicity depends on both angle and amplitude.
recurrence_homogeneous__complex_roots.definition: For a linear homogeneous recurrence with real constant coefficients, a pair of simple nonreal conjugate roots $re^{\pm i\theta}$ (r>0) contributes $r^n(C\cos n\theta+D\sin n\theta)$ to the real general solution, with real C,D. If each root has multiplicity m, the contribution is $r^n(P(n)\cos n\theta+Q(n)\sin n\theta)$, where P,Q are real polynomials of degree at most m−1. Real initial values and real coefficients still produce a real sequence despite complex roots.
recurrence_homogeneous__complex_roots.explanation: The angle θ controls oscillation; r^n controls growth or decay. Even if the sine and cosine factors repeat periodically, the full sequence is usually not periodic when r≠1. Proving a least period requires finding a period and ruling out every smaller positive integer period.
notation: Roots ±i give $C\cos(n\pi/2)+D\sin(n\pi/2)$.
recurrence_homogeneous__complex_roots.example: Roots ±2i give four-step oscillation multiplied by 2^n. The normalized sequence may be periodic while the original amplitude grows.
common_mistakes: Claiming a sequence cannot be real because there are complex roots.
Looking only at repeated angles and ignoring the changing exponential amplitude.

recurrence_nonhomogeneous.title: Nonhomogeneous recurrences
recurrence_nonhomogeneous.summary: When a linear recurrence has a nonzero forcing term, find a particular solution and add the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous recurrence.
recurrence_nonhomogeneous.definition: A linear nonhomogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients has the form $a_n-c_1a_{n-1}-\cdots-c_ka_{n-k}=f(n)$, where f is not identically zero. Replacing f by 0 gives its homogeneous recurrence. If p_n is a particular solution and h_n is the general homogeneous solution, all solutions are a_n=p_n+h_n; initial conditions then determine the homogeneous constants.
recurrence_nonhomogeneous.explanation: A linear operator applied to p+h equals the sum of its actions, explaining this structure. Find a particular solution by rearrangement, iteration, or undetermined coefficients. For f(n)=P(n)λ^n with λ≠0, try a polynomial of the same degree times λ^n. If λ is a homogeneous characteristic root of multiplicity s, multiply the trial by n^s to avoid overlap with homogeneous solutions. A particular solution need not satisfy the initial values; apply those to the full homogeneous-plus-particular solution.
notation: If $L(a)=f$, $L(h)=0$, and $L(p)=f$, then $L(h+p)=f$.
In resonance, try $p_n=n^sQ(n)\lambda^n$, with Q of the same degree as the forcing polynomial.
The difference of two particular solutions is homogeneous, but their sum generally does not solve the same nonhomogeneous recurrence.
recurrence_nonhomogeneous.example: For $a_n=2a_{n-1}+1$, a constant particular solution is −1, so the general solution is $C2^n-1$. If a_0=0, C=1 and a_n=2^n−1.
common_mistakes: Solving only the homogeneous part and ignoring the forcing term.
Failing to multiply by the required power of n when a trial overlaps with the homogeneous solution.
Requiring the particular solution alone to satisfy all initial values and incorrectly concluding that no solution exists.

recurrence_nonhomogeneous__superposition.title: Superposition of homogeneous and particular solutions
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__superposition.summary: The nonhomogeneous solution set is one particular solution plus all homogeneous solutions; subtraction of two particular solutions cancels the forcing term.
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__superposition.definition: If a linear recurrence operator L satisfies L(p)=f, then L(a)=f exactly when a=p+h with L(h)=0. Thus the nonhomogeneous solution set is a translate of the corresponding homogeneous solution space and is generally not itself a vector space.
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__superposition.explanation: Linearity gives L(p+h)=L(p)+L(h). Conversely, set h=a−p. Subtracting two particular solutions of the same equation gives a homogeneous solution, but adding them generally produces 2f. Apply initial conditions to the complete solution p+h.
notation: $L(p-q)=0$ when L(p)=L(q)=f.
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__superposition.example: For a_n−2a_(n−1)=3, the constant sequence −3 is a particular solution, and all solutions are −3+C2^n.
common_mistakes: Assuming the forcing term remains f after adding two particular solutions.
Keeping only a particular solution and omitting the homogeneous freedom.

recurrence_nonhomogeneous__nonresonant.title: Nonresonant forcing and undetermined coefficients
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__nonresonant.summary: If the exponential base of the forcing term is not a homogeneous characteristic root, try a matching polynomial times that exponential.
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__nonresonant.definition: For a linear recurrence with constant coefficients and forcing $P_d(n)\lambda^n$, with λ≠0 and λ not a characteristic root, try $Q_d(n)\lambda^n$, where Q_d is a polynomial of degree at most d with undetermined coefficients, then substitute and compare coefficients.
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__nonresonant.explanation: A constant forcing term has λ=1,d=0; exponential forcing has d=0. The recurrence itself determines the particular coefficients, independently of the initial values; the latter then determine the homogeneous part. If substitution yields identically 0 where a nonzero forcing term is needed, check for resonance.
notation: For first-order L(a)=a_n-ca_(n−1), $L(A\lambda^n)=A(1-c/\lambda)\lambda^n$ (λ≠0).
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__nonresonant.example: For a_n=3a_(n−1)+2^n, try A2^n because 2 is not the homogeneous characteristic root 3.
common_mistakes: Failing to check whether the exponential base is a characteristic root.
Determining a particular-solution coefficient from initial values rather than substituting into the recurrence.

recurrence_nonhomogeneous__resonance.title: Resonance and adjusting particular solutions
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__resonance.summary: When forcing overlaps with homogeneous solutions, multiply by an appropriate extra power of n to avoid terms annihilated by the operator.
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__resonance.definition: If the forcing is $P_d(n)\lambda^n$ and λ is a characteristic root of multiplicity s, try $n^sQ_d(n)\lambda^n$. The required power n^s is determined by root multiplicity, rather than guessed arbitrarily.
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__resonance.explanation: For λ=1, resonance often appears as discrete summation increasing the polynomial degree. Substitute the trial to verify it, compare all polynomial coefficients, and use the homogeneous-plus-particular solution to satisfy the initial values.
notation: For a simple root 2 and forcing 2^n, try An2^n.
For a double root 1 and constant forcing, try An².
recurrence_nonhomogeneous__resonance.example: The homogeneous root of a_n−a_(n−1)=n² is 1, so quadratic polynomial forcing requires consideration of a cubic particular solution.
common_mistakes: Always multiplying by just one n regardless of multiplicity s.
Assuming the adjusted trial form is already a solution without substituting it.

recurrence_initial.title: Initial conditions
recurrence_initial.summary: Initial conditions select a particular sequence from the recurrence solution family; check their number, valid indices, independence, and consistency.
recurrence_initial.definition: For the forward recurrence $a_n=c_1a_{n-1}+\cdots+c_ka_{n-k}+f(n)$ (n≥k), specifying $a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}$ determines every later term uniquely in order. These k values are standard initial conditions. Conditions at other indices or on linear combinations may also determine the sequence, but their independence and compatibility must be checked.
recurrence_initial.explanation: The valid range matters: if a second-order formula starts only at n=3, it cannot compute a_2 without another condition. The number of written conditions is not necessarily the number of independent conditions; an equation already forced by the recurrence removes no further freedom. Inconsistent conditions give no solution. Recovering earlier terms backward also requires the relevant coefficient to be nonzero; forward computability does not guarantee unique recovery in every direction.
notation: Standard kth-order initial values: $(a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{k-1})$.
Existence means some sequence satisfies all given conditions simultaneously. Uniqueness means at most one does.
To compare two solutions, apply the homogeneous recurrence and zero initial values to their difference and prove equality by induction.
recurrence_initial.example: For $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$ (n≥2), a_0=1 alone leaves a_1 arbitrary. Adding a_1=2 uniquely gives 1,2,3,5,8,…. Requiring a_2=9 as well contradicts a_2=3, so there is no solution.
common_mistakes: Assuming k written conditions are necessarily independent.
Ignoring the recurrence starting index and calculating early terms without justification.
Checking only some initial values and overlooking incompatibility of others.

recurrence_initial__forward_unique.title: Existence and uniqueness for forward recurrences
recurrence_initial__forward_unique.summary: Consecutive standard initial values give a starting point; construction term by term proves existence, and comparison term by term proves uniqueness.
recurrence_initial__forward_unique.definition: If each a_n for n≥k is explicitly determined by the preceding k terms and known f(n), any given a_0 through a_(k−1) constructs a sequence satisfying the recurrence in order. No second distinct sequence can have those same initial values.
recurrence_initial__forward_unique.explanation: Existence means the rule actually allows continuation; uniqueness means a common start cannot branch. For a linear recurrence, take the difference of two solutions: the initial differences are 0, hence all later differences are 0. A general explicit functional recurrence can also be compared directly by induction.
notation: The induction base must cover all early terms required on the right side.
recurrence_initial__forward_unique.example: For the second-order recurrence a_n=a_(n−1)+a_(n−2), given a_0,a_1, the terms a_2,a_3,… are produced uniquely in turn.
common_mistakes: Showing one formula satisfies the conditions without showing that every solution agrees with it.
Confusing forward uniqueness with backward invertibility.

recurrence_initial__boundary_range.title: Valid indices and completing boundary data
recurrence_initial__boundary_range.summary: The starting index determines which early terms must be supplied separately; backward recovery from later data also requires an invertible coefficient.
recurrence_initial__boundary_range.definition: The valid index range is part of a recurrence definition. An early term not determined by equations in that range is free boundary data. For a_n=ca_(n−1), backward recovery by division is possible only if c≠0.
recurrence_initial__boundary_range.explanation: Writing n≥2 rather than n≥3 can produce a different solution family. Substitute the first valid index to see exactly which undetermined quantities the right side needs. If later values replace initial values, verify that they uniquely recover standard initial values.
notation: The first valid equation need not determine the unknown term with the smallest index.
recurrence_initial__boundary_range.example: If a_n=a_(n−1)+a_(n−2) holds only for n≥3, a_2 does not follow from a_0,a_1.
common_mistakes: Applying a formula outside its stated range.
Dividing by a zero coefficient when solving backward.

recurrence_initial__compatibility.title: Independence and compatibility of initial information
recurrence_initial__compatibility.summary: Additional conditions may be redundant, contradictory, or determine free parameters; counting written conditions alone is insufficient.
recurrence_initial__compatibility.definition: Independence means a condition does not follow automatically from the others and the recurrence. Compatibility means some sequence satisfies all conditions simultaneously. Substituting the general solution gives a linear system that distinguishes unique, multiple, and nonexistent solutions.
recurrence_initial__compatibility.explanation: Two values on the same parity subsequence may provide only one piece of information. An equality already forced by the recurrence removes no freedom, while data contradicting it immediately give no solution. Retain the original valid index range when checking conditions.
notation: For linear conditions, all parameters determined means a unique solution; remaining free parameters mean multiple solutions; a contradiction means no solution.
recurrence_initial__compatibility.example: The recurrence a_n=a_(n−2) makes even-index terms equal and odd-index terms equal. Giving a_0 and a_2 does not determine the odd-index terms.
common_mistakes: Assuming two conditions always determine a second-order recurrence.
Failing to check whether extra conditions contradict already determined terms.

graph_basic.title: Basic graph concepts
graph_basic.summary: Graphs represent objects and their relationships using vertices and edges; the handshake theorem relates undirected degree sums to edge counts.
graph_basic.definition: A finite undirected graph G=(V,E) consists of a finite vertex set V and an edge set E. A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges; each edge joins two distinct vertices. The degree deg(v) is the number of edge ends incident to v, with a loop counted twice, so Σdeg(v)=2|E|. Directed arcs have a tail and a head, contributing to outdegree and indegree respectively.
graph_basic.explanation: Specify the graph type before discussing edge counts and degrees. Each nonloop undirected edge contributes 1 at each endpoint; a loop contributes 2 at one vertex. Thus the handshake theorem also holds for finite undirected graphs with loops or parallel edges. In a simple n-vertex graph, each degree is at most n−1 and there are at most n(n−1)/2 edges. The number of odd-degree vertices is even. In a directed graph, total outdegree and total indegree both equal the number of arcs.
notation: G=(V,E); |V| is the vertex count and |E| the edge count.
deg(v) is undirected degree; d⁺(v),d⁻(v) are outdegree and indegree.
Σv∈V deg(v)=2|E|; Σd⁺(v)=Σd⁻(v)=|E|.
graph_basic.example: For the simple undirected graph V={a,b,c,d}, E={ab,ac,bc,cd}, the degrees are 2,2,3,1. Their sum 8 is twice the 4 edges. Here ab denotes the unordered endpoint pair {a,b}.
common_mistakes: Using a simple-graph maximum edge formula without specifying whether loops or parallel edges are allowed.
Counting a loop as only 1 toward undirected degree.
Adding indegrees and outdegrees and treating that sum as the number of arcs.

graph_basic__simple_graph.title: Simple graphs and complete graphs
graph_basic__simple_graph.summary: Simple graphs forbid loops and parallel edges; complete graphs contain every pair of distinct vertices.
graph_basic__simple_graph.definition: In an undirected simple graph, each edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices, with at most one edge per pair. The complete graph Kₙ joins every pair of distinct vertices.
graph_basic__simple_graph.explanation: A simple graph has maximum degree n−1 and at most n(n−1)/2 edges; the complete graph attains both bounds. A general simple graph may omit edges or have isolated vertices, and need not be connected.
notation: Kₙ has n(n−1)/2 edges and degree n−1 at each vertex.
E is a subfamily of the two-element subsets of V.
graph_basic__simple_graph.example: The complete graph on 4 vertices has 6 edges and degree 3 at every vertex. Removing any edge leaves a simple graph that is no longer complete.
common_mistakes: Assuming simple graphs must be connected.
Assuming every degree list with an even sum is realizable by a simple graph.

graph_basic__degree.title: Undirected degree and isolated vertices
graph_basic__degree.summary: Undirected degree counts incident edge ends; isolated vertices and leaves have degrees 0 and 1 respectively.
graph_basic__degree.definition: The undirected degree deg(v) counts edge ends incident to v. An ordinary edge contributes 1 at each endpoint, and a loop contributes 2 at its vertex. A degree-0 vertex is isolated; a degree-1 vertex is often called a leaf.
graph_basic__degree.explanation: Degree is a local statistic and does not directly determine whether the graph is connected or the vertex is a cut vertex. In a simple graph every distinct neighbor contributes exactly 1, so degree equals neighbor count. With loops or parallel edges these counts can differ.
notation: deg(v) is the degree and N(v) the neighbor set.
For an undirected simple graph, deg(v)=|N(v)|.
graph_basic__degree.example: If a and b have two parallel edges, a has just one distinct neighbor b but receives degree 2 from those edges.
common_mistakes: Using distinct-neighbor count as degree in a multigraph.
Removing an isolated vertex from the vertex set because it has no edges.

graph_basic__directed_degree.title: Indegree and outdegree in directed graphs
graph_basic__directed_degree.summary: Indegree counts incoming arcs and outdegree counts outgoing arcs; each total equals the number of arcs.
graph_basic__directed_degree.definition: In a directed graph, d⁻(v) counts arcs ending at v and d⁺(v) counts arcs starting at v. A directed loop contributes 1 to both at its vertex. Every finite directed graph satisfies Σd⁻(v)=Σd⁺(v)=|E|.
graph_basic__directed_degree.explanation: An arc is counted once in the outdegree of its tail and once in the indegree of its head. A vertex of outdegree 0 cannot leave along an arc; a vertex of indegree 0 cannot be entered from other vertices along arcs, apart from allowing a length-0 stay.
notation: d⁺ is outdegree and d⁻ is indegree.
graph_basic__directed_degree.example: With only a→b and b→c, the (indegree,outdegree) pairs are (0,1) for a, (1,1) for b, and (1,0) for c. Both degree totals are 2.
common_mistakes: Counting an arrowhead toward outdegree.
Assuming indegree equals outdegree at every vertex; only the whole-graph totals must agree.

graph_basic__undirected_graph.title: Undirected graphs and unordered endpoints
graph_basic__undirected_graph.summary: An undirected edge has no starting or ending direction; exchanging endpoints does not create a new edge.
graph_basic__undirected_graph.definition: An undirected graph expresses a symmetric relationship through unordered endpoints. In a simple graph uv and vu denote the same edge, the unordered set {u,v}, and the edge can be traversed in either direction.
graph_basic__undirected_graph.explanation: Mutual acquaintance and two-way roads can be modeled by undirected graphs. If only one direction is allowed or the two directions have different attributes, use a directed graph; written vertex order cannot implicitly supply a direction.
notation: uv=vu denotes one undirected edge, not two parallel edges.
In G=(V,E), V must include objects with no incident edges.
graph_basic__undirected_graph.example: If a and b know each other, record one undirected edge ab rather than counting ab and ba separately.
common_mistakes: Counting the two written orientations of an edge twice.
Using an undirected graph for one-way travel without explanation.

graph_basic__directed_graph.title: Directed graphs and arc directions
graph_basic__directed_graph.summary: Directed arcs are ordered relationships; a reverse arc, if present, is a separate arc.
graph_basic__directed_graph.definition: An arc u→v has tail u and head v and is usually recorded as (u,v). The arcs u→v and v→u differ; only one may exist. In a loopless simple directed graph, every ordered pair of distinct vertices has at most one arc.
graph_basic__directed_graph.explanation: Direction determines allowable traversal, indegree and outdegree, and strong connectivity. Models of one-way roads or precedence dependencies must follow arrows; connectivity of the underlying undirected graph does not imply reachability in every direction.
notation: u→v and v→u are different.
A loopless simple directed graph on n vertices has at most n(n−1) arcs.
graph_basic__directed_graph.example: With only a→b, a reaches b but b cannot reach a. Adding b→a adds a new arc.
common_mistakes: Traversing an arc backward without justification.
Incorrectly dividing the maximum arc count of a simple directed graph by 2.

graph_basic__parallel_edges.title: Parallel edges and multigraphs
graph_basic__parallel_edges.summary: Parallel edges share endpoints but have distinct identities; retain each separately in counting and traversal.
graph_basic__parallel_edges.definition: Different edges joining the same endpoint pair are parallel edges. An undirected graph allowing them may be called a multigraph. Whether loops are allowed needs a separate convention: multiplicity and loops are independent features.
graph_basic__parallel_edges.explanation: Each parallel edge contributes separately to edge count and degrees and must be used separately in an Euler traversal. Storing edges only as a set of endpoint pairs incorrectly merges parallel edges.
notation: e₁≠e₂ may have the same two endpoints.
Each nonloop parallel edge adds 1 to the degree of each endpoint.
graph_basic__parallel_edges.example: Three parallel edges between a and b give 3 edges and degree 3 at each vertex, despite there being only one distinct endpoint pair.
common_mistakes: Counting parallel edges only once because they have the same endpoints.
Confusing parallel edges with opposite directed arcs.

graph_basic__loops.title: Loops and degree counting
graph_basic__loops.summary: A loop has both ends at one vertex; it counts 2 toward undirected degree, or 1 each toward directed indegree and outdegree.
graph_basic__loops.definition: A loop is an edge whose endpoints coincide, or a directed arc whose tail equals its head. An undirected loop contributes 2 to its vertex degree; a directed loop contributes 1 each to indegree and outdegree. Simple graphs do not allow loops.
graph_basic__loops.explanation: A loop still counts as only one edge. Undirected degree counts edge ends rather than edge objects, which explains its contribution of 2. Textbooks may use different adjacency-matrix conventions for loops, so state the convention before use.
notation: Undirected loop: add 1 edge and 2 to degree.
Directed loop: add 1 arc and 1 each to indegree and outdegree.
graph_basic__loops.example: With only vertex a and one undirected loop, |E|=1 and deg(a)=2, consistent with the handshake theorem.
common_mistakes: Counting a loop as two edges.
Giving a loop only 1 toward undirected degree.

graph_basic__handshake.title: The handshake theorem and parity of odd-degree vertices
graph_basic__handshake.summary: Each edge contributes two edge ends, so the total degree sum is even.
graph_basic__handshake.definition: Every finite undirected graph satisfies Σv deg(v)=2|E|, allowing parallel edges and loops with each loop counted twice in degree. Consequently, the number of odd-degree vertices is even.
graph_basic__handshake.explanation: Double-count the two endpoints of every edge. An even number of odd-degree vertices and an even degree sum are necessary constraints, but do not guarantee that an arbitrary list is realizable as a simple graph.
notation: |E|=½Σv deg(v).
An odd number of odd integers has odd sum, so the number of odd-degree vertices cannot be odd.
graph_basic__handshake.example: A degree sum of 18 gives 9 edges. Exactly three odd-degree vertices are impossible regardless of the other degrees.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to divide the degree sum by 2.
Treating the necessary handshake condition as sufficient for realizability of a degree list.

graph_isomorphism.title: Graph isomorphism
graph_isomorphism.summary: Isomorphic graphs differ only in vertex names or drawings and have exactly the same adjacency structure.
graph_isomorphism.definition: Two undirected simple graphs G=(V,E) and H=(W,F) are isomorphic if there is a bijection f:V→W such that for all distinct vertices u,v, uv∈E if and only if f(u)f(v)∈F. The map f is an isomorphism. For directed graphs it must also preserve arc directions; weighted isomorphisms additionally require equal corresponding edge weights.
graph_isomorphism.explanation: Verify both a bijection on vertices and correspondence of edges and nonedges. Vertex count, edge count, degree multiset, number of components, and cycle lengths are isomorphism invariants that can rule out isomorphism; agreement of these invariants usually does not prove it. An automorphism is an isomorphism from a graph to itself, describing structural symmetry regardless of visual symmetry in a drawing.
notation: G≅H means G and H are isomorphic.
f(uv)=f(u)f(v) denotes the edge correspondence.
Aut(G) is the set of all automorphisms of G.
graph_isomorphism.example: The paths a—b—c—d and 1—3—4—2 are isomorphic via f(a)=1,f(b)=3,f(c)=4,f(d)=2. Their positions on the page do not affect this conclusion.
common_mistakes: Assuming equal vertex and edge counts suffice for isomorphism.
Checking only some edges without verifying the bijection and remaining adjacencies.
Using segment lengths, crossing positions, or vertex names to judge abstract graph isomorphism.

graph_isomorphism__mapping.title: Adjacency preservation and isomorphism maps
graph_isomorphism__mapping.summary: An isomorphism is a bijection on vertices that preserves adjacency in both directions.
graph_isomorphism__mapping.definition: An isomorphism between undirected simple graphs is a vertex bijection f such that uv is an edge of the source exactly when f(u)f(v) is an edge of the target. This equivalence preserves both edges and nonedges.
graph_isomorphism__mapping.explanation: First check that no vertex is omitted or repeated, then check each edge. For finite graphs with equal edge counts, a vertex bijection mapping every source edge to an edge automatically covers all target edges. These hypotheses cannot generally be omitted.
notation: G≅H; f:V(G)→V(H) is a bijection.
A composition of isomorphisms is an isomorphism; the inverse of an isomorphism is also an isomorphism.
graph_isomorphism__mapping.example: Map a—b—c to 2—1—3 by f(a)=2,f(b)=1,f(c)=3: endpoints map to endpoints and the middle vertex to the middle.
common_mistakes: Giving a many-to-one map without checking bijectivity.
Claiming all adjacencies are preserved after checking only a few edges.

graph_isomorphism__invariants.title: Isomorphism invariants and detecting nonisomorphism
graph_isomorphism__invariants.summary: Invariants can quickly rule out isomorphism, but graphs may still be nonisomorphic after passing several invariant checks.
graph_isomorphism__invariants.definition: An isomorphism invariant is a graph property or value preserved by isomorphisms, such as vertex count, edge count, degree multiset, component count, and triangle count. Any differing invariant proves two graphs nonisomorphic.
graph_isomorphism__invariants.explanation: Isomorphisms map paths, cycles, and neighborhoods to corresponding structures, preserving their counts. The converse fails: equal degree lists and equal connectivity may coexist with different triangles or other structures.
notation: The degree multiset records the multiplicity of each degree independently of vertex names.
The triangle count counts unordered triples of pairwise adjacent vertices.
graph_isomorphism__invariants.example: K₃,₃ and the triangular prism graph are both connected, have 6 vertices, and have degree 3 at every vertex. The former has no triangles and the latter has two, so they are nonisomorphic.
common_mistakes: Treating matching invariants as a proof of isomorphism.
Using the number of drawn edge crossings as an invariant of an abstract graph.

graph_isomorphism__automorphism.title: Automorphisms and structural symmetry
graph_isomorphism__automorphism.summary: Automorphisms are vertex permutations preserving graph structure and describe abstract symmetry.
graph_isomorphism__automorphism.definition: An automorphism of G is an isomorphism from G to itself. All automorphisms include the identity and can be counted as vertex permutations. They must preserve degree, adjacency, and each vertex’s structural role.
graph_isomorphism__automorphism.explanation: Use invariants such as unique degrees to fix special vertices, then determine whether the others can be interchanged freely. An asymmetric drawing does not remove automorphisms; visually similar vertices need not be interchangeable.
notation: Aut(G) is the automorphism set; |Aut(G)| is its size.
The identity is always an automorphism.
graph_isomorphism__automorphism.example: A path with 5 vertices has only two automorphisms: identity and reversal. It cannot move an internal degree-2 vertex to an endpoint.
common_mistakes: Counting every vertex permutation as an automorphism.
Assuming vertices with equal degrees may be freely permuted.

graph_adjacency.title: Adjacency matrices
graph_adjacency.summary: An adjacency matrix records adjacency in a fixed vertex order, and its powers count walks of a specified length.
graph_adjacency.definition: For an undirected simple graph ordered v₁,…,vₙ, the adjacency matrix A has aᵢⱼ=1 when vᵢ,vⱼ are adjacent and 0 otherwise. It is symmetric with zero diagonal. For a loopless simple directed graph, take aᵢⱼ=1 when vᵢ→vⱼ exists; row sums are outdegrees and column sums are indegrees.
graph_adjacency.explanation: The matrix depends on vertex order; reordering vertices reorders rows and columns together. In an undirected simple graph, a row sum is the corresponding degree and the total sum is twice the edge count. Under ordinary integer matrix multiplication, (Aᵏ)ᵢⱼ counts length-k walks from vᵢ to vⱼ. Walks allow repeated vertices and edges and cannot always be interpreted as simple paths. If parallel edges or loops are allowed, separately state the matrix-counting convention.
notation: A=(aᵢⱼ) is the adjacency matrix; first fix vertex order.
(Aᵏ)ᵢⱼ counts length-k walks, k≥1.
Undirected simple graph: aᵢⱼ=aⱼᵢ, aᵢᵢ=0, Σⱼaᵢⱼ=deg(vᵢ).
graph_adjacency.example: For a—b—c ordered (a,b,c), A=[[0,1,0],[1,0,1],[0,1,0]]. (A²)ₐ𝚌=1 represents the unique two-step walk a—b—c.
common_mistakes: Writing a matrix without specifying vertex order, leaving row and column meanings unclear.
Interchanging directed row-sum and column-sum degrees.
Mistaking walks counted by Aᵏ for simple paths with no repeated vertices.

graph_adjacency__construction.title: Constructing and validating adjacency matrices
graph_adjacency__construction.summary: Each matrix entry represents a fixed vertex pair; an undirected simple graph requires symmetry and no diagonal ones.
graph_adjacency__construction.definition: In order v₁,…,vₙ, entry (i,j) is 1 if vᵢ,vⱼ are adjacent and 0 otherwise. Adjacency matrices of undirected simple graphs are exactly symmetric 0/1 square matrices with zero diagonal.
graph_adjacency__construction.explanation: Symmetry corresponds to undirected edges, the zero diagonal to no loops, and 0/1 entries to at most one edge per endpoint pair. An isolated vertex gives an all-zero row and column.
notation: A=Aᵀ, aᵢᵢ=0, aᵢⱼ∈{0,1}.
Fix vertex order before constructing the matrix.
graph_adjacency__construction.example: [[0,1],[1,0]] represents one edge between two vertices; [[0,1],[0,0]] cannot represent an undirected graph in the same vertex order.
common_mistakes: Filling an undirected edge in only one triangular half.
Checking symmetry but overlooking loops or entries other than 0 and 1.

graph_adjacency__degree_sums.title: Row sums, column sums, and degrees
graph_adjacency__degree_sums.summary: Adjacency matrices turn local degree calculations into row and column sums.
graph_adjacency__degree_sums.definition: For an undirected simple graph, row i sums to deg(vᵢ) and all entries sum to 2|E|. For a loopless simple directed graph with rows as tails and columns as heads, row i sums to outdegree and column i to indegree.
graph_adjacency__degree_sums.explanation: State the direction convention first. In a directed matrix, the sum of all entries directly equals the arc count, without division by 2. Each undirected edge occupies two symmetric positions.
notation: Undirected: deg(vᵢ)=Σⱼaᵢⱼ.
Directed: d⁺(vᵢ)=Σⱼaᵢⱼ, d⁻(vᵢ)=Σⱼaⱼᵢ.
graph_adjacency__degree_sums.example: The directed matrix [[0,1],[0,0]] has only v₁→v₂. Vertex v₁ has outdegree 1 and indegree 0; the total matrix sum is 1.
common_mistakes: Dividing the total sum of a directed matrix by 2.
Assuming all adjacency matrices are symmetric.

graph_adjacency__walk_powers.title: Adjacency matrix powers and fixed-length walks
graph_adjacency__walk_powers.summary: Integer matrix powers count walks, allowing repeated vertices and edges.
graph_adjacency__walk_powers.definition: Let A be a graph’s 0/1 adjacency matrix, with ordinary integer addition and multiplication. For k≥1, (Aᵏ)ᵢⱼ counts walks from vᵢ to vⱼ traversing exactly k edges. A⁰=I corresponds to length-0 stays.
graph_adjacency__walk_powers.explanation: Multiplication classifies by the penultimate vertex, adjoining a final edge to a length-k walk; this also gives an induction proof. Boolean multiplication records only existence, while ordinary integer multiplication retains counts.
notation: (Aᵏ⁺¹)ᵢⱼ=Σℓ(Aᵏ)ᵢℓaℓⱼ.
tr(Aᵏ) counts length-k closed walks with a specified starting point.
graph_adjacency__walk_powers.example: If the only edge is a—b, then A²=I, representing a—b—a and b—a—b. Both are valid walks but not paths with distinct vertices.
common_mistakes: Interpreting matrix powers as simple-path counts.
Treating a closed-walk total as the number of cycles without regard to starting point or direction.

graph_adjacency__vertex_order.title: Vertex reordering and adjacency-matrix permutations
graph_adjacency__vertex_order.summary: Reordering vertices must reorder rows and columns together; a changed numerical arrangement need not mean changed graph structure.
graph_adjacency__vertex_order.definition: If A uses order v₁,…,vₙ and A′ uses vₚ₁,…,vₚₙ, then A′ᵢⱼ=Aₚᵢₚⱼ. This simultaneously applies the same vertex permutation to rows and columns.
graph_adjacency__vertex_order.explanation: A row and column jointly belong to one vertex. Permuting rows alone makes row and column orders inconsistent. Isomorphism of undirected simple graphs can be expressed as equality of adjacency matrices after a vertex reordering.
notation: A′ᵢⱼ=Aₚᵢₚⱼ.
Two graphs are isomorphic exactly when simultaneous row and column reordering by one vertex permutation makes their adjacency matrices agree.
graph_adjacency__vertex_order.example: Reordering a—b—c as (b,a,c) moves the degree-2 middle vertex’s row and column to the first position.
common_mistakes: Swapping rows without swapping columns.
Declaring graphs nonisomorphic because their matrices differ entry by entry.

graph_matrix.title: Matrix representations of graphs
graph_matrix.summary: Adjacency, incidence, and Laplacian matrices encode different aspects of a graph; distinguish their row and column objects and sign conventions.
graph_matrix.definition: Fix vertex and edge orders for an undirected simple graph. The unsigned incidence matrix M has vertices as rows and edges as columns, with entry 1 when the vertex is an endpoint, otherwise 0. After arbitrarily orienting every edge, the oriented incidence matrix B records −1 at the tail and +1 at the head. With adjacency matrix A and degree diagonal matrix D, the Laplacian is L=D−A and BBᵀ=L.
graph_matrix.explanation: Every column of M has two ones, and row sums give degrees. Every column of B has one −1 and one +1 and sums to 0. Reversing an edge’s chosen orientation negates that column without changing BBᵀ. For a loopless directed graph, Boolean unions of powers of A give reachability matrices; specify whether length-0 walks count. Reflexive reachability has ones on the diagonal. Matrix representations convert combinatorial properties into computable algebraic relations.
notation: M is the unsigned vertex–edge incidence matrix; B uses tail −1 and head +1.
D=diag(deg(v₁),…,deg(vₙ)); L=D−A=BBᵀ.
xᵀLx=Σuv∈E(xᵤ−xᵥ)² for undirected simple graphs.
graph_matrix.example: For a single edge a—b oriented a→b, B=[[-1],[1]], so BBᵀ=[[1,-1],[-1,1]], also the degree matrix I minus adjacency matrix [[0,1],[1,0]].
common_mistakes: Confusing vertex–edge incidence matrices with vertex–vertex adjacency matrices.
Mixing unsigned M with signed B and incorrectly writing MMᵀ=D−A.
Claiming reachability diagonals must all be 0 or all be 1 without stating whether length 0 is allowed.

graph_matrix__unsigned_incidence.title: Unsigned vertex–edge incidence matrices
graph_matrix__unsigned_incidence.summary: An unsigned incidence matrix records endpoint membership, with two ones per simple undirected edge.
graph_matrix__unsigned_incidence.definition: Fix vertex and edge orders for an undirected simple graph. In M, rows represent vertices and columns edges; an entry is 1 if the vertex is an endpoint, otherwise 0. With n vertices and m edges, M is n×m.
graph_matrix__unsigned_incidence.explanation: Every column has exactly two ones and row sums equal degrees. MMᵀ has degrees on its diagonal and common incident-edge counts off diagonal, so MMᵀ=D+A for simple graphs.
notation: M is an n×m 0/1 matrix.
For an undirected simple graph, MMᵀ=D+A.
graph_matrix__unsigned_incidence.example: For a—b—c with edges ordered ab,bc, M=[[1,0],[1,1],[0,1]].
common_mistakes: Treating the product for unsigned M as D−A.
Reversing the row and column roles of vertices and edges without stating it.

graph_matrix__laplacian.title: Laplacian matrices and edge energy
graph_matrix__laplacian.summary: The Laplacian combines adjacency and degrees, using squared differences to reflect connectivity.
graph_matrix__laplacian.definition: For an undirected simple graph, L=D−A, where D is the degree diagonal matrix. If B uses tail −1 and head +1 in every column, then L=BBᵀ.
graph_matrix__laplacian.explanation: The diagonal of L records degrees, adjacent off-diagonal positions are −1, other entries are 0, and each row sums to 0. The quadratic form xᵀLx sums squared endpoint-value differences over edges. In a connected graph it vanishes exactly when all vertex values are equal.
notation: L=D−A=BBᵀ.
xᵀLx=Σuv∈E(xᵤ−xᵥ)².
graph_matrix__laplacian.example: For a—b—c, L=[[1,-1,0],[-1,2,-1],[0,-1,1]], with diagonal entry 2 at the middle vertex.
common_mistakes: Writing +1 in adjacent off-diagonal entries of L.
Mistaking the unsigned incidence-matrix product for D−A as well.

graph_matrix__reachability.title: Reachability matrices and Boolean operations
graph_matrix__reachability.summary: Reachability matrices record only whether a path exists; Boolean addition and multiplication reduce counts to truth values.
graph_matrix__reachability.definition: For a directed graph, the reachability matrix R has rᵢⱼ=1 if a walk of length at least 1 exists from vᵢ to vⱼ. Allowing length 0 gives the reflexive reachability matrix R*=I∨R. Boolean matrix multiplication replaces addition by OR and multiplication by AND.
graph_matrix__reachability.explanation: Ordinary Aᵏ counts walks; Boolean Aᵏ only tests existence of a length-k walk. In a finite graph, reflexive reachability is the Boolean union of I,A,…,Aⁿ⁻¹. Diagonal entries of nonreflexive R additionally require considering nonempty closed walks.
notation: (A⊙B)ᵢⱼ=∨k(aᵢk∧bkⱼ).
R*=I∨A∨A²∨…∨Aⁿ⁻¹, with Boolean powers and unions.
graph_matrix__reachability.example: In the directed diamond s→a,s→b,a→t,b→t, ordinary (A²)ₛₜ=2, while the same entry in the Boolean square is 1.
common_mistakes: Writing the count 2 into a reachability matrix restricted to 0/1.
Unconditionally omitting or imposing reflexive diagonal entries.

graph_matrix__signed_incidence.title: Oriented incidence matrices and sign conventions
graph_matrix__signed_incidence.summary: After orienting edges, each incidence column has one negative and one positive entry and sums to 0.
graph_matrix__signed_incidence.definition: For a finite loopless directed graph with n≥1 vertices, fix vertex and arc orders. Its oriented incidence matrix B records −1 at the tail and +1 at the head of each arc, with zeros elsewhere. An undirected simple graph may also be arbitrarily oriented to construct B; this algebraic representation does not change its undirected traversal rules.
graph_matrix__signed_incidence.explanation: Reversing an arc or a chosen edge orientation negates its column, leaving BBᵀ unchanged. Since each column sums to 0, all row vectors sum to zero, and rank is at most n−1 for n≥1. The equality BBᵀ=D−A uses B obtained by orienting an undirected simple graph and D,A from that original undirected graph. Its D,A cannot be replaced directly by a directed outdegree matrix and directed adjacency matrix.
notation: For a loopless graph, each column has exactly one −1 and one +1, and 1ᵀB=0.
For B from an arbitrary orientation of an undirected simple graph, BBᵀ=D−A, where D,A both come from that original undirected graph.
graph_matrix__signed_incidence.example: The column for a→b is [-1,1]ᵀ; reversing it gives [1,-1]ᵀ.
common_mistakes: Mixing the tail −1, head +1 convention with another convention.
Interpreting an artificial orientation as making an originally undirected edge one-way.

graph_connectivity.title: Paths and connectivity
graph_connectivity.summary: Paths express reachability; connected components divide an undirected graph into maximal internally reachable parts with no reachability between them.
graph_connectivity.definition: A walk is a sequence of adjacent vertices joined successively by edges, with length equal to edges traversed. Here a path specifically means a simple path, with no repeated vertices. An undirected graph is connected if every two vertices have a path between them. A connected component is a maximal connected subgraph, including an isolated vertex by itself. A directed graph is strongly connected if every pair is mutually reachable, and weakly connected if ignoring directions gives a connected graph.
graph_connectivity.explanation: “Maximal” means it cannot be extended by adding other vertices of the graph while staying in the same connected part, rather than having the largest vertex count. Undirected reachability uniquely partitions vertices into components. Breadth-first search visits layers and finds minimum edge-count distances from a source in an unweighted graph. Depth-first search also finds components, but its first path need not be shortest. Strong connectivity must respect arc directions; weak connectivity alone guarantees neither one-way nor mutual reachability.
notation: u⇝v means a directed path from u to v, or reachability in an undirected context.
c(G) is the number of connected components of an undirected graph.
d(u,v) is the minimum path edge count in an unweighted graph; use ∞ if unreachable.
graph_connectivity.example: The graph with vertices {a,b,c,d,e,f} and edges {ab,bc,de} has three components with vertex sets {a,b,c},{d,e},{f}. Although a and c are not adjacent, b connects them.
common_mistakes: Confusing nonadjacency with unreachability.
Omitting isolated vertices or calling every connected subgraph a component.
Ignoring directed arcs and mistaking weak for strong connectivity.

graph_connectivity__simple_paths.title: Simple paths and reachability
graph_connectivity__simple_paths.summary: Simple paths have no repeated vertices; deleting repeated portions turns any reaching walk into a simple path.
graph_connectivity__simple_paths.definition: A path here means a simple path: consecutive vertices are joined by edges and all vertices are distinct; its length counts edges. A directed simple path must also follow every arc direction.
graph_connectivity__simple_paths.explanation: If a walk repeats a vertex, remove the closed segment between two occurrences without changing its endpoints. Repeated deletion produces a simple path. Thus reachability does not require repeated traversal, though counting and negative-weight optimization require separate distinctions.
notation: A simple path with r edges has r+1 distinct vertices.
u⇝v denotes a path from u to v.
graph_connectivity__simple_paths.example: a—b—c—d is a simple path of length 3; a—b—a—c is not, since a repeats.
common_mistakes: Counting vertices instead of edges as path length.
Ignoring that directed paths must follow arrows.

graph_connectivity__components.title: Undirected reachability and connected components
graph_connectivity__components.summary: Undirected reachability uniquely partitions vertices into maximal connected parts.
graph_connectivity__components.definition: Vertices u,v of an undirected graph are reachable if a path connects them. Reachability is an equivalence relation; each equivalence class with all its internal edges forms a connected component. An isolated vertex is a component by itself.
graph_connectivity__components.explanation: There are no edges between different components, since such an edge would make them mutually reachable. Adding an edge between two components merges them and reduces the component count by 1. Adding an edge within one component does not change the count.
notation: c(G) is the number of connected components.
A component is a maximal connected subgraph; it need not be a largest component.
graph_connectivity__components.example: Edges {ab,cd} and isolated vertex e give 3 components. Adding bc leaves 2 components, with e still separate.
common_mistakes: Counting only parts containing edges as components.
Assuming one edge connecting two components connects all components.

graph_connectivity__strong_components.title: Strong connectivity and strongly connected components
graph_connectivity__strong_components.summary: Strong connectivity requires mutual reachability; strong components are maximal mutually reachable parts.
graph_connectivity__strong_components.definition: A directed graph is strongly connected if every pair u,v has directed paths both from u to v and from v to u. A strongly connected component is a maximal strongly connected subgraph. One vertex may form a strong component.
graph_connectivity__strong_components.explanation: An arc going only from one side to another cannot merge those sides into a single strong component. Mutual reachability partitions vertices into disjoint strong components; degrees or drawing distances do not determine this grouping.
notation: u,v share a strong component exactly when u⇝v and v⇝u.
Length 0 permits each vertex to reach itself.
graph_connectivity__strong_components.example: If a↔b and b→c, the strong components are {a,b} and {c}; c cannot return to a or b.
common_mistakes: Treating one-way reachability as sufficient for a common strong component.
Forgetting that a single vertex without a cycle can still be a strong component.

graph_connectivity__walks.title: Walks and repeated traversal
graph_connectivity__walks.summary: A walk requires an edge at every step and may repeat vertices and edges.
graph_connectivity__walks.definition: A walk is a finite alternating sequence of vertices and connecting edges, allowing repeated vertices and edges. It is closed if its starting and ending vertices coincide. A length-0 stay at one vertex may also be a walk.
graph_connectivity__walks.explanation: Adjacency-matrix powers count walks rather than only simple paths. Traversing an undirected edge and returning is legal, but both traversals use the same edge. In negative-weight problems, allowing repetition can determine whether a minimum cost exists.
notation: Length counts edge traversals, including repetitions.
A closed walk has equal endpoints and may repeat internally.
graph_connectivity__walks.example: With only edge ab, a—b—a is a closed walk of length 2 despite having only two distinct vertices and one distinct edge.
common_mistakes: Assuming walks must have distinct edges.
Excluding repeated traversals from the length count.

graph_connectivity__trails.title: Trails and the no-repeated-edge restriction
graph_connectivity__trails.summary: Trails do not repeat edges but may repeat vertices.
graph_connectivity__trails.definition: A trail is a walk with no repeated edges. A closed trail has equal endpoints and still uses each edge at most once. In a directed graph repetition is judged by arc identity; traversing an undirected edge backward repeats the same edge.
graph_connectivity__trails.explanation: Every simple path is a trail, but a trail need not be a simple path. An Euler trail covers all edges and may therefore revisit vertices where parts meet.
notation: Trail: all traversed edges are distinct.
Simple path ⇒ trail ⇒ walk; the reverse implications generally fail.
graph_connectivity__trails.example: For two triangles sharing vertex c, c—a—b—c—d—e—c is a closed trail: c repeats but no edge does.
common_mistakes: Rejecting a trail because a vertex repeats.
Failing to label parallel edges and mistaking two distinct ones for one repeated edge.

graph_connectivity__cycles.title: Simple cycles versus closed walks
graph_connectivity__cycles.summary: A simple cycle repeats no vertex except its common start and end, imposing stronger restrictions than a general closed walk.
graph_connectivity__cycles.definition: In an undirected simple graph, a simple cycle is a closed trail of length at least 3 whose vertices are distinct except for its endpoints. A directed simple cycle must follow arc directions and have distinct vertices apart from the endpoints. If loops or opposite arcs are allowed, specify minimum-length conventions separately.
graph_connectivity__cycles.explanation: Cycles supply alternative routes between vertices and underlie bridges, two-colorability, Hamiltonicity, and other concepts. A closed walk can traverse an edge back and forth or join several cycles, so it need not itself be a simple cycle.
notation: An undirected simple cycle Cₖ requires k≥3.
Repeating the initial vertex at the end only denotes closure.
graph_connectivity__cycles.example: The triangle a—b—c—a is a simple cycle. Although a—b—a is closed, it repeats one edge and is not a simple cycle in an undirected simple graph.
common_mistakes: Calling every closed walk a simple cycle.
Counting the repeated start at the end as an extra new vertex.

graph_connectivity__connected_graph.title: Connected graphs and maximal connected subgraphs
graph_connectivity__connected_graph.summary: Connectivity requires reachability between every two vertices, without requiring direct adjacency or unique paths.
graph_connectivity__connected_graph.definition: An undirected graph with at least one vertex is connected if a path joins every pair of vertices. A connected subgraph requires only internal reachability; a connected component must additionally admit no extension within the original graph to a larger connected part.
graph_connectivity__connected_graph.explanation: Connected does not mean complete: many pairs may connect through intermediate vertices. It does not mean a tree either, since cycles are allowed. A path connecting two vertices need not be shortest.
notation: A connected graph has c(G)=1.
Maximal means unable to be extended, rather than largest among all subgraphs.
graph_connectivity__connected_graph.example: The path a—b—c is connected although a,c are not adjacent. Edge ab alone is a connected subgraph, but is not a component of the entire graph.
common_mistakes: Equating connected with pairwise direct adjacency.
Treating every connected subgraph as a connected component.

graph_connectivity__weak_connectivity.title: Weak connectivity and the underlying undirected graph
graph_connectivity__weak_connectivity.summary: Weak connectivity checks connections after ignoring arrows and does not guarantee actual directed reachability.
graph_connectivity__weak_connectivity.definition: The underlying undirected graph of a directed graph is obtained by ignoring every arc direction. The directed graph is weakly connected if this underlying graph is connected; its undirected components correspond to weak components.
graph_connectivity__weak_connectivity.explanation: Strong connectivity implies weak connectivity, but generally not conversely. Weak connectivity identifies whether a structure is separated, but does not directly determine whether directed transport or dependency routes are feasible.
notation: Strongly connected ⇒ weakly connected.
Reversing every arc leaves the underlying undirected graph unchanged.
graph_connectivity__weak_connectivity.example: With only a→b,b→c, the underlying graph is a—b—c. It is weakly connected, but c cannot reach a.
common_mistakes: Treating a route found after ignoring directions as a legal directed route.
Assuming weak and strong connectivity differ only in wording.

graph_connectivity__condensation.title: Condensation of strongly connected components
graph_connectivity__condensation.summary: Contracting strong components to vertices separates internal cycles from one-way dependencies between components.
graph_connectivity__condensation.definition: The condensation of a directed graph has its strong components as vertices. An arc between two different components exists whenever the original graph has an arc from the first to the second. Internal arcs are omitted.
graph_connectivity__condensation.explanation: The condensation is a directed acyclic graph: a cycle between components would make their union mutually reachable, contradicting maximality. It can analyze precedence between strong components.
notation: Condensation vertices are strong components, not individual original vertices.
Internal loops of components are not retained.
common_mistakes: Using weak components as condensation vertices.
Retaining internal cycles and incorrectly claiming condensations may have cycles.

graph_cut.title: Cut vertices and bridges
graph_cut.summary: Cut vertices and bridges identify vertices and edges essential to connectivity.
graph_cut.definition: In a finite undirected graph G, a vertex v is a cut vertex if deleting v and all its incident edges increases the component count. An edge e is a cut edge or bridge if deleting e while retaining all vertices increases that count. In an undirected simple graph, an edge is a bridge exactly when it lies on no simple cycle.
graph_cut.explanation: Compare component counts before and after deletion; degrees alone do not decide. Internal vertices of paths are usually cut vertices, while cycle edges have alternative routes and are not bridges. Two cycles sharing one vertex may have a cut vertex with no bridge. For a connected graph on at least two vertices, edge connectivity λ(G) is the minimum number of edges whose deletion disconnects it, measuring resistance to edge failures beyond single bridges.
notation: G−v deletes v and its incident edges; G−e deletes only e.
Cut vertex: c(G−v)>c(G); bridge: c(G−e)>c(G).
λ(G) is the edge connectivity of a connected graph.
graph_cut.example: If triangles abc and def are joined only by cd, then cd is the unique bridge and c,d are cut vertices. Any triangle edge can be bypassed using its other two edges.
common_mistakes: Confusing deleting an edge with deleting its two endpoints.
Assuming a high-degree vertex must be a cut vertex, or no bridges means no cut vertices.
For a disconnected graph, asking only whether deletion leaves it disconnected rather than comparing component counts.

graph_cut__articulation.title: Cut vertices and vertex deletion
graph_cut__articulation.summary: Cut vertices are defined by an increase in component count after vertex deletion, not directly by degree.
graph_cut__articulation.definition: A vertex v is a cut vertex if deleting it and all incident edges increases the original component count. This also applies to disconnected graphs and affects only the original component containing v.
graph_cut__articulation.explanation: Removing a leaf does not break routes among the other vertices. Removing a vertex from a cycle leaves a path. A shared connection vertex of several cycles may be a cut vertex even if none of its incident edges is a bridge.
notation: v is a cut vertex exactly when c(G−v)>c(G).
Vertex deletion also deletes all incident edges.
graph_cut__articulation.example: The cut vertices of a—b—c—d are b,c; endpoints a,d are not cut vertices.
common_mistakes: Replacing increased component count with merely remaining disconnected.
Assuming every vertex of degree at least 2 is a cut vertex.

graph_cut__bridges.title: Bridges and alternative routes
graph_cut__bridges.summary: An edge is a bridge exactly when its endpoints have no alternative route after it is deleted.
graph_cut__bridges.definition: A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the component count of an undirected graph. In an undirected simple graph, uv is a bridge exactly when u,v are unreachable in G−uv, equivalently when uv lies on no simple cycle.
graph_cut__bridges.explanation: Deleting one cycle edge leaves its endpoints connected by the rest, so it is not a bridge. Every tree edge has no alternative route, so every tree edge is a bridge. The graph as a whole need not be connected to test for bridges.
notation: For a bridge e, c(G−e)=c(G)+1.
A bridge lies on no simple cycle.
graph_cut__bridges.example: In triangle abc with added edge cd, cd is a bridge and the three triangle edges are not.
common_mistakes: Equating no bridges with no cut vertices.
Assuming deletion of one bridge can split its original component into three or more parts.

graph_cut__edge_connectivity.title: Edge cuts and edge connectivity
graph_cut__edge_connectivity.summary: Edge connectivity measures the minimum number of edges that must fail to destroy connectivity.
graph_cut__edge_connectivity.definition: For a finite connected undirected graph on at least two vertices, an edge cut is a set of edges whose deletion disconnects the graph. The smallest size is its edge connectivity λ(G). A single bridge is an edge cut of size 1.
graph_cut__edge_connectivity.explanation: To prove λ(G)=k, show that k edges suffice and fewer than k cannot disconnect the graph. Deleting all edges incident to a vertex isolates it, so λ(G) is at most minimum degree, though this upper bound need not be attained.
notation: λ(G)=min{|F|:G−F is disconnected}.
A connected graph has a bridge exactly when λ(G)=1.
graph_cut__edge_connectivity.example: Deleting any one triangle edge leaves it connected; deleting the two edges at one vertex disconnects it. Thus λ(K₃)=2.
common_mistakes: Claiming λ=k from one k-edge cut without proving a lower bound.
Confusing edge connectivity, which deletes edges, with vertex connectivity, which deletes vertices.

graph_weighted.title: Weighted graphs
graph_weighted.summary: Weighted graphs attach numbers to edges to represent cost, length, and other quantities; path comparison requires adding edge weights.
graph_weighted.definition: A weighted graph consists of G=(V,E) with a weight function w:E→ℝ. Weights may represent length, time, cost, or another specified quantity. The weight w(P) of a path or walk sums the weights of traversed edges, counting repetitions. State explicitly whether negative weights, directions, or repeated traversal are allowed.
graph_weighted.explanation: A path with the fewest edges need not have minimum total weight. A zero-weight edge is still present and must be distinguished from a missing edge. Cost matrices usually use ∞ for missing edges and 0 for the cost of an empty walk at a vertex. Being weighted implies neither nonnegative weights nor the triangle inequality. With repeated traversal, negative closed walks may make cost unbounded below, so algorithmic assumptions matter.
notation: w(e) is the weight of e; w(P)=Σe along P w(e), counting each traversal.
A missing direct edge is usually ∞ in a cost matrix; an empty-walk diagonal cost is 0.
In an undirected weighted graph, both directions use the same edge and weight.
graph_weighted.example: If st has weight 9 and s—a—b—t has three edges of weight 2, the direct edge uses fewer edges but the three-edge path has lower cost, 6.
common_mistakes: Confusing fewest edges with minimum total weight.
Using 0 for both missing edges and valid zero-weight edges.
Applying any shortest-path algorithm without checking negative weights or directions.

graph_weighted__path_cost.title: Edge weights, path costs, and optimization objectives
graph_weighted__path_cost.summary: Path cost is the sum of edge weights; edge count, cost, and bottleneck objectives differ.
graph_weighted__path_cost.definition: A weight function w:E→ℝ assigns a number to every edge. Total walk cost sums edge weights with multiplicity. A minimum edge-count path is a minimum-cost path when every edge has weight 1.
graph_weighted__path_cost.explanation: Costs may represent time, distance, or price, and different meanings of weights may give different optimal routes on the same graph. If a problem instead minimizes the maximum edge weight as a bottleneck objective, optimize that quantity rather than the sum.
notation: w(P)=Σ along P w(e).
Name edge-count length and weighted cost separately.
graph_weighted__path_cost.example: A route with weights 1 and 8 costs 9; a route with three edges of weight 2 costs 6. The latter has more edges but is cheaper.
common_mistakes: Ignoring weights and counting only steps.
Calling a route best without specifying the objective.

graph_weighted__cost_matrix.title: Cost matrices and zero-weight edges
graph_weighted__cost_matrix.summary: A cost matrix must distinguish actual zero-cost edges from missing direct edges.
graph_weighted__cost_matrix.definition: Fix a vertex order. In a cost matrix C, cᵢⱼ is the weight of the direct edge from vᵢ to vⱼ; use ∞ when no direct edge exists and usually 0 on the diagonal for an empty walk. C is symmetric for undirected graphs but generally not for directed graphs.
graph_weighted__cost_matrix.explanation: A cost matrix is not an all-pairs shortest-distance matrix: an indirect route must not fill a missing-edge entry. Special structures such as negative loops need separate diagonal conventions; this entry uses loopless models.
notation: cᵢⱼ=∞ means no direct edge, not necessarily that no route through intermediate vertices exists.
For undirected graphs, cᵢⱼ=cⱼᵢ.
graph_weighted__cost_matrix.example: With only a→b of weight 0 and b→c of weight 2, cₐ𝚌=∞ although the minimum total cost from a to c is 2.
common_mistakes: Replacing direct costs by shortest distances without explanation.
Forcing a directed cost matrix to be symmetric.

graph_weighted__negative_walks.title: Negative closed walks and repetition rules
graph_weighted__negative_walks.summary: Whether negative weights cause unbounded cost depends on repeatability and reachability from the source and to the target.
graph_weighted__negative_walks.definition: A closed walk has identical endpoints and is a negative-cost closed walk if its total weight is negative. If the source can reach it and the target remains reachable afterward, repeat it arbitrarily many times to make source-to-target cost unbounded below.
graph_weighted__negative_walks.explanation: One negative directed edge need not create a negative cycle. A directed acyclic graph has only finitely many simple paths even with negative edges. An undirected negative edge can be traversed back and forth to create a negative closed walk, but repetition is forbidden if only simple paths are allowed.
notation: If w(C)<0, k repetitions cost kw(C).
A negative closed walk affects s-to-t cost only if s can reach it and it can reach t.
graph_weighted__negative_walks.example: A directed edge a→b of weight −2, without any route back to a, does not by itself imply all costs are unbounded below.
common_mistakes: Assuming any negative edge guarantees a negative cycle.
Repeating a negative edge in a problem allowing only simple paths.

graph_weighted__optimization_objectives.title: Total cost, edge count, and bottleneck objectives
graph_weighted__optimization_objectives.summary: An optimal route must be defined relative to a specific numerical objective.
graph_weighted__optimization_objectives.definition: The total-cost objective minimizes the sum of edge weights; the fewest-edges objective minimizes edge count; the bottleneck objective minimizes the largest individual edge weight along the path. These are three different optimization problems.
graph_weighted__optimization_objectives.explanation: The objectives may select different routes. Giving weights does not automatically specify an objective; both model and answer should state the quantity optimized. Fewest edges and minimum total cost naturally agree when all edges have the same positive weight.
notation: Total cost Σw(e); edge count |E(P)|; bottleneck maxe along P w(e).
Routes can be compared as better only under the same objective.
graph_weighted__optimization_objectives.example: Weights 1,8 give total cost 9 and bottleneck 8; weights 4,4,4 give total cost 12 and bottleneck 4. The two objectives prefer opposite routes.
common_mistakes: Assuming more uniform weights mean lower total cost.
Replacing minimum maximum-edge weight with minimum total weight.

graph_euler.title: Eulerian graphs
graph_euler.summary: Euler traversals use each edge exactly once; their key conditions involve connectivity of the nonisolated part and vertex degrees.
graph_euler.definition: An Euler trail traverses every edge exactly once and may repeat vertices. If its endpoints coincide, it is an Euler circuit. A finite undirected graph with at least one edge has an Euler circuit exactly when all nonzero-degree vertices lie in one component and all degrees are even. It has an Euler trail with distinct endpoints exactly when the nonzero-degree part is connected and precisely two vertices have odd degree.
graph_euler.explanation: Many textbooks call a connected undirected graph with an Euler circuit Eulerian. When asking only whether all edges can be traversed, isolated vertices can be ignored. Every visit to an internal vertex consumes one entering and one leaving edge, pairing its degree contributions; an open trail’s endpoints are exceptions. Directed graphs must respect arc directions: strong connectivity of the nonzero-degree part and equality of indegree and outdegree at each vertex guarantee an Euler circuit. Euler problems cover edges, rather than requiring each vertex to appear once.
notation: Euler trail: every edge exactly once; Euler circuit: additionally equal endpoints.
An open undirected Euler trail starts and ends at the two odd-degree vertices.
A directed Euler circuit requires d⁺(v)=d⁻(v) at every vertex and the connectivity condition on the nonzero-degree part.
graph_euler.example: Add diagonal ac to a—b—c—d—a. Vertices a,c have degree 3 and the others degree 2. The sequence a—b—c—d—a—c uses all five edges once, giving an Euler trail from a to c, but no Euler circuit exists.
common_mistakes: Remembering each vertex once instead of each edge once.
Checking degree parity without checking that all edges lie in one traversable connected part.
Applying undirected degree criteria to directed graphs while ignoring indegrees, outdegrees, and directions.

graph_euler__undirected_circuit.title: The even-degree criterion for undirected Euler circuits
graph_euler__undirected_circuit.summary: An undirected Euler circuit requires all edges to be continuously accessible and edge ends to pair at each vertex.
graph_euler__undirected_circuit.definition: A finite undirected graph with at least one edge has an Euler circuit exactly when all nonzero-degree vertices lie in one connected component and all vertex degrees are even. An Euler circuit uses every edge once and returns to its start.
graph_euler__undirected_circuit.explanation: Isolated vertices have no edges to traverse and may be ignored in the existence test. Even degrees come from pairing each entry with an exit. Connectivity ensures no edges remain in an unreachable part.
notation: The nonzero-degree part is connected and ∀v, deg(v) is even.
A loop contributes degree 2 and therefore does not disrupt even parity.
graph_euler__undirected_circuit.example: A triangle plus an isolated vertex still has an Euler circuit covering all edges; two disjoint triangles do not.
common_mistakes: Checking only even degrees and overlooking connectivity of the part containing edges.
Rejecting every graph with an isolated vertex as having no closed traversal of all edges.

graph_euler__directed_balance.title: Directed Euler circuits and degree balance
graph_euler__directed_balance.summary: A directed Euler circuit must balance entries and exits at each vertex and access all arcs.
graph_euler__directed_balance.definition: A directed Euler circuit follows directions and uses every arc exactly once. If there is at least one arc, strong connectivity of the nonzero-degree part and d⁺(v)=d⁻(v) at every vertex are sufficient and necessary for its existence.
graph_euler__directed_balance.explanation: Equality of total indegree and total outdegree holds in every directed graph and is far from sufficient. Check each vertex and exclude arcs scattered among parts that cannot all be visited together.
notation: A directed Euler circuit requires ∀v, d⁺(v)=d⁻(v).
A directed Euler trail with distinct endpoints has indegree/outdegree imbalances of 1 at its two endpoints.
graph_euler__directed_balance.example: In a→b→c→a, every indegree and outdegree is 1, giving a directed Euler circuit. Two disjoint directed cycles are balanced at every vertex but cannot form one circuit.
common_mistakes: Using undirected parity in place of directed indegree/outdegree balance.
Checking only total degrees rather than each vertex.

graph_euler__construction.title: Constructing Euler traversals and tracking edge identities
graph_euler__construction.summary: Splicing closed trails or adding and removing an auxiliary edge constructs Euler traversals; parallel edges must be used by their own identities.
graph_euler__construction.definition: In a finite connected undirected graph with even degrees, start anywhere and follow unused edges to form a closed trail. If unused edges remain, start another closed trail at an existing trail vertex incident to an unused edge and splice it in, continuing until all edges are used. Parallel edges are distinct, and each loop is also used once.
graph_euler__construction.explanation: This is construction by splicing closed trails. With two odd-degree vertices, first add an auxiliary edge to make all degrees even, then cut the Euler circuit at that edge. An algorithm should record unique edge identifiers rather than just endpoint pairs.
notation: Distinguish used and unused edges by edge identifiers.
A loop contributes degree 2 but appears only once in an Euler traversal.
graph_euler__construction.example: Two parallel edges e₁,e₂ between a,b give the Euler circuit a—e₁—b—e₂—a; this does not repeat the same edge.
common_mistakes: Merging two parallel edges into one.
Interpreting a loop’s degree contribution of 2 as requiring two traversals.

graph_euler__open_trail.title: Open Euler trails and two odd-degree vertices
graph_euler__open_trail.summary: An all-edge traversal with distinct endpoints requires exactly two odd-degree endpoints.
graph_euler__open_trail.definition: A finite undirected graph with at least one edge has an open Euler trail exactly when the nonzero-degree part is connected and exactly two vertices have odd degree. Those two vertices must be its endpoints; every other vertex has even degree.
graph_euler__open_trail.explanation: Internal entries and exits pair, leaving one unpaired incidence at each endpoint. Add an auxiliary edge between the odd vertices to obtain an even-degree Euler circuit, then cut it open to construct a trail in the original graph.
