algebra_system__commutativity.explanation: A finite operation table is commutative exactly when it is symmetric about the main diagonal. On infinite sets, a general verification is usually needed. A group need not be commutative; a commutative group is called abelian.
notation: a*b=b*a.
A finite operation table is symmetric about the main diagonal.
algebra_system__commutativity.example: Since max(a,b)=max(b,a), maximum is commutative. Integer subtraction is not: 4−2≠2−4.
common_mistakes: Inferring commutativity from associativity.
Checking only a=b, which cannot reveal any difference on swapping inputs.

algebra_system__identity_elements.title: Left, right, and two-sided identities
algebra_system__identity_elements.summary: Distinguish left and right identities. A two-sided identity, if it exists, is unique.
algebra_system__identity_elements.definition: A left identity e satisfies e*a=a for every a; a right identity satisfies a*e=a. A two-sided identity must satisfy both. A two-sided identity is unique whenever it exists, while one-sided identities may be nonunique.
algebra_system__identity_elements.explanation: Uniqueness of a two-sided identity does not require associativity. One-sided identities can be nonunique: for a*b=a, every element is a right identity, but on a set with at least two elements there is no left identity.
notation: Left: e*a=a.
Right: a*e=a.
A two-sided identity must satisfy both equations.
algebra_system__identity_elements.example: On {0,1,2}, define a*b=a. Every b satisfies a*b=a, so all three elements are right identities. No fixed e can satisfy e*a=a for every a.
common_mistakes: Checking only one side of the identity property.
Treating multiple one-sided identities as a counterexample to uniqueness of a two-sided identity.

algebra_system__inverse_elements.title: Inverses relative to an identity
algebra_system__inverse_elements.summary: An inverse requires products in both orders to equal the specified identity.
algebra_system__inverse_elements.definition: Suppose * has a two-sided identity e. An element b is a two-sided inverse of a if a*b=b*a=e. If only one equality holds, call it a left or right inverse as appropriate; it cannot automatically be treated as two-sided.
algebra_system__inverse_elements.explanation: Inverses are relative to the same operation and identity. In an associative operation with identity, each two-sided inverse is unique. Noninvertible elements are allowed in a monoid, but prevent it from being a group.
notation: a*b=b*a=e.
a⁻¹ denotes a two-sided inverse whose existence has been established.
algebra_system__inverse_elements.example: For the integer operation a*b=a+b+2, the identity is −2 and the inverse of a is −a−4, rather than the ordinary additive inverse −a.
common_mistakes: Writing −a as the inverse without checking the operation.
Verifying one side and ignoring the other.

algebra_system__semigroups_monoids.title: Semigroups and monoids
algebra_system__semigroups_monoids.summary: An associative operation gives a semigroup; adding an identity gives a monoid, without requiring every element to be invertible.
algebra_system__semigroups_monoids.definition: A nonempty set with an associative binary operation is a semigroup. If it also has a two-sided identity, it is a monoid. If every element of the monoid has an inverse, it is a group.
algebra_system__semigroups_monoids.explanation: These structures add axioms successively. Compare them using the same set and operation. Positive integers under addition form a semigroup with no identity. Nonnegative integers under addition have identity 0 but no additive inverse for any nonzero element.
notation: Semigroup: closed and associative.
Monoid: a semigroup with a two-sided identity.
algebra_system__semigroups_monoids.example: The set {0,1} with min is a commutative monoid with identity 1. The element 0 has no inverse relative to 1, so it is not a group.
common_mistakes: Assuming a semigroup has an identity.
Assuming a monoid automatically has inverses for every element.

algebra_homomorphism.title: Homomorphisms and isomorphisms
algebra_homomorphism.summary: A homomorphism preserves operations; an isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism and expresses complete structural correspondence.
algebra_homomorphism.definition: For groups (G,*) and (H,∘), a map φ:G→H is a group homomorphism if φ(a*b)=φ(a)∘φ(b). A bijective homomorphism is an isomorphism. Its kernel is kerφ={g∈G:φ(g)=e_H}, and its image is imφ={φ(g):g∈G}. Group homomorphisms automatically preserve identities and inverses.
algebra_homomorphism.explanation: Proving an isomorphism requires well-definedness, operation preservation, injectivity, and surjectivity. Equal cardinality is only one necessary condition for finite groups to be isomorphic. Element orders and commutativity can disprove isomorphism. The kernel is a subgroup of G, and a homomorphism is injective exactly when its kernel contains only the identity.
notation: φ(a⁻¹)=φ(a)⁻¹.
kerφ≤G, imφ≤H.
G≅H means G and H are isomorphic.
algebra_homomorphism.example: The map φ:ℤ₆→ℤ₃, φ([x]₆)=[x]₃, is surjective with kernel {[0]₆,[3]₆}, so it is neither injective nor an isomorphism.
common_mistakes: Inferring isomorphism solely from equal group sizes.
Failing to prove well-definedness when using integer representatives.
Writing the kernel as identities in H instead of their preimage in the domain.

algebra_homomorphism__images.title: Images and surjectivity of group homomorphisms
algebra_homomorphism__images.summary: The image consists of the elements actually reached in the target group and is a subgroup.
algebra_homomorphism__images.definition: For a group homomorphism φ:G→H, imφ={φ(g):g∈G} is a subgroup of H. The map is surjective exactly when imφ=H. For finite group homomorphisms, every nonempty fiber has the same size as the kernel.
algebra_homomorphism__images.explanation: Image elements belong to the target group, while kernel elements belong to the domain. Compute the image by enumerating representatives or describing all possible outputs. For finite groups, counting fibers gives |G|=|kerφ|·|imφ|.
notation: imφ≤H.
For finite groups, |G|=|kerφ|·|imφ|.
algebra_homomorphism__images.example: On ℤ₈, the doubling homomorphism φ(x)=2x has image {0,2,4,6}, so it is not surjective onto ℤ₈.
common_mistakes: Calling the whole codomain H the image without checking it.
Comparing kernel and image elements without regard to which group they belong to.

algebra_homomorphism__isomorphism_invari.title: Group isomorphisms
algebra_homomorphism__isomorphism_invari.summary: An operation-preserving bijection makes two group structures correspond.
algebra_homomorphism__isomorphism_invari.definition: A bijective group homomorphism is a group isomorphism. Constructing one requires well-definedness, operation preservation, injectivity, and surjectivity.
algebra_homomorphism__isomorphism_invari.explanation: A bijection gives an element correspondence; operation preservation gives structural correspondence. The inverse of an isomorphism also preserves the operation, so structural properties translate both ways.
notation: G≅H.
ord(φ(g))=ord(g) when φ is an isomorphism.
algebra_homomorphism__isomorphism_invari.example: The map [x]↦2ˣ from ℤ₄ to the multiplicative unit group modulo 5 has successive images 1,2,4,3 and is an isomorphism.
common_mistakes: Deciding isomorphism solely by element count.
Replacing the isomorphism requirement with an arbitrary bijection.

algebra_homomorphism__kernels.title: Kernels and the trivial-kernel test
algebra_homomorphism__kernels.summary: The kernel contains all domain elements mapped to the target identity.
algebra_homomorphism__kernels.definition: For a group homomorphism φ:G→H, kerφ={g∈G:φ(g)=e_H}. It is a subgroup of the domain G. The map φ is injective if and only if kerφ contains only e_G.
algebra_homomorphism__kernels.explanation: The kernel describes what the map collapses. If φ(a)=φ(b), then ab⁻¹ is in the kernel; when the kernel consists only of the identity, this yields a=b. Kernel elements must be domain elements, not target elements.
notation: kerφ=φ⁻¹({e_H}).
φ injective ⇔ kerφ={e_G}.
algebra_homomorphism__kernels.example: Reduction φ:ℤ₆→ℤ₃ has kernel {0,3}, so it is not injective.
common_mistakes: Writing the kernel as the identity itself in the image.
Assuming surjectivity implies a trivial kernel.

algebra_homomorphism__operation_preserva.title: Operation preservation and well-defined group homomorphisms
algebra_homomorphism__operation_preserva.summary: A homomorphism must be a well-defined function, including on quotient structures, and preserve the operation.
algebra_homomorphism__operation_preserva.definition: A map φ:G→H is a group homomorphism if φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b) for all a,b. If its formula uses representatives of residue classes, also prove that different representatives give the same image class.
algebra_homomorphism__operation_preserva.explanation: First check that the map is well-defined, then that it preserves operations. Even a bijective formula is not a homomorphism or isomorphism if it fails to preserve the identity or operation.
notation: φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b).
In additive groups: φ(a+b)=φ(a)+φ(b).
algebra_homomorphism__operation_preserva.example: For the additive integers, g(x)=2x is a homomorphism, but f(x)=x+1 is not, since f(0)=1≠0.
common_mistakes: Calling a map a homomorphism merely because it exists.
Omitting independence from representative choice for residue-class maps.

algebra_homomorphism__structural_invaria.title: Isomorphism invariants and element orders
algebra_homomorphism__structural_invaria.summary: Invariants can disprove isomorphism without enumerating every bijection.
algebra_homomorphism__structural_invaria.definition: An isomorphism preserves element orders, group size, and commutativity. Any difference in one such property disproves isomorphism; agreement usually does not suffice to prove it.
algebra_homomorphism__structural_invaria.explanation: Necessary conditions cannot be reversed into sufficient ones. Comparing element-order distributions is particularly useful for small finite groups, but proving isomorphism still requires a construction or a complete structural argument.
notation: Isomorphisms preserve ord(g).
Different invariants ⇒ not isomorphic.
algebra_homomorphism__structural_invaria.example: ℤ₄ has an element of order 4, whereas every nonidentity element of ℤ₂×ℤ₂ has order 2. Although both have 4 elements, they are not isomorphic.
common_mistakes: Assuming matching invariants automatically imply isomorphism.
Comparing only set sizes and ignoring group structure.

algebra_group.title: Groups and subgroups
algebra_group.summary: A group has an associative operation, an identity, and inverses for all elements. A subgroup is a group under the inherited operation.
algebra_group.definition: A group (G,*) is a nonempty set with a binary operation satisfying associativity, a two-sided identity e, and a two-sided inverse a⁻¹ for every a∈G. A subset H⊆G is a subgroup if it is a group under the same operation. A nonempty H is a subgroup exactly when ab⁻¹∈H for all a,b∈H.
algebra_group.explanation: Groups need not be commutative; a commutative group is abelian. In a finite cyclic group, the order of an element is the smallest positive k with aᵏ=e. In additive notation, powers mean repeated addition, the identity is 0, and inverses are additive negatives. A subgroup must contain the original identity.
notation: H≤G means H is a subgroup of G.
⟨a⟩ is the cyclic subgroup generated by a.
The additive group ℤₙ uses addition modulo n.
algebra_group.example: In (ℤ₁₂,+), 4 has order 3 because 4+4+4≡0, while 4 and 8 are nonzero. It generates {0,4,8}.
common_mistakes: Inferring subgroup status from closure alone, omitting identity and inverses.
Assuming all groups are commutative.
Confusing an element’s order with its numerical value or the group’s size.

algebra_group__axioms_inverses.title: Inverse formulas and cancellation in groups
algebra_group__axioms_inverses.summary: Inverses allow common factors in group equations to be canceled on the correct side.
algebra_group__axioms_inverses.definition: A group has an associative operation, a two-sided identity, and two-sided inverses. These imply left and right cancellation, uniqueness of inverses, and (ab)⁻¹=b⁻¹a⁻¹. Commutativity is not required.
algebra_group__axioms_inverses.explanation: Cancel a common left factor by multiplying on the left by its inverse; cancel a common right factor on the right. The product-inverse formula reverses order because general groups do not commute; a⁻¹b⁻¹ cannot be used without further conditions.
notation: ab=ac ⇒ b=c.
ba=ca ⇒ b=c.
(ab)⁻¹=b⁻¹a⁻¹.
algebra_group__axioms_inverses.example: If every g in a group satisfies g²=e, every element is self-inverse. Hence ab=(ab)⁻¹=b⁻¹a⁻¹=ba.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the inverse on the wrong side during cancellation.
Assuming every group commutes.

algebra_group__cyclic_subgroups.title: Cyclic subgroups generated by an element
algebra_group__cyclic_subgroups.summary: All integer powers of one element form the smallest subgroup containing it.
algebra_group__cyclic_subgroups.definition: For a∈G, ⟨a⟩={aᵏ:k∈ℤ} is the cyclic subgroup generated by a. In additive notation it is the set of integer multiples {ka:k∈ℤ}. Every subgroup containing a must contain this set.
algebra_group__cyclic_subgroups.explanation: Positive, zero, and negative powers come from closure, the identity, and inverses respectively. For finite order, powers repeat periodically, and the generated subgroup size equals the element’s order.
notation: In additive groups, use ka instead of aᵏ.
algebra_group__cyclic_subgroups.example: In the additive group ℤ₁₂, ⟨4⟩={0,4,8}, the smallest subgroup that every subgroup containing 4 must include.
common_mistakes: Taking only positive powers and omitting the identity and inverses.
Assuming the generated subgroup always equals the entire group.

algebra_group__element_orders.title: Orders of group elements
algebra_group__element_orders.summary: An element’s order is the first positive repetition count that returns to the identity.
algebra_group__element_orders.definition: If some k>0 has aᵏ=e, the least such k is the order of a. If none exists, a has infinite order. The identity has order 1. Every element of a finite group has finite order.
algebra_group__element_orders.explanation: In an additive group, find the least positive k with ka=0. For a in ℤₙ this means n∣ka, so its order is n/gcd(n,a).
notation: ord(a)=min{k>0:aᵏ=e}.
In ℤₙ, ord(a)=n/gcd(n,a).
algebra_group__element_orders.example: The element 4 in ℤ₁₂ has order 3: 4 and 8 are nonzero, but 3·4≡0.
common_mistakes: Assigning order 0 to an element.
Confusing group order with element order.

algebra_group__generators.title: Cyclic groups and generators
algebra_group__generators.summary: A group generated by one element is cyclic, and that element is a generator.
algebra_group__generators.definition: If G=⟨a⟩ for some a∈G, G is cyclic and a is a generator. In a finite group, a generates the whole group exactly when its order equals the group’s size.
algebra_group__generators.explanation: In additive ℤₙ, generators are exactly the residue classes relatively prime to n. Not every nonidentity element of a cyclic group generates it; some generate only proper subgroups.
notation: Generators of ℤₙ satisfy gcd(a,n)=1.
algebra_group__generators.example: The generators of ℤ₁₀ are 1,3,7,9. The element 2 has order 5 and generates only the subgroup of even residue classes.
common_mistakes: Assuming any nonidentity element generates a cyclic group.
Declaring a group cyclic solely from its size.

algebra_group__group_axioms.title: Group axioms
algebra_group__group_axioms.summary: A group has an associative operation, an identity, and a two-sided inverse for every element.
algebra_group__group_axioms.definition: A nonempty set G with a binary operation is a group if the operation is associative, has a two-sided identity, and every element has a two-sided inverse. Commutativity is not a general group axiom; groups satisfying it are abelian.
algebra_group__group_axioms.explanation: For a specific system, first check closure on the underlying set. The same identity must work for every element, and every inverse must also belong to the underlying set.
notation: e is the identity shared by all elements.
algebra_group__group_axioms.example: The invertible residues {1,3,5,7} modulo 8 form a group under multiplication. All nonzero residues {1,…,7} do not even form a closed set under multiplication, since 2·4=0.
common_mistakes: Forgetting closure or that inverses must lie in the underlying set.
Listing commutativity as a required property of every group.

algebra_group__subgroups.title: The subgroup test and the inherited operation
algebra_group__subgroups.summary: A nonempty subset is a subgroup only if it retains the group structure under the original operation.
algebra_group__subgroups.definition: A nonempty subset H of a group G is a subgroup if and only if ab⁻¹∈H for every a,b∈H. Equivalently, H contains the identity and is closed under multiplication and inverses.
algebra_group__subgroups.explanation: Nonemptiness lets us choose a∈H and obtain the identity aa⁻¹. Multiplicative closure alone generally fails for infinite groups: the positive integers within additive ℤ omit 0 and negative integers.
notation: H≤G.
A common test is nonempty H with ab⁻¹∈H.
algebra_group__subgroups.example: The even residue classes {0,2,4,6} in additive ℤ₈ contain 0 and are closed under addition and additive inverses, so they are a subgroup.
common_mistakes: Omitting nonemptiness.
Proving the subset is a group with another operation and claiming it is a subgroup of the original group.

algebra_ring_field.title: Rings and fields
algebra_ring_field.summary: A ring combines addition and multiplication; a field requires multiplicative inverses for every nonzero element.
algebra_ring_field.definition: Here rings have a multiplicative identity 1 with 1≠0. Addition forms an abelian group, multiplication is associative, and both distributive laws hold. A general ring need not have commutative multiplication. A field is such a ring with commutative multiplication and every nonzero element invertible. An integral domain is a commutative ring with no nonzero zero divisors.
algebra_ring_field.explanation: For integers n≥2, the residue ring ℤₙ has multiplicative identity 1, and a is invertible exactly when gcd(a,n)=1. The ring ℤₙ is a field exactly when n is prime. Division in a ring is allowed only by a unit, using multiplication by its inverse. Every finite integral domain is a field; finiteness is essential.
notation: A unit is an invertible element a: some b satisfies ab=ba=1.
Nonzero a,b with ab=0 give nonzero zero divisors.
For prime p, ℤₚ is a finite field.
algebra_ring_field.example: In ℤ₆, 1 and 5 are invertible, but 2·3=0 with both factors nonzero, so ℤ₆ is not a field. In ℤ₇, 3⁻¹=5 since 3·5≡1(mod7).
common_mistakes: Assuming all nonzero elements are invertible in any ring.
Confusing “has a multiplicative identity” with “every element is a unit.”
Ignoring differing textbook conventions about whether rings must contain 1.

algebra_ring_field__finite_fields.title: Fields and finite fields
algebra_ring_field__finite_fields.summary: A field is a commutative ring in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
algebra_ring_field__finite_fields.definition: A field is a commutative ring with 1≠0 and every nonzero element invertible. It is finite if its underlying set is finite. For n>1, ℤₙ under usual modular addition and multiplication is a field exactly when n is prime.
algebra_ring_field__finite_fields.explanation: In a field, division by a nonzero element is defined and there are no nonzero zero divisors. A prime p gives the finite field ℤₚ. Finite integral domains are fields, but this does not imply every finite field has prime size; more general finite fields can have prime-power size.
notation: Finite integral domain ⇒ field.
For n>1, ℤₙ is a field ⇔ n is prime.
algebra_ring_field__finite_fields.example: ℤ₁₁ is a field. In ℤ₉, 3·3=0 with 3 nonzero, so it is not a field.
common_mistakes: Dropping finiteness and asserting every integral domain is a field.
Overlooking zero divisors in ℤₙ for composite n.

algebra_ring_field__integral_domains.title: Integral domains
algebra_ring_field__integral_domains.summary: An integral domain is a commutative ring with identity and no nonzero zero divisors.
algebra_ring_field__integral_domains.definition: Under the convention 1≠0, a ring is an integral domain if multiplication is commutative and there are no nonzero zero divisors. Nonzero factors can be canceled, but need not all be invertible.
algebra_ring_field__integral_domains.explanation: The integers ℤ form a standard integral domain. The element 2 has no multiplicative inverse there, so integral domains need not be fields. A finite integral domain is a field, because an injection of a finite set to itself is surjective.
notation: ab=0 ⇒ a=0 or b=0.
Nonzero factors can be canceled in an integral domain.
algebra_ring_field__integral_domains.example: ℤ is an infinite integral domain but not a field. ℤ₇ is a finite integral domain and a field. ℤ₉ is not an integral domain, since 3·3=0.
common_mistakes: Equating absence of zero divisors with invertibility of every nonzero element.
Omitting commutativity or the convention 1≠0.

algebra_ring_field__ring_axioms.title: Axioms of rings with identity
algebra_ring_field__ring_axioms.summary: A ring connects additive and multiplicative structures through two operations and distributive laws.
algebra_ring_field__ring_axioms.definition: Here a ring contains 1 with 1≠0. Addition forms an abelian group. Multiplication is associative, has identity 1, and distributes over addition on both sides. General rings need not have commutative multiplication.
algebra_ring_field__ring_axioms.explanation: Check both operations on the same set and the distributive laws connecting them. Additive inverses always exist; multiplicative inverses are not general ring axioms. State the convention about identity, which varies between textbooks.
notation: a(b+c)=ab+ac.
(a+b)c=ac+bc.
Multiplication need not commute.
algebra_ring_field__ring_axioms.example: The 2×2 matrices over ℤ₂ form a finite ring under entrywise addition and matrix multiplication. Some matrices A,B have AB≠BA.
common_mistakes: Assuming multiplication is commutative in every ring.
Reading existence of additive inverses as existence of all multiplicative inverses.

algebra_ring_field__units.title: Units and inverses in residue rings
algebra_ring_field__units.summary: The invertible residues modulo n are exactly those relatively prime to n.
algebra_ring_field__units.definition: In a ring with multiplicative identity 1≠0, an element a is a unit if some b satisfies ab=ba=1. For integers n≥2 in ℤₙ, this is equivalent to gcd(a,n)=1; Bézout’s identity can compute the inverse.
algebra_ring_field__units.explanation: The identity 1 is a specified neutral element, while a “unit” in ring theory is any invertible element; distinguish their roles by context. Division is defined only for invertible divisors.
notation: U(ℤₙ)={a:gcd(a,n)=1}.
a/b means a·b⁻¹, provided b is invertible.
algebra_ring_field__units.example: The units of ℤ₁₂ are 1,5,7,11. The inverse of 5 is 5, since 25≡1(mod12).
common_mistakes: Assuming every nonzero element of any ring is invertible.
Treating an ordinary real quotient directly as an element of a residue ring.

algebra_ring_field__zero_divisors.title: Nonzero zero divisors and multiplicative cancellation
algebra_ring_field__zero_divisors.summary: A product of nonzero elements can be 0, causing ordinary factor cancellation to fail.
algebra_ring_field__zero_divisors.definition: A ring has nonzero zero divisors if nonzero a,b satisfy ab=0. In a commutative ring, absence of nonzero zero divisors is equivalent to cancellation by nonzero factors. In noncommutative rings, distinguish left and right zero divisors.
algebra_ring_field__zero_divisors.explanation: From ab=ac obtain a(b−c)=0. Only when a≠0 and zero divisors are absent can one conclude b=c. With zero divisors, the implication generally fails.
notation: ab=ac ⇒ a(b−c)=0.
algebra_ring_field__zero_divisors.example: In ℤ₆, 2·3=0, and 2·1=2·4 although 1≠4. In ℤ₈, 2·4=0.
common_mistakes: Canceling nonzero factors unconditionally in congruences or ring equations.
Giving zero itself when a nonzero zero divisor is requested.

algebra_lattice_bool.title: Lattices and Boolean algebras
algebra_lattice_bool.summary: A lattice gives every pair a greatest lower bound and least upper bound; Boolean algebras add distributivity and complements.
algebra_lattice_bool.definition: A partially ordered set L is a lattice if every a,b have a greatest lower bound a∧b and least upper bound a∨b. It is bounded if it has least element 0 and greatest element 1. A bounded distributive lattice in which every a has a complement a′ satisfying a∧a′=0 and a∨a′=1 is a Boolean algebra.
algebra_lattice_bool.explanation: The power set P(U), ordered by inclusion, is a standard Boolean algebra: meet is intersection, join is union, and complement is relative to fixed U. A general lattice need not be distributive; being bounded and distributive does not guarantee complements. Finite chains have meets and joins but no complements for internal elements, so finite chains with at least 3 elements are not Boolean algebras.
notation: The lattice symbols 0,1 mean least and greatest elements and need not be the integers 0,1.
In P(U), A∧B=A∩B, A∨B=A∪B, A′=U\A.
algebra_lattice_bool.example: The positive divisors of 12 ordered by divisibility form a bounded lattice with meet gcd, join lcm, least element 1, and greatest element 12. The element 2 has no complement: the only divisors coprime to 2 are 1,3, and neither has lcm 12 with 2.
common_mistakes: Treating every partially ordered set as a lattice.
Assuming boundedness and distributivity automatically give complements.
Taking set complements without a fixed universal set.

algebra_lattice_bool__boolean_algebras.title: Distributive lattices and the set model of Boolean algebra
algebra_lattice_bool__boolean_algebras.summary: Boolean algebra unifies distributivity, bounds, and complements with logic and set operations.
algebra_lattice_bool__boolean_algebras.definition: A Boolean algebra can be defined as a bounded complemented distributive lattice. It satisfies distributivity, absorption, and De Morgan’s laws. The power set P(U) with intersection, union, and complement is the standard model, with 0=∅ and 1=U.
algebra_lattice_bool__boolean_algebras.explanation: Distributivity permits systematic simplification; for example, (A∩B)∪(A∩B′)=A∩(B∪B′)=A. Complements must use the same fixed universal set. Boundedness and distributivity are insufficient without a complement for every element.
algebra_lattice_bool__boolean_algebras.example: All subsets of a finite set U form a Boolean algebra. If U has n elements, the underlying set P(U) has 2ⁿ elements.
common_mistakes: Automatically treating a bounded distributive lattice as a Boolean algebra.
Mixing complements relative to different universal sets.

algebra_lattice_bool__bounded_lattices.title: Bounded lattices and least and greatest elements
algebra_lattice_bool__bounded_lattices.summary: In addition to lattice operations, a bounded lattice has global lower and upper bounds.
algebra_lattice_bool__bounded_lattices.definition: A lattice L is bounded if it has a least element 0 and greatest element 1, so 0≤x≤1 for every x. These symbols describe order roles, not necessarily the integers 0,1.
algebra_lattice_bool__bounded_lattices.explanation: Boundedness differs from existence of meets and joins for pairs, and does not guarantee complements. In the divisor lattice D(N), the least element is integer 1 and the greatest is integer N.
algebra_lattice_bool__bounded_lattices.example: The positive-divisor lattice of 12 has least element 1 and greatest element 12. The three-element chain 0<a<1 is also a bounded lattice.
common_mistakes: Assuming all lattices have global bounds by definition.
Writing integer 0 as the least element of a divisor lattice where 0 is absent.

algebra_lattice_bool__complements.title: Complements in bounded lattices
algebra_lattice_bool__complements.summary: A complement must meet to the least element and join to the greatest; both conditions are required.
algebra_lattice_bool__complements.definition: In a bounded lattice with least element 0 and greatest element 1, b complements a if a∧b=0 and a∨b=1. Not every bounded lattice gives each element a complement, and complements in a general lattice need not be unique.
algebra_lattice_bool__complements.explanation: The lattice symbols 0,1 describe roles, not necessarily the corresponding integers. A divisor lattice can have integer 1 as its least element and N as its greatest; there the complement conditions become gcd(a,b)=1 and lcm(a,b)=N.
notation: Complement: a∧b=0 and a∨b=1.
In P(U), the complement of A is U\A.
algebra_lattice_bool__complements.example: In the divisor lattice of 6, 1 and 6 are complements, as are 2 and 3. The middle element a of the chain 0<a<1 has no complement.
common_mistakes: Checking only meet 0 without checking join 1.
Interpreting the order symbol 0 as an integer absent from the underlying set.

algebra_lattice_bool__distributive_latti.title: Distributive lattices
algebra_lattice_bool__distributive_latti.summary: In a distributive lattice, meet and join distribute over each other.
algebra_lattice_bool__distributive_latti.definition: A lattice is distributive if it satisfies x∧(y∨z)=(x∧y)∨(x∧z) and the dual identity. The two laws are equivalent within lattice theory, but both can be stated directly when verifying them.
algebra_lattice_bool__distributive_latti.explanation: A total chain with min as meet and max as join is distributive. A distributive lattice need not have complements: the middle element of a bounded three-element chain has none, so this is not a Boolean algebra.
algebra_lattice_bool__distributive_latti.example: Set intersection and union distribute. A three-element chain is distributive and bounded, yet the complement requirement fails at its middle element.
common_mistakes: Taking distributivity as an axiom of every lattice.
Inferring a Boolean algebra from distributivity and boundedness alone.

algebra_lattice_bool__meets_joins.title: Lattices, greatest lower bounds, and least upper bounds
algebra_lattice_bool__meets_joins.summary: A lattice requires the meet and join of every pair to exist in its underlying set.
algebra_lattice_bool__meets_joins.definition: In a partially ordered set L, a∧b is the greatest of all common lower bounds of a,b, and a∨b is the least of all common upper bounds. If both exist for every pair, L is a lattice. The bounds must themselves belong to L.
algebra_lattice_bool__meets_joins.explanation: In a complete set of divisors ordered by divisibility, meet is gcd and join is lcm. Arbitrarily removing elements can remove a needed upper bound, so the remaining partial order may cease to be a lattice.
notation: a∧b is the greatest lower bound; a∨b is the least upper bound.
“Greatest” and “maximal” are different concepts.
algebra_lattice_bool__meets_joins.example: In {1,2,3} ordered by divisibility, 2 and 3 have no common upper bound inside the set, so it is not a lattice. The external element 6 cannot serve as their join.
common_mistakes: Choosing bounds outside the underlying set.
Mistaking a maximal lower bound for the greatest of all lower bounds.

q01.title: Identifying propositions
q01.statement: Which of the following statements is a false proposition?
q01.explanation: “9 is even” is a statement with a definite truth value, and it is false. A is an imperative sentence; D contains an unspecified free variable x and is not yet a definite proposition; B is a true proposition.
q01.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing C. Explaining that A is not a declarative proposition and that D contains a free variable may be used as feedback on the reasoning.

options.text: Please write this problem on paper.

q02.title: Truth value of an implication
q02.statement: When proposition p is false and proposition q is true, what is the truth value of p→q?
q02.explanation: An implication is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false. When p is false, p→q is true whether q is true or false.

options.text: p and q must both be true

q03.title: An equivalent form of implication
q03.statement: By the equivalence law for implication, p→q is equivalent to ______.
q03.explanation: p→q is false only when p is true and q is false. ¬p∨q is also false in exactly that case, so the two have the same truth value under every truth assignment.
q03.grading_criteria: Full credit for “¬p∨q” or a correctly written expression with the same meaning.

q04.title: Negating a universal statement
q04.statement: Negate the proposition “For every integer n, n²≥0.” Retain the complete domain.
q04.answer_text: There exists an integer n such that n²<0.
q04.explanation: Negating a universal quantifier changes it to an existential quantifier and negates the predicate: ¬(∀n∈ℤ, n²≥0) is equivalent to ∃n∈ℤ such that n²<0.
q04.grading_criteria: Both “there exists an integer n” and “n²<0” are required. An inequality without the existential quantifier does not receive full credit.

q05.title: Set operations
q05.statement: Let U={1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8} be the universal set, A={1,2,3,5}, and B={2,4,5,7}. Find A∪B, A∩B, A∖B, and the complement of A in U.
q05.explanation: The union contains elements belonging to at least one set; the intersection contains only elements belonging to both sets; A∖B contains elements of A that are not in B. The complement must be calculated relative to the specified universal set U.
q05.grading_criteria: Each of the four results is worth 25%. Different orders of the same set of elements are accepted.

q06.title: Properties of a relation
q06.statement: Let A={1,2,3} and R={(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1)}. Which of the following properties hold?
q06.explanation: All three diagonal pairs are in R, so R is reflexive. The non-diagonal pair (1,2) has its reverse (2,1), so R is symmetric. Since 1≠2 and the relation holds in both directions, R is not antisymmetric. Checking compositions of pairs within {1,2}, together with the diagonal pair for 3, shows that R is transitive.
q06.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting A, B, and D and excluding C. Extra selections or omissions receive partial credit.

q07.title: Equivalence classes of congruence
q07.statement: On the integers define a relation by: a is related to b if and only if 4 divides a−b. List all its distinct equivalence classes, and determine whether 7 and −1 belong to the same class.
q07.answer_text: There are four equivalence classes, [0], [1], [2], and [3], consisting respectively of integers with remainders 0, 1, 2, and 3 modulo 4. Since 7−(−1)=8 is divisible by 4, 7 and −1 belong to the same class.
q07.explanation: Two integers are congruent modulo 4 if and only if they have the same remainder upon division by 4. The only possible remainders are 0, 1, 2, and 3, so there are exactly four equivalence classes.
q07.grading_criteria: Describing the four classes by their remainders is worth 70%; correctly placing 7 and −1 in the same class and giving their difference is worth 30%.

q08.title: Injectivity and surjectivity
q08.statement: Let f:ℤ→ℤ be defined by f(n)=2n+1. Prove that f is injective but not surjective.
q08.answer_text: Injectivity: If f(a)=f(b), then 2a+1=2b+1, hence a=b, so f is injective. Failure of surjectivity: Take any even integer 2k. If an integer n satisfied f(n)=2k, then 2n+1=2k would give n=k−1/2, which is not an integer. Thus no even integer is in the image, and f is not surjective.
q08.explanation: For injectivity, equal function values must imply equal inputs. To disprove surjectivity it suffices to find one element of the codomain with no preimage. Here every even integer has no integer preimage.
q08.grading_criteria: A correct proof of injectivity is worth 40%; identifying even integers as having no preimages and explaining why is worth 60%. A single input-output example cannot replace a proof.

q09.title: A partial order given by divisibility
q09.statement: On A={1,2,3,6}, define the relation “a divides b.” Give the least and greatest elements of this partially ordered set, and identify a pair of incomparable elements.
q09.answer_text: The least element is 1 and the greatest element is 6; 2 and 3 are incomparable.
q09.explanation: 1 divides every element of A, so 1 is the least element. Every element of A divides 6, so 6 is the greatest element. Neither 2 divides 3 nor 3 divides 2, so they are incomparable.
q09.grading_criteria: Full credit requires all three conclusions to be correct. Distinguish a least element from a minimal element.

q10.title: The handshaking theorem
q10.statement: A finite undirected graph has four vertices of degrees 3, 2, 2, and 1, respectively. Find its number of edges.
q10.explanation: By the handshaking theorem, the sum of all vertex degrees is twice the number of edges. The degree sum is 3+2+2+1=8, so the number of edges is 8÷2=4.
q10.grading_criteria: Full credit for stating the handshaking theorem and calculating 4 edges.

q11.title: Connected components
q11.statement: An undirected graph has vertex set {A,B,C,D} and edge set {{A,B},{B,C}}. List all its connected components.
q11.answer_text: There are two connected components: one consists of vertices A, B, and C and edges {A,B} and {B,C}; the other is the isolated vertex D.
q11.explanation: There are paths connecting A, B, and C, so they belong to one connected component. D has no connection to any other vertex and forms a component on its own.
q11.grading_criteria: Full credit for identifying the two components {A,B,C} and {D}. Do not omit the isolated vertex.

q12.title: Edges of a tree and deleting an edge
q12.statement: A tree has 9 vertices. How many edges does it have? How many connected components result after any one of its edges is deleted?
q12.answer_text: The original tree has 8 edges. Deleting any edge splits the graph into two connected components.
q12.explanation: A tree with n vertices has n−1 edges, so this tree has 9−1=8 edges. Every edge of a tree is a bridge; deleting it disconnects the graph into exactly two connected components.
q12.grading_criteria: The number of edges and the number of connected components are each worth 50%. Explain that every edge of a tree is a bridge.

q13.title: Applying the pigeonhole principle
q13.statement: Prove that among any 13 people, at least two were born in the same month.
q13.answer_text: View the 12 months as 12 boxes and the 13 people as 13 objects. Put each person into the box corresponding to their birth month. Since there are 13 objects and only 12 boxes, the pigeonhole principle implies that some box contains at least 2 people. Therefore at least two people were born in the same month.
q13.explanation: Identify the objects and boxes: the people are the objects and the months are the boxes. There is no need to identify the particular two people or to know how many people were born in each month.
q13.grading_criteria: Correctly matching 13 people to 12 months is worth 40%; correctly applying the pigeonhole principle and concluding the proof is worth 60%.

q14.title: Proving the sum of odd integers by induction
q14.statement: Use mathematical induction to prove that for every positive integer n, 1+3+5+⋯+(2n−1)=n².
q14.answer_text: Base case: For n=1, the left side is 1 and the right side is 1²=1, so the claim holds. Induction hypothesis: Assume the claim holds for n=k, that is, 1+3+⋯+(2k−1)=k². Inductive step: For n=k+1, the left side is k²+[2(k+1)−1]=k²+2k+1=(k+1)², which equals the right side. Thus the claim holds for k+1. By mathematical induction, it holds for every positive integer n.
q14.explanation: The proof must include a base case, an induction hypothesis, and an inductive step. In the inductive step, add the (k+1)st odd integer, 2k+1, to the sum of the first k terms.
q14.grading_criteria: Base case: 20%; correct induction hypothesis: 20%; correct algebra in the inductive step: 40%; complete conclusion: 20%.

q_logic_truth_01.title: Open sentences and closed propositions
q_logic_truth_01.statement: Let n be an integer variable that has not been assigned a value. Which of the following is itself a closed proposition?
q_logic_truth_01.explanation: “31 is odd” asserts a property of a fixed integer and has a definite truth value. In A, n remains free; C is a command; D is a question.
q_logic_truth_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing only B. The explanation should distinguish free variables, imperative sentences, and questions.

q_logic_truth_02.title: Does an unknown truth value prevent a statement from being a proposition?
q_logic_truth_02.statement: A student has not tested whether the fixed integer N=10^20+39 is prime. Is the statement “N is prime” a proposition? Discuss only whether it is a proposition; no primality test is required.
q_logic_truth_02.answer_text: Yes. N is fixed, so the statement has a definite truth value, true or false. The student’s present lack of knowledge does not prevent it from being a proposition.
q_logic_truth_02.explanation: The criterion is whether a statement has a definite truth value, not whether someone already knows that value. There is no need to claim that N is actually prime or composite.
q_logic_truth_02.grading_criteria: Answering “yes” is worth 40%; explaining that N is fixed and that an unknown truth value is still a truth value is worth 60%.

q_logic_truth_03.title: Closing an open sentence by assignment and quantification
q_logic_truth_03.statement: Over the integers, let P(n) mean n²=n. Give the truth values of P(0), P(2), and “For every integer n, P(n),” and explain how these differ from P(n) with n unassigned.
q_logic_truth_03.answer_text: P(0) is true because 0²=0. P(2) is false because 4≠2. The universal statement is false, with n=2 as a counterexample. P(n) with n unassigned is an open sentence; it cannot be assigned a single truth value without an assignment or a quantifier.
q_logic_truth_03.explanation: The first two statements replace the free variable with a constant; the third binds it with a universal quantifier. All three are therefore closed propositions, but their truth values need not agree.
q_logic_truth_03.grading_criteria: Each of the three truth values is worth 20%; the universal counterexample and explanation of the open sentence together are worth 40%.

q_logic_truth_04.title: Truth values in a fixed context
q_logic_truth_04.statement: The context is the first lesson of Class A on October 12, 2026, and the attendance record shows 24 students present. Is “25 students in this class attended today’s first lesson” a proposition, and what is its truth value? If exactly 25 students attend on another day, making the same sentence true in that new context, is there a logical contradiction?
q_logic_truth_04.answer_text: In the given context, it is a proposition and is false. The statement on the other day concerns a different date and expresses a different specific fact. Different truth values in different contexts do not make one and the same proposition both true and false.
q_logic_truth_04.explanation: References such as “this class” and “today” depend on context. The class, date, and lesson must be fixed to interpret the assertion; these conditions must remain the same when comparing truth values.
q_logic_truth_04.grading_criteria: Identifying it as a false proposition is worth 40%; explaining that the two dates give different specific propositions and hence no contradiction is worth 60%.

q_logic_connectives_01.title: Evaluating compound connectives using parentheses
q_logic_connectives_01.statement: Suppose p is true and q is false. Evaluate (¬p∨q)∧(p∨¬q), giving the truth values at both levels of subformulas.
q_logic_connectives_01.answer_text: ¬p is false and ¬q is true. Thus ¬p∨q is false and p∨¬q is true, so the whole conjunction is false.
q_logic_connectives_01.explanation: Evaluate the negations first, then the two parenthesized formulas, and finally the conjunction. An outer ∧ is false whenever either component is false.
q_logic_connectives_01.grading_criteria: The two negations together are worth 20%; the two parenthesized formulas together are worth 40%; the final value false is worth 40%.

q_logic_connectives_02.title: Expressing that exactly one proposition holds
q_logic_connectives_02.statement: Let p and q be arbitrary propositions. Which formulas are true exactly when one of p and q is true? Select all correct options.
q_logic_connectives_02.explanation: A requires at least one to be true and excludes both being true. B lists the cases “p true, q false” and “p false, q true.” C is also true when both are true. D is true when both are true or both are false, so it has a different meaning.
q_logic_connectives_02.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting both A and B and excluding C and D. Explaining the differences between exclusive disjunction, inclusive disjunction, and the biconditional can earn reasoning credit.

q_logic_connectives_03.title: Recovering an unknown truth value from a biconditional
q_logic_connectives_03.statement: The formula s↔(p∧q) is true, p is true, and s is false. Find the truth value of q and justify your answer.
q_logic_connectives_03.answer_text: q is false. A true biconditional requires s and p∧q to have the same truth value, so p∧q is false. Since p is true, the conjunction can be false only if q is false.
q_logic_connectives_03.explanation: A true biconditional does not mean that both sides are true; it also holds when both sides are false.
q_logic_connectives_03.grading_criteria: Using equality of truth values to show the conjunction is false is worth 50%; using p true to conclude q false is worth 50%.

q_logic_connectives_04.title: The direction of an “only if” condition and its converse
q_logic_connectives_04.statement: Let s, l, and n mean “submission succeeds,” “the user is logged in,” and “the network is available,” respectively. Express “Submission can succeed only if the user is logged in and the network is available” as a formula. Does it imply “If the user is logged in and the network is available, submission succeeds”? If not, give a counterexample assignment.
q_logic_connectives_04.answer_text: The original statement is s→(l∧n). It does not imply (l∧n)→s. Set s=false, l=true, n=true; the original formula is true and the converse is false.
q_logic_connectives_04.explanation: An “only if” statement gives necessary conditions for success, without giving sufficient conditions. Other restrictions may apply in addition to login and network availability.
q_logic_connectives_04.grading_criteria: Symbolization: 40%; identifying that the converse does not follow: 20%; a counterexample making the original true and converse false: 40%.

q_logic_truth_table_01.title: Distinct letters determine the number of truth-table rows
q_logic_truth_table_01.statement: A formula contains exactly five distinct propositional letters p, q, r, s, and t, with p occurring three times. Its complete truth table has ______ rows.
q_logic_truth_table_01.explanation: Each of the five distinct letters has two possible truth values, giving 2^5=32 assignments. Every occurrence of p must have the same value within an assignment, so repetitions do not add independent variables.
q_logic_truth_table_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for 32. Explaining that only distinct propositional letters are counted can earn reasoning credit.

q_logic_truth_table_02.title: The complete truth column for a three-variable implication chain
q_logic_truth_table_02.statement: Let F=(p→q)∧(q→r). Give its eight truth values in the order (p,q,r)=000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111, and list the assignments making F true. Here 0 means false and 1 means true.
q_logic_truth_table_02.answer_text: The truth column is 1,1,0,1,0,0,0,1. The true assignments are 000, 001, 011, and 111, for a total of 4.
q_logic_truth_table_02.explanation: For both implications to be true, p=1,q=0 and q=1,r=0 must both be excluded. Hence the values must satisfy p≤q≤r, giving exactly the four listed rows.
q_logic_truth_table_02.grading_criteria: The complete eight-row column is worth 80%; listing exactly the four true assignments without omissions is worth 20%.

q_logic_truth_table_03.title: Classifying a disjunction of opposite implications
q_logic_truth_table_03.statement: For arbitrary propositions p and q, how is (p→q)∨(q→p) classified?
q_logic_truth_table_03.explanation: In the order 00, 01, 10, 11, its truth values are 1, 1, 1, 1. In the only case where p→q is false, namely p=1,q=0, q→p is true. Thus the whole disjunction cannot be false.
q_logic_truth_table_03.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing only A. A truth table or an explanation using the incompatible conditions for falsity is accepted.

options.text: A contingency, with both true and false rows
An open sentence without a definite truth value

q_logic_truth_table_04.title: Enumerating every differing row of two similar formulas
q_logic_truth_table_04.statement: Let A=p→(q∧r) and B=(p→q)∧r. Enumerate all binary assignments to p, q, and r and find every assignment where A and B differ. Use this to decide whether they are equivalent.
q_logic_truth_table_04.answer_text: They differ only at (p,q,r)=(0,0,0) and (0,1,0). In both rows A is true and B is false. Therefore A and B are not equivalent.
q_logic_truth_table_04.explanation: If p=1, both formulas equal q∧r. If p=0, A is always true and B equals r. They therefore differ exactly when p=0 and r=0, with q arbitrary, which accounts for all differing rows.
q_logic_truth_table_04.grading_criteria: A complete case split or eight-row enumeration: 40%; the two differing assignments and their truth values: 40%; concluding non-equivalence: 20%.

q_logic_equivalence_01.title: De Morgan’s law for a negated disjunction
q_logic_equivalence_01.statement: Which formula is logically equivalent to ¬(p∨q)?
q_logic_equivalence_01.explanation: The negation of the disjunction requires both p and q to be false, so it is equivalent to ¬p∧¬q. By contrast, ¬p∨¬q requires only at least one to be false and is weaker.
q_logic_equivalence_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing only B.

q_logic_equivalence_02.title: Simplifying a common antecedent with incompatible consequents
q_logic_equivalence_02.statement: Use equivalence laws to simplify (p→q)∧(p→¬q) to a formula containing just one literal. Show the main steps.
q_logic_equivalence_02.explanation: First eliminate both implications, then use distribution to combine the common ¬p. Since q∧¬q is always false, the formula depends only on ¬p.
q_logic_equivalence_02.grading_criteria: Eliminating implications: 30%; correct distribution and simplification of the contradiction: 50%; the result ¬p: 20%.

q_logic_equivalence_03.title: Expressing a biconditional by matching truth values
q_logic_equivalence_03.statement: Prove that p↔q and (p∧q)∨(¬p∧¬q) are logically equivalent. Your proof must cover all truth-value cases for p and q.
q_logic_equivalence_03.answer_text: Take any truth assignment to p and q. If both are true, the biconditional is true and p∧q on the right is true. If both are false, the biconditional is true and ¬p∧¬q on the right is true. If exactly one is true, the biconditional is false and both conjunctions on the right are false. These three cases cover all four assignments, so the formulas agree under every assignment and are logically equivalent.
q_logic_equivalence_03.explanation: The right side lists exactly the two kinds of cases where the biconditional is true. A row-by-row truth table or correct equivalence-law derivation is also accepted, but checking a single assignment is insufficient.
q_logic_equivalence_03.grading_criteria: Covering both true, both false, and exactly one true: 60%; correct comparisons in those cases: 25%; concluding equivalence under every assignment: 15%.

q_logic_equivalence_04.title: Combining two implications with a common consequent
q_logic_equivalence_04.statement: Use equivalence laws to prove (p→r)∧(q→r)≡(p∨q)→r, and name the laws for the main steps.
q_logic_equivalence_04.answer_text: (p→r)∧(q→r)≡(¬p∨r)∧(¬q∨r) (elimination of implication) ≡(¬p∧¬q)∨r (distribution) ≡¬(p∨q)∨r (De Morgan’s law) ≡(p∨q)→r (implication equivalence). Each step is an unconditional equivalence, so the claimed equivalence holds.
q_logic_equivalence_04.explanation: The common consequent r can be combined, but the antecedent becomes p∨q, not p∧q. Each step preserves truth under every assignment.
q_logic_equivalence_04.grading_criteria: Eliminating implications: 20%; combining by distribution: 35%; De Morgan’s law and restoring implication: 30%; giving reasons and the conclusion: 15%.

q_logic_normal_form_01.title: Recognizing disjunctive normal form by definition
q_logic_normal_form_01.statement: Under the syntactic definitions “a literal is a propositional letter or its negation” and “disjunctive normal form is a disjunction of conjunctive terms,” which formula is already in disjunctive normal form? A single literal is allowed as a conjunctive term.
q_logic_normal_form_01.explanation: A is the disjunction of the conjunctive term p∧¬q and the single-literal term r. B contains a disjunction under an outer conjunction and is not already in disjunctive normal form; C contains implication; D applies negation directly to a compound formula. The other formulas can be converted to DNF, but the question concerns their present written form.
q_logic_normal_form_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing only A. Distinguish “already in normal form” from “can be converted to normal form.”

q_logic_normal_form_02.title: The two principal normal forms of exclusive disjunction
q_logic_normal_form_02.statement: Fix the complete variable set as p and q. Find the principal disjunctive normal form and principal conjunctive normal form of F=(p∨q)∧¬(p∧q).
q_logic_normal_form_02.answer_text: Principal disjunctive normal form: (¬p∧q)∨(p∧¬q). Principal conjunctive normal form: (p∨q)∧(¬p∨¬q).
q_logic_normal_form_02.explanation: F is true on rows 01 and 10, which give two minterms, and false on rows 00 and 11, which give two maxterms. Each term contains p and q exactly once.
q_logic_normal_form_02.grading_criteria: True rows and principal DNF: 45%; false rows and principal CNF: 45%; complete variable occurrence and correct parentheses: 10%.

q_logic_normal_form_03.title: Minterms and maxterms of an implication
q_logic_normal_form_03.statement: Fix the variable order as (p,q). Find the principal disjunctive and principal conjunctive normal forms of p→q, and identify the false row used to construct the principal conjunctive normal form.
q_logic_normal_form_03.answer_text: Principal DNF: (¬p∧¬q)∨(¬p∧q)∨(p∧q). Principal CNF: ¬p∨q. The unique false row is (p,q)=(1,0).
q_logic_normal_form_03.explanation: The implication is true on 00, 01, and 11, giving three minterms. The maxterm for the false row 10 must be false on that row, so p is negated and q is left unnegated, giving ¬p∨q.
q_logic_normal_form_03.grading_criteria: The three minterms: 50%; the maxterm: 30%; the unique false row and explanation of the negation rule: 20%.

q_logic_normal_form_04.title: Completing principal normal forms with three variables
q_logic_normal_form_04.statement: Fix the variable order as (p,q,r). Find the principal disjunctive and principal conjunctive normal forms of F=p∧(q∨r). Every term must contain p, q, and r exactly once.
q_logic_normal_form_04.explanation: The true rows 101, 110, and 111 give three minterms. The other rows, 000, 001, 010, 011, and 100, are false; each gives a maxterm that is false on that row. Although the original formula is ordinary CNF, its clauses do not each contain all three variables, so it is not already principal CNF.
q_logic_normal_form_04.grading_criteria: The three minterms from true rows: 40%; the five maxterms from false rows: 50%; complete variables and the distinction between ordinary and principal normal forms: 10%.

q_logic_reasoning_01.title: The conclusion of modus ponens
q_logic_reasoning_01.statement: The premises p→q and p are both true. Which of the following must be true?
q_logic_reasoning_01.explanation: Modus ponens gives q. If p were true and q false, p→q would be false, contradicting the premise. The other options conflict with the premises or do not follow from them.
q_logic_reasoning_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing only B.

q_logic_reasoning_02.title: A counterexample to affirming the consequent
q_logic_reasoning_02.statement: Is the inference “p→q; q; therefore p” valid? If not, give an assignment making all premises true and the conclusion false.
q_logic_reasoning_02.answer_text: It is invalid. Set p=false and q=true. Then p→q and q are true, but the conclusion p is false.
q_logic_reasoning_02.explanation: This is the fallacy of affirming the consequent. A counterexample must make all premises hold together while the conclusion fails; making a premise fail does not suffice.
q_logic_reasoning_02.grading_criteria: Identifying invalidity: 20%; p false and q true: 40%; verifying both premises true and conclusion false: 40%.

q_logic_reasoning_03.title: Reasoning by cases from a disjunctive premise
q_logic_reasoning_03.statement: Prove r from the premises p∨q, p→r, and q→r. Explain why your two cases cover all possibilities.
q_logic_reasoning_03.answer_text: Assume all premises hold and split into cases. If p is true, p→r gives r. If p is false, p∨q forces q to be true, and q→r gives r. Since p is either true or false, the cases cover all assignments and both yield r. Therefore the inference is valid.
q_logic_reasoning_03.explanation: A case proof must do more than say that p might imply r. It must also handle the case where p fails and the disjunctive premise guarantees q.
q_logic_reasoning_03.grading_criteria: Correct derivation in each case: 35% each; explaining coverage and concluding validity: 30%.

q_logic_reasoning_04.title: An implication chain and disjunctive syllogism
q_logic_reasoning_04.statement: Given p→q, q→r, ¬r∨s, and p, derive s step by step, citing the premise or rule used at each step.
q_logic_reasoning_04.answer_text: From p→q and p, obtain q by modus ponens. From q→r and q, obtain r by modus ponens again. Treat ¬r∨s as r→s, or apply disjunctive syllogism directly: r rules out the disjunct ¬r, so s follows. Thus s must hold whenever all the premises hold.
q_logic_reasoning_04.explanation: First derive r, then eliminate ¬r from the disjunction. You cannot choose s merely because ¬r∨s holds.
q_logic_reasoning_04.grading_criteria: Deriving q from p: 25%; deriving r from q: 25%; deriving s from r and ¬r∨s: 35%; naming the rules: 15%.

q_predicate_domain_01.title: The truth set of a unary predicate
q_predicate_domain_01.statement: Let D={−1,0,1,2} and let P(x) mean x²≤1. The set {x∈D:P(x) is true} is ______.
q_predicate_domain_01.explanation: Substituting each element gives squares 1, 0, 1, and 4. The first three are at most 1, while 2²=4, so 2 is excluded.
q_predicate_domain_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for exactly the three correct elements, without 2. An answer consisting only of elements outside the domain receives no credit.

q_predicate_domain_02.title: Ordered argument positions in a binary predicate
q_predicate_domain_02.statement: Let D={1,2} and let R(x,y) mean x<y. Give its four truth values in the order (1,1),(1,2),(2,1),(2,2).
q_predicate_domain_02.explanation: Strict inequality excludes equal pairs, and 1<2 is true whereas 2<1 is false. Swapping arguments can change the truth value.
q_predicate_domain_02.grading_criteria: Each truth value is worth 25%. Preserve the order given in the question.

q_predicate_domain_03.title: Changing the domain can change a universal statement’s truth
q_predicate_domain_03.statement: Is “Every x satisfies x²≥x” true over the integers? Is it true over the rationals? Give a reason or counterexample for each.
q_predicate_domain_03.answer_text: It is true over the integers: if x≤0, then x²≥0≥x; if x≥1, then x²≥x, and no integer lies strictly between 0 and 1. It is false over the rationals: for example, x=1/2 gives x²=1/4<1/2.
q_predicate_domain_03.explanation: Universal statements of similar form can have different truth values when their quantification ranges differ. The integer case must cover positive and nonpositive integers, rather than merely checking a few integers.
q_predicate_domain_03.grading_criteria: An exhaustive argument for the integer case: 55%; a rational counterexample with verification: 45%.

q_predicate_domain_04.title: Writing a divisibility predicate as a set of ordered pairs
q_predicate_domain_04.statement: Let D={1,2,3}, and let R(x,y) mean that y=kx for some integer k. List all ordered pairs in D×D making R true.
q_predicate_domain_04.explanation: 1 divides all three elements; 2 divides only 2 within this domain; 3 divides only 3. Since divisibility is defined by y=kx, (1,2) must not be reversed to (2,1).
q_predicate_domain_04.grading_criteria: The five true pairs: 80%; no extra pairs and the correct direction: 20%.

q_predicate_quantifier_01.title: Choosing a larger integer for each integer
q_predicate_quantifier_01.statement: The domain is the integers. Symbolize “Every integer has an integer larger than it,” and give an existential witness depending on the original integer.
q_predicate_quantifier_01.answer_text: ∀x∈Z ∃y∈Z(y>x). For any integer x, take y=x+1, which is still an integer and satisfies y>x.
q_predicate_quantifier_01.explanation: First take arbitrary x, then choose y depending on it. This shows how the later witness in ∀x∃y can depend on the earlier object.
q_predicate_quantifier_01.grading_criteria: Quantifier order, domain, and inequality: 50%; the witness x+1 and its verification: 50%.

q_predicate_quantifier_02.title: Exchanging quantifiers does not preserve meaning
q_predicate_quantifier_02.statement: Let D={1,2}. Evaluate A=∀x∃y(x≠y) and B=∃y∀x(x≠y), and explain how y is chosen in each.
q_predicate_quantifier_02.answer_text: A is true: for x=1 choose y=2, and for x=2 choose y=1. B is false: for any fixed y∈D, setting x=y makes x≠y false.
q_predicate_quantifier_02.explanation: A allows a different y for each x. B requires the same y to differ from every x, including itself, which is impossible.
q_predicate_quantifier_02.grading_criteria: The truth value of A and its two witnesses: 50%; refuting B for every fixed y: 50%.

q_predicate_quantifier_03.title: Restricted universal and existential quantification
q_predicate_quantifier_03.statement: The domain is all students at a school. Let S(x) mean “x enrolled in discrete mathematics” and P(x) mean “x passed the examination.” Which symbolizations are accurate? Select all correct options.
q_predicate_quantifier_03.explanation: “All enrolled students passed” imposes no condition on students who did not enroll, so it is ∀x(S(x)→P(x)); A is correct. B instead asserts that everyone enrolled and passed. “Some enrolled student passed” requires the same object to satisfy S and P, so C is correct. D merely requires someone satisfying S→P, which a non-enrolled student can satisfy, and does not express the intended meaning.
q_predicate_quantifier_03.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting both A and C and excluding B and D. Explaining that universal restrictions use → and existential restrictions use ∧ can earn reasoning credit.

q_predicate_quantifier_04.title: A single witness versus a witness for each object
q_predicate_quantifier_04.statement: Let D be a nonempty domain and R any binary predicate on D. Prove that ∃x∀y R(x,y) implies ∀y∃x R(x,y), and use a finite model to show that the converse does not hold in general.
q_predicate_quantifier_04.answer_text: If ∃x∀yR(x,y) is true, take a witness a. Then R(a,y) holds for every y. For each y, choosing x=a establishes ∃xR(x,y), so ∀y∃xR(x,y). The converse fails: let D={0,1} and let R(x,y) mean x=y. For each y choose x=y, so ∀y∃xR is true. But no x equals both 0 and 1, so ∃x∀yR is false.
q_predicate_quantifier_04.explanation: One fixed witness that works for all objects also works for each individual object. Separate witnesses for individual objects need not be the same.
q_predicate_quantifier_04.grading_criteria: The forward argument with an arbitrary object: 50%; a defined finite model and verification of both truth values for the converse: 50%.

q_predicate_variable_01.title: Free and bound occurrences of the same letter
q_predicate_variable_01.statement: For A=∀x(P(x,y)→∃y Q(x,y,z)), the set of free variables FV(A) is ______. Distinguish the y in P from the y in Q.
q_predicate_variable_01.answer_text: FV(A)={y,z}. The y in P is free, while the y in Q is bound by ∃y. z is free, and all occurrences of x are bound by the outer ∀x.
q_predicate_variable_01.explanation: Whether a variable occurrence is free depends on that occurrence and its scope, not merely on whether some quantifier elsewhere uses the letter y.
q_predicate_variable_01.grading_criteria: The set {y,z}: 50%; explaining the bindings of the different occurrences: 50%.

q_predicate_variable_02.title: Correctly renaming nested bound variables
q_predicate_variable_02.statement: In ∀x(P(x,y)∨∃x Q(x,y)), rename the two bound variables to the fresh variables u and v, respectively. Keep the free variable y unchanged, and explain why renaming the outer variable must not change the x in Q.
q_predicate_variable_02.answer_text: The result is ∀u(P(u,y)∨∃v Q(v,y)). The x in Q is originally bound by the inner ∃x, which shadows the outer binding. Renaming the outer x to u therefore affects only the x in P; the inner bound variable is then independently renamed to v.
q_predicate_variable_02.explanation: Safe renaming preserves the original binding of every occurrence. Changing the x in Q to u as well would incorrectly change the formula’s meaning.
q_predicate_variable_02.grading_criteria: The complete new formula: 60%; explaining shadowing and preservation of free y: 40%.

q_predicate_variable_03.title: Avoiding capture when substituting for a free variable
q_predicate_variable_03.statement: Let F(x)=∃y R(x,y). To replace its free x with the free variable y, what renaming is needed first, and what formula results? Next let D={0,1}, let R(u,v) mean u≠v, and assign free y the value 0. Compare the truth values of the correct result and the direct replacement ∃yR(y,y).
q_predicate_variable_03.answer_text: First rename the original bound y to a fresh variable z, then substitute, obtaining ∃z R(y,z). With y=0, choose z=1, so the correct result is true. Writing ∃yR(y,y) directly captures the substituted free y. It requires an object unequal to itself and is false in this model.
q_predicate_variable_03.explanation: Substitution must preserve the freedom of positions that were free originally. The same variable name does not mean that a quantifier may automatically bind both occurrences.
q_predicate_variable_03.grading_criteria: Correct substitution after renaming: 50%; the correct result true with a witness: 25%; the incorrect result false and explanation of capture: 25%.

q_predicate_variable_04.title: Parentheses change quantifier scope and truth values
q_predicate_variable_04.statement: Let D={0,1}, with P and Q both true only at 0. Assign free x the value 0. Compare F=(∀xP(x))∨Q(x) and G=∀x(P(x)∨Q(x)), and identify the free occurrence of x in F.
q_predicate_variable_04.answer_text: F is true: ∀xP(x) is false, but free x=0 makes Q(x) true. G is false: within the quantifier’s scope, x=1 makes P(1)∨Q(1) false. In F the x in Q(x) is free, while the x in P is bound.
q_predicate_variable_04.explanation: The outer disjunction in F limits the quantifier’s scope to P(x); the quantifier cannot simply be extended to Q(x). In G it binds every x inside the parentheses.
q_predicate_variable_04.grading_criteria: The truth values of F and G: 30% each; identifying the free occurrence and explaining the scopes: 40%.

q_predicate_reasoning_01.title: Negating an existential conjunction
q_predicate_reasoning_01.statement: Over a nonempty domain, which formula is equivalent to ¬∃x(P(x)∧Q(x))?
q_predicate_reasoning_01.explanation: First change the negated existential quantifier to a universal quantifier, then apply De Morgan’s law: ¬∃x(P∧Q)≡∀x¬(P∧Q)≡∀x(¬P∨¬Q).
q_predicate_reasoning_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing only C.

q_predicate_reasoning_02.title: Transferring existence through a universal condition
q_predicate_reasoning_02.statement: On the same nonempty domain, suppose ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)) and ∃xP(x). Prove ∃xQ(x), and explain the role of the temporary witness.
q_predicate_reasoning_02.answer_text: From ∃xP(x), introduce a fresh temporary name a for an object satisfying P, so P(a). The universal premise gives P(a)→Q(a), and modus ponens gives Q(a). Existential introduction yields ∃xQ(x). The conclusion contains no a and thus does not depend on the temporary name; a was not assumed to be any previously designated object.
q_predicate_reasoning_02.explanation: An existential witness cannot simply be treated as a known special constant. Use a fresh name within a subproof to derive an existential conclusion that no longer contains that name.
q_predicate_reasoning_02.grading_criteria: Legally introducing a witness: 25%; instantiation and modus ponens: 45%; existential introduction and explanation of independence: 30%.

q_predicate_reasoning_03.title: Valid distribution of quantifiers over connectives
q_predicate_reasoning_03.statement: Let P and Q be arbitrary unary predicates on the same nonempty domain. Which equivalences hold for every such interpretation?
q_predicate_reasoning_03.explanation: A says each object has both properties, equivalent to every object having P and every object having Q separately. B says some object has P or Q, equivalent to a P witness existing or a Q witness existing. C and D fail in general: let D={1,2}, with P true only at 1 and Q true only at 2. C then has a true left side and false right side; D has a false left side and true right side.
q_predicate_reasoning_03.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting both A and B and excluding C and D. A two-element model refuting both C and D can earn reasoning credit.

q_predicate_reasoning_04.title: Two existential assertions cannot automatically share a witness
q_predicate_reasoning_04.statement: Someone reasons from ∃xP(x) and ∃xQ(x): “Take a witness a. Then P(a) and Q(a), so ∃x(P(x)∧Q(x)).” Identify the invalid step, and give an interpretation on D={1,2} making the premises true and the conclusion false.
q_predicate_reasoning_04.answer_text: The invalid step is assuming, without proof, that both existential assertions can use the same witness a. Let P be true only at 1 and Q only at 2. The premises are true, witnessed by 1 and 2 respectively, but no object satisfies both P and Q, so the conclusion is false.
q_predicate_reasoning_04.explanation: Each existential quantifier guarantees at least one object separately; it does not guarantee that the witnesses coincide. The two existential eliminations require suitable fresh temporary names and cannot simply be merged.
q_predicate_reasoning_04.grading_criteria: Identifying the shared-witness error: 40%; defining P and Q: 20%; verifying all premises true and conclusion false: 40%.

q_predicate_prenex_01.title: Recognizing a formula already in prenex form
q_predicate_prenex_01.statement: Which formula is already in prenex normal form? Here P and Q are predicates; prenex normal form requires all quantifiers to be in a prefix and the matrix to contain no quantifiers.
q_predicate_prenex_01.explanation: A has quantifier prefix ∀x∃y and quantifier-free matrix P(x,y)∨¬Q(y). In B and C, quantifiers occur in local subformulas after connectives. In D, negation precedes the quantifier, so an equivalence transformation is still needed.
q_predicate_prenex_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing only A.

q_predicate_prenex_02.title: Pushing negations inward and converting to prenex form
q_predicate_prenex_02.statement: Over a nonempty domain, convert ¬∀x(P(x)→∃yQ(x,y)) to an equivalent prenex normal form. Show the transformations of negations and quantifiers.
q_predicate_prenex_02.explanation: Eliminate implication, then apply quantifier negation and De Morgan’s law in turn. Moving ∀y outward in the final step is valid because y does not occur free in P(x).
q_predicate_prenex_02.grading_criteria: Changing negated ∀x to ∃x: 20%; eliminating implication and negating the inner existential: 40%; valid outward movement and the final matrix: 40%.

q_predicate_prenex_03.title: Separating bound variables with the same name before moving quantifiers
q_predicate_prenex_03.statement: Over a nonempty domain, convert (∀xP(x))∨(∃xQ(x)) to an equivalent prenex normal form. Use different fresh bound variables and explain the free-variable conditions for moving the quantifiers.
q_predicate_prenex_03.answer_text: First rename to (∀uP(u))∨(∃vQ(v)), where u and v are fresh. Moving the quantifiers outward gives ∀u∃v(P(u)∨Q(v)). Since u does not occur free in Q(v) and v does not occur free in P(u), both movements satisfy the required conditions.
q_predicate_prenex_03.explanation: The original two x variables belong to separate quantifiers and must not be treated as the same object merely because their names agree. The equivalent form ∃v∀u(P(u)∨Q(v)) is also accepted, with an explanation of the independence conditions used; it is incorrect to claim that ∀ and ∃ can always be interchanged.
q_predicate_prenex_03.grading_criteria: Separating the bound variables: 30%; the prenex formula: 40%; free-variable conditions and the nonempty-domain convention: 30%.

q_predicate_prenex_04.title: Handling an antecedent quantifier while preserving a free parameter
q_predicate_prenex_04.statement: Over a nonempty domain, in A=(∃xP(x))→∀yR(x,y), the x in R on the right is free. Convert A to an equivalent prenex normal form while preserving this free parameter x. Let u be a fresh variable.
q_predicate_prenex_04.answer_text: First rename the bound x in the antecedent to u: A≡(∃uP(u))→∀yR(x,y)≡¬∃uP(u)∨∀yR(x,y)≡(∀u¬P(u))∨∀yR(x,y)≡∀u∀y(¬P(u)∨R(x,y)). The x in R remains free in the final formula.
q_predicate_prenex_04.explanation: Moving the antecedent’s ∃x straight to the front would capture the free x on the right. Also, negating the antecedent changes the original ∃u to ∀u.
q_predicate_prenex_04.grading_criteria: Renaming first and preserving free x: 35%; eliminating implication and switching the quantifier: 35%; valid outward movement and the final formula: 30%.

q_proof_direct_contradiction_01.title: A direct proof that a product of odd integers is odd
q_proof_direct_contradiction_01.statement: Use a direct proof to show that the product of any two odd integers a and b is an odd integer.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_01.answer_text: Take arbitrary odd integers a and b. By definition there are integers r and s with a=2r+1 and b=2s+1. Then ab=4rs+2r+2s+1=2(2rs+r+s)+1. Since 2rs+r+s is an integer, ab satisfies the definition of an odd integer. Thus the product of any two odd integers is odd.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_01.explanation: State that r and s are integers when introducing them, and finish by checking the definition, rather than merely asserting that “odd times odd is odd.”
q_proof_direct_contradiction_01.grading_criteria: Arbitrary objects and their integer representations: 35%; algebraic manipulation: 40%; linking back to the definition of odd integers: 25%.

q_proof_direct_contradiction_02.title: A proof by contradiction that there are infinitely many primes
q_proof_direct_contradiction_02.statement: Assume that every positive integer greater than 1 has at least one prime divisor. Prove by contradiction that there are infinitely many primes. You need not construct the next prime.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_02.answer_text: Suppose there are only finitely many primes, listed as p₁,…,pₖ. Let N=p₁p₂⋯pₖ+1. Then N>1, so the given fact supplies a prime divisor q. If q were some pᵢ, then q would divide both N and p₁⋯pₖ, hence their difference 1, which is impossible. Therefore q is absent from the list, contradicting its assumed completeness. Thus there are infinitely many primes.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_02.explanation: There is no need to claim that N itself is prime. Taking a prime divisor of N suffices to find an object contradicting the finite-list assumption.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_02.grading_criteria: Assuming a finite complete list: 20%; constructing N and correctly applying existence of a prime divisor: 30%; showing q is absent from the list and obtaining the contradiction: 40%; the conclusion: 10%.

q_proof_direct_contradiction_03.title: Finding and repairing a parity argument based on a square root
q_proof_direct_contradiction_03.statement: For an integer n, a proof says: “n² is even, so n²=2k. Hence n=√(2k), so n is even.” Identify the essential gap and give a complete repair using proof by contradiction.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_03.answer_text: The expression n=√(2k) does not imply that n is even; for negative n, this equality also ignores the sign. A correct proof is as follows. Suppose n² is even but n is not even. By the odd-even dichotomy for integers, n=2t+1 for some integer t. Then n²=2(2t²+2t)+1 is odd, contradicting its assumed evenness. Therefore n is even.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_03.explanation: A square-root expression does not supply an integer m such that n=2m. The repair must use the definitions of integer parity and a contradiction argument, rather than merely restating the conclusion.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_03.grading_criteria: Identifying the unsupported parity inference: 30%; the contrary assumption and odd representation: 25%; deriving an odd square and a contradiction: 35%; the conclusion: 10%.

q_proof_direct_contradiction_04.title: A proof by contradiction using residues modulo 5
q_proof_direct_contradiction_04.statement: Given six indexed integers a₁,…,a₆, whose values may repeat, prove by contradiction that there exist distinct indices i and j such that 5 divides aᵢ−aⱼ.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_04.answer_text: Suppose, to the contrary, that no difference between distinct indices is divisible by 5. Each aᵢ has a unique remainder rᵢ∈{0,1,2,3,4} upon division by 5. If rᵢ=rⱼ, then aᵢ−aⱼ=5(qᵢ−qⱼ), contradicting the assumption. Thus the six indices would require six distinct remainders, but the remainder set has only five elements, which is impossible. The assumption is false, so such i and j exist.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_04.explanation: Even if two original integers have equal values, their indices can be distinct, and their difference 0 is divisible by 5. The witnesses must have distinct indices; the six values need not be distinct.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_04.grading_criteria: Precisely negating the existential conclusion: 20%; remainder representations and the difference of congruent integers: 35%; the contradiction of six distinct remainders among five: 35%; the existence conclusion: 10%.

q_proof_induction_01.title: An induction proof of divisibility starting at zero
q_proof_induction_01.statement: Use mathematical induction to prove that for every integer n≥0, 3^n−1 is even.
