q_proof_induction_01.answer_text: For n=0, 3^0−1=0 is even. Take any k≥0 and assume 3^k−1=2t for some integer t. Then 3^(k+1)−1=3(3^k−1)+2=6t+2=2(3t+1), which is again even. By mathematical induction, the claim holds for all n≥0.
q_proof_induction_01.explanation: Zero is even, so n=0 is a valid starting point. The inductive step should write the new expression as an integer multiple of the old one plus an even number; checking only n=1 is insufficient.
q_proof_induction_01.grading_criteria: The zero base case: 20%; a clear hypothesis: 20%; an even-integer representation of the new expression: 45%; the conclusion for the full range: 15%.

q_proof_induction_02.title: Induction for an exponential-linear inequality
q_proof_induction_02.statement: Use mathematical induction to prove that 2^n≥n+1 for every integer n≥0.
q_proof_induction_02.answer_text: For n=0, 1≥1. Take any k≥0 and assume 2^k≥k+1. Then 2^(k+1)=2·2^k≥2(k+1)=2k+2≥k+2, since k≥0. Thus P(k+1) holds. By mathematical induction, the claim holds for every n≥0.
q_proof_induction_02.explanation: The induction hypothesis establishes only the first inequality. You must also explain why 2k+2≥k+2 holds throughout the permitted range of k.
q_proof_induction_02.grading_criteria: The base case and hypothesis together: 35%; both inequality steps after using the hypothesis, with their conditions: 50%; the conclusion for the full range: 15%.

q_proof_induction_03.title: Choosing the correct starting point for a factorial inequality
q_proof_induction_03.statement: Use mathematical induction to prove that n!≥2^n for every integer n≥4. Explain why n=3 cannot be a valid starting point for this claim.
q_proof_induction_03.answer_text: For n=4, 4!=24≥16=2^4. Take any k≥4 and assume k!≥2^k. Then (k+1)!=(k+1)k!≥(k+1)2^k≥2·2^k=2^(k+1), since k+1≥5≥2. Thus the claim holds for every n≥4. At n=3, 3!=6<8=2^3, so the claim fails and this cannot be a true base case.
q_proof_induction_03.explanation: The successor step must match the stated index range. A false base case invalidates the induction proof even if the subsequent algebra is correct.
q_proof_induction_03.grading_criteria: The n=4 base case: 20%; the induction hypothesis and successor inequalities: 55%; the n=3 counterexample: 15%; the conclusion: 10%.

q_proof_induction_04.title: A false induction that all integers are equal
q_proof_induction_04.statement: Someone claims that for every positive integer n, any n integers are equal. Their proof: the case n=1 is clear; assume any k integers are equal. Given k+1 integers a₁,…,aₖ₊₁, the first k are equal and the last k are equal. The two groups share an element, so all are equal. Identify the first failing inductive step and give a counterexample.
q_proof_induction_04.answer_text: The step from k=1 to k+1=2 fails. The first group contains only a₁ and the last only a₂, so there is no common element connecting their equality statements. Taking a₁=0 and a₂=1 gives a counterexample to P(2). A correct base case P(1) cannot repair this failed successor step.
q_proof_induction_04.explanation: The intersection consists of a₂,…,aₖ and is guaranteed nonempty only when k≥2. The proof misses precisely the smallest inductive step. Merely saying the conclusion is obviously false does not identify the gap.
q_proof_induction_04.grading_criteria: Identifying k=1 as the failed step: 45%; explaining the lack of a shared element: 30%; a counterexample with two different integers: 25%.

q_proof_strong_induction_01.title: Stating the available strong induction hypothesis
q_proof_strong_induction_01.statement: To prove P(n) for every integer n≥2 by strong induction, the necessary base cases have been verified. When proving P(k+1), the standard strong induction hypothesis is ______. Do not merely write “P holds for all integers.”
q_proof_strong_induction_01.answer_text: For every integer j with 2≤j≤k, P(j) holds.
q_proof_strong_induction_01.explanation: Strong induction permits all already covered cases from the starting point 2 through the current index k. It does not include P(k+1), larger indices, or the out-of-range case P(1).
q_proof_strong_induction_01.grading_criteria: Including “every j” and the range 2≤j≤k: 70%; clearly excluding the current target from the assumption: 30%.

q_proof_strong_induction_02.title: Every integer greater than 1 is a product of primes
q_proof_strong_induction_02.statement: Use strong induction to prove that every integer n≥2 is a product of one or more primes. Repeated prime factors are allowed; uniqueness need not be proved.
q_proof_strong_induction_02.answer_text: Base case: n=2 is itself prime. Take any k≥2 and assume the claim holds for every integer j with 2≤j≤k. Consider k+1. If it is prime, the single factor k+1 suffices. Otherwise, by the definition of a composite integer, k+1=ab with 2≤a,b<k+1, so a and b both lie between 2 and k. By the strong induction hypothesis, each is a product of primes. Combining these products gives a prime-factor product for k+1. Hence the claim holds for all n≥2.
q_proof_strong_induction_02.explanation: Strong induction is useful because the two factors of a composite number need not equal k, but both are smaller than the current number. This proves existence of a factorization and does not by itself establish uniqueness.
q_proof_strong_induction_02.grading_criteria: Base case: 15%; complete strong induction hypothesis: 20%; prime/composite cases and the ranges of the factors: 35%; combining factorizations and concluding: 30%.

q_proof_strong_induction_03.title: Representing consecutive integers with two denominations
q_proof_strong_induction_03.statement: Only tickets of denominations 3 and 5 may be used, with a nonnegative integer number of each. Use strong induction to prove that every integer n≥8 can be written as 3a+5b, and then show that 7 cannot be so written.
q_proof_strong_induction_03.answer_text: Base cases: 8=3+5, 9=3+3+3, and 10=5+5. For any m≥11, assume every j with 8≤j<m has a representation. Since 8≤m−3<m, write m−3=3a+5b. Then m=3(a+1)+5b, where a+1 and b remain nonnegative. By strong induction, every n≥8 has a representation. For 7, if b≥2, then 5b>7; if b=0, then 7 is not divisible by 3; if b=1, the remainder 2 is not a nonnegative multiple of 3. Thus 7 cannot be represented.
q_proof_strong_induction_03.explanation: An inductive step subtracting 3 requires the three consecutive base cases 8, 9, and 10, or else 9 or 10 may not belong to an established chain. Proving impossibility for 7 requires excluding every possible b, rather than trying a few combinations.
q_proof_strong_induction_03.grading_criteria: The three base cases: 25%; strong induction and the valid range of m−3: 30%; adding one denomination-3 ticket and concluding: 20%; exhaustively excluding representations of 7: 25%.

q_proof_strong_induction_04.title: A closed form for a recurrence depending on two previous terms
q_proof_strong_induction_04.statement: An integer sequence satisfies a₁=1, a₂=3, and aₙ=aₙ₋₁+2aₙ₋₂ for n≥3. Use strong induction to prove that aₙ=(2^(n+1)+(−1)^n)/3 for every n≥1.
q_proof_strong_induction_04.answer_text: For n=1, (4−1)/3=1, and for n=2, (8+1)/3=3, matching both initial values. Let n≥3 and assume the formula holds for all 1≤j<n. Since n−1 and n−2 are both in this range, aₙ=[2^n+(−1)^(n−1)+2(2^(n−1)+(−1)^(n−2))]/3. The powers of 2 sum to 2^(n+1). Also, (−1)^(n−1)=−(−1)^n and (−1)^(n−2)=(−1)^n, so the signed terms sum to (−1)^n. Hence aₙ=(2^(n+1)+(−1)^n)/3. By strong induction, the formula holds for all n≥1.
q_proof_strong_induction_04.explanation: The recurrence uses two previous terms, so both initial values must be checked, and the inductive step must ensure n−2≥1. Division in the formula does not imply that the sequence is nonintegral; the proof establishes agreement with the integer recurrence.
q_proof_strong_induction_04.grading_criteria: Both initial values: 25%; the hypothesis range and valid use of both previous terms: 20%; simplifying powers and signed terms: 40%; the conclusion for the full range: 15%.

q_logic_truth_05.title: Commands cannot be answered true or false
q_logic_truth_05.statement: Which of the following sentences do not themselves assert truth or falsity in classical logic? Interpret variables and context as explicitly stated in each sentence. Select all correct options.

options.text: Please write 15 as the product of two positive integers.
How many positive divisors does 15 have?
There exists an integer k such that 15=3k.

q_logic_truth_05.explanation: B is a request and C is a question. A asserts a property of a fixed integer and is false; D is a complete existential statement and is true. A false statement can still be a proposition.
q_logic_truth_05.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting both B and C and neither A nor D.

q_logic_truth_06.title: Both free variables must be handled
q_logic_truth_06.statement: Over the integers, let R(x,y) mean x+y=5. After fixing x at 2, is R(2,y) already a closed proposition? Close it once by assignment and once by existential quantification, and determine the truth of both statements you give.
q_logic_truth_06.answer_text: It is not yet closed because y remains free. Assignment example: R(2,3) is true because 2+3=5. Existential closure: ∃y∈Z R(2,y) is true with witness y=3. Other valid complete assignments are acceptable; for example, R(2,0) is a false proposition.
q_logic_truth_06.explanation: Closure requires eliminating all free variables, rather than fixing just one. Closure by assignment and closure by quantification are different operations.
q_logic_truth_06.grading_criteria: Identifying the remaining free y: 30%; two valid closed statements with reasons for their truth values: 70%.

q_logic_truth_07.title: Distinguishing proposition status from truth and closing sentences
q_logic_truth_07.statement: Over the integers, compare A: ‘n+2=8’ with n unspecified; B: ‘6+2=8’; and C: ‘There exists an integer n such that n+2=8’. State whether each is a closed proposition and determine the truth of the closed propositions.
q_logic_truth_07.answer_text: A is an open sentence, not a closed proposition. B is a true proposition. C is also a true proposition, with witness n=6. B is closed by fixing an object; C is closed by existential quantification.
q_logic_truth_07.explanation: The same equation structure can produce a complete assertion in different ways. Do not confuse the free n in A with the quantified n in C.
q_logic_truth_07.grading_criteria: Classifying all three: 60%; the calculation for B and the witness for C: 40%.

q_logic_truth_08.title: A proposition cannot change value within one assignment
q_logic_truth_08.statement: Let p denote the fixed statement ‘the integer 26 is divisible by 2’. Someone assigns true to the first occurrence of p and false to the second within the same logical assignment, then claims p∧¬p can be true. Explain the error and give the formula's truth value.
q_logic_truth_08.answer_text: The error is assigning different truth values to the same propositional letter within one assignment. Here p is true, so ¬p is false and p∧¬p is false. More generally, this formula is false under every fixed assignment.
q_logic_truth_08.explanation: An assignment acts on propositional letters, rather than on individual text occurrences. Repeated p must be consistent, and negation is computed from that same value.
q_logic_truth_08.grading_criteria: Identifying the consistency error: 50%; the current false value and general explanation: 50%.

q_logic_connectives_05.title: Not both passing differs from neither passing
q_logic_connectives_05.statement: Let p mean the first person passes and q mean the second person passes. Given that the first passes and the second does not, find the truth values of ‘not both people pass’ and ‘neither person passes’.
q_logic_connectives_05.answer_text: ‘Not both people pass’ is true and corresponds to ¬(p∧q). ‘Neither person passes’ is false and corresponds to ¬p∧¬q.
q_logic_connectives_05.explanation: With p true and q false, p∧q is false. But ¬p is false, so the conjunction of the two negations is also false. The sentences differ in the scope of negation.
q_logic_connectives_05.grading_criteria: Each symbolic formula: 20%; each truth value: 30%.

q_logic_connectives_06.title: Allowed truth rows under a sufficient condition
q_logic_connectives_06.statement: Suppose p is sufficient for q, so p→q is true. Which (p,q) truth-value combinations remain possible? 1 denotes true and 0 false.
q_logic_connectives_06.explanation: Material implication excludes only row 10, with a true antecedent and a false consequent. Rows 00, 01, and 11 all make p→q true and hence remain possible.
q_logic_connectives_06.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting all of A, B, D and not C.

q_logic_connectives_07.title: One-way and two-way registration conditions
q_logic_connectives_07.statement: Let p mean registration succeeds, q mean the documents are complete, and r mean the fee has been paid. Formalize ‘successful registration requires complete documents and payment’ and ‘registration succeeds if and only if the documents are complete and the fee is paid’, and explain the difference.
q_logic_connectives_07.answer_text: The first is p→(q∧r); the second is p↔(q∧r). The first gives only necessary conditions for success; the second also guarantees that q∧r suffices for success. The assignment p=0,q=r=1 satisfies the first but not the second.
q_logic_connectives_07.explanation: ‘Requires’ gives no sufficient guarantee of success; ‘if and only if’ requires both directions.
q_logic_connectives_07.grading_criteria: The two formulas: 60%; their difference and a distinguishing assignment: 40%.

q_logic_connectives_08.title: Satisfying assignments for three conjoined conditions
q_logic_connectives_08.statement: Find every assignment (p,q,r) making F=(p∨q)∧(p→r)∧(q→¬r) true.
q_logic_connectives_08.explanation: p∨q requires at least one to be true. If p is true, r is true and q cannot be true, since that would also require r false; this gives 101. If p is false, q is true and hence r is false, giving 010. The two branches are exhaustive and both assignments check correctly.
q_logic_connectives_08.grading_criteria: Exhaustive cases: 40%; the two assignments: 40%; verification and explanation of completeness: 20%.

q_logic_truth_table_05.title: Can the conjunction's constraints hold together?

options.text: Not a propositional formula because no values have been assigned

q_logic_truth_table_05.explanation: If the conjunction were true, p would be true and q false, making p→q false, a contradiction. Thus there are no true rows and the formula is a contradiction.
q_logic_truth_table_05.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting only B.

q_logic_truth_table_06.title: Testing an inference of one disjunct
q_logic_truth_table_06.statement: Use truth-table counterexamples to test whether ‘p∨q, therefore p’ is valid. Give every assignment (p,q) that makes the premise true and the conclusion false.
q_logic_truth_table_06.answer_text: It is invalid. The unique counterexample is (p,q)=(0,1). A false conclusion requires p=0, and then making p∨q true requires q=1.
q_logic_truth_table_06.explanation: A counterexample must meet the conditions on both the premise and conclusion. At 00 the conclusion is false but the premise is also false, so it is not a counterexample to this inference.
q_logic_truth_table_06.grading_criteria: Invalidity: 20%; the unique counterexample and completeness argument: 60%; ruling out 00: 20%.

q_logic_truth_table_07.title: Classifying a formula by counting all assignments
q_logic_truth_table_07.statement: F=(p↔q)∧(q∨r) contains three distinct letters. Find all assignments making F true, count its true rows, and determine whether it is a tautology.
q_logic_truth_table_07.answer_text: The true assignments are 001, 110, 111, for a total of 3 rows. It is not a tautology.
q_logic_truth_table_07.explanation: p↔q requires p=q. If both are 0, q∨r forces r=1. If both are 1, r may be 0 or 1. Only 3 of the 8 rows are true, so the formula is satisfiable but not a tautology.
q_logic_truth_table_07.grading_criteria: Cases based on p=q: 30%; the three rows and their count: 50%; classification: 20%.

q_logic_truth_table_08.title: Checking a distributive law with a truth table
q_logic_truth_table_08.statement: In the order (p,q,r)=000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111, give the truth columns for A=p∨(q∧r) and B=(p∨q)∧(p∨r), and determine whether they are equivalent.
q_logic_truth_table_08.answer_text: Both columns are 0,0,0,1,1,1,1,1, so A and B are logically equivalent.
q_logic_truth_table_08.explanation: When p=0, both formulas equal q∧r and are true only on row 011. When p=1, both are true. These cases also provide a check on all eight rows.
q_logic_truth_table_08.grading_criteria: Both eight-row columns correct: 70%; complete coverage and equivalence conclusion: 30%.

q_logic_equivalence_05.title: Pushing nested negations inward one level at a time
q_logic_equivalence_05.statement: Transform ¬(p∨(q∧¬r)) into an equivalent formula whose negations apply only to propositional letters.
q_logic_equivalence_05.explanation: First obtain ¬p∧¬(q∧¬r). De Morgan's law then gives ¬p∧(¬q∨¬¬r), and eliminating double negation gives the result.
q_logic_equivalence_05.grading_criteria: Outer De Morgan step: 35%; inner De Morgan step: 40%; double negation: 25%.

q_logic_equivalence_06.title: The precise failure condition of a conditional
q_logic_equivalence_06.answer_text: ¬((p∧q)→r)≡¬(¬(p∧q)∨r)≡¬¬(p∧q)∧¬r≡p∧q∧¬r. The steps use implication elimination, De Morgan's law, double negation, and associativity.
q_logic_equivalence_06.explanation: Failure of a conditional requires the entire antecedent p∧q to hold while the consequent r fails; it is not enough that just one of p and q holds.
q_logic_equivalence_06.grading_criteria: Implication elimination: 30%; pushing negation inward: 45%; conclusion and named rules: 25%.

q_logic_equivalence_07.title: Simplifying after distributing a common component
q_logic_equivalence_07.statement: Use equivalence laws to simplify F=p∨(¬p∧q), with no → or ↔ in the result.
q_logic_equivalence_07.explanation: Distributing disjunction over conjunction produces the excluded-middle formula p∨¬p. The term ¬p∧q cannot simply be deleted to leave p.
q_logic_equivalence_07.grading_criteria: Correct distribution: 50%; excluded middle and identity simplification: 35%; result: 15%.

q_logic_equivalence_08.title: Distinguishing the converse and the contrapositive
q_logic_equivalence_08.statement: Among A=p→q, B=q→p, and C=¬q→¬p, determine which must be logically equivalent. Give an assignment showing why the others are not equivalent.
q_logic_equivalence_08.answer_text: A and C are equivalent because both simplify to ¬p∨q. B is generally not equivalent. With p=0,q=1, A and C are true but B is false.
q_logic_equivalence_08.explanation: The contrapositive both exchanges positions and negates them; merely exchanging antecedent and consequent gives the converse and does not preserve equivalence in general.
q_logic_equivalence_08.grading_criteria: Simplifying A and C: 50%; checking the counterexample: 35%; explaining the distinction: 15%.

q_logic_normal_form_05.title: Single literals can form both ordinary normal forms
q_logic_normal_form_05.statement: Assume a single literal can be a term. Which of these formulas, in their current syntactic form, are both DNF and CNF?
q_logic_normal_form_05.explanation: A can be viewed as a one-literal term or a one-literal clause. B is a single conjunction term, hence DNF, and also a conjunction of two single-literal clauses, hence CNF. C is DNF but is not currently in CNF; D contains implication.
q_logic_normal_form_05.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting both A and B and neither C nor D.

q_logic_normal_form_06.title: Constructing principal CNF from specified false rows
q_logic_normal_form_06.statement: Fix variable order (p,q,r). A formula is false exactly on rows 001 and 110 and true on the remaining six rows. Write its principal CNF.
q_logic_normal_form_06.explanation: Row 001 gives maxterm p∨q∨¬r, with every literal false there. Row 110 gives ¬p∨¬q∨r. Their conjunction excludes exactly those two rows.
q_logic_normal_form_06.grading_criteria: Each maxterm: 40%; conjoining the terms and explaining the excluded rows: 20%.

q_logic_normal_form_07.title: Adding an absent variable to principal DNF
q_logic_normal_form_07.statement: Fix the complete variable set as p, q, r. F=p∧q does not originally contain r. Find its principal DNF over all three variables.
q_logic_normal_form_07.explanation: F is true when p=q=1 and r is either 0 or 1. Alternatively, distribute F≡F∧(r∨¬r) to obtain two terms, each containing all three variables.
q_logic_normal_form_07.grading_criteria: Adding the excluded-middle term or listing the two true rows: 40%; the two minterms: 50%; explaining the complete variable set: 10%.

q_logic_normal_form_08.title: Reading the negated formula from principal DNF
q_logic_normal_form_08.statement: Use variable order (p,q). The principal DNF of F is (¬p∧q)∨(p∧q). Find the principal DNF and principal CNF of ¬F.
q_logic_normal_form_08.answer_text: The principal DNF of ¬F is (¬p∧¬q)∨(p∧¬q); its principal CNF is (p∨¬q)∧(¬p∨¬q).
q_logic_normal_form_08.explanation: F is true on 01 and 11, so ¬F is true on 00 and 10 and false on 01 and 11. Use the true rows for minterms and false rows for maxterms. Alternatively, first simplify F≡q and ¬F≡¬q, then add the missing p.
q_logic_normal_form_08.grading_criteria: Complementary truth set: 30%; each principal normal form: 35%.

q_logic_reasoning_05.title: Denying the antecedent is not a valid rule
q_logic_reasoning_05.statement: Is the inference “p→q; ¬p; therefore ¬q” valid? If not, give a counterexample assignment.
q_logic_reasoning_05.answer_text: It is invalid. Let p=0,q=1. Then p→q and ¬p are both true, but ¬q is false.
q_logic_reasoning_05.explanation: A false antecedent does not rule out the consequent holding for other reasons. This is not the valid rule of modus tollens.
q_logic_reasoning_05.grading_criteria: The validity judgment: 20%; the assignment and verification of all three truth values: 80%.

q_logic_reasoning_06.title: Reaching a common goal by cases on the premises
q_logic_reasoning_06.statement: Derive t from p∨q, p→r, q→s, r→t, and s→t, showing the case split.
q_logic_reasoning_06.answer_text: If p is true, p→r gives r, and r→t gives t. If p is false, p∨q forces q true; q→s gives s, and s→t gives t. The cases p true and p false cover every situation in which all premises are true, so t must be true.
q_logic_reasoning_06.explanation: The two branches need not have the same intermediate conclusion; each only needs to reach the common goal t through valid steps.
q_logic_reasoning_06.grading_criteria: The p branch: 35%; the non-p branch: 40%; coverage and conclusion: 25%.

q_logic_reasoning_07.title: A consequent is not guaranteed without affirming its antecedent
q_logic_reasoning_07.statement: Given only p→q and q→r, which conclusions necessarily follow?
q_logic_reasoning_07.explanation: A follows by hypothetical syllogism. C follows by contraposition of A. B is not guaranteed: p=q=r=0 makes both premises true but r false. D is not guaranteed: p=0,q=1,r=1 makes both premises true but q→p false.
q_logic_reasoning_07.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting both A and C and excluding B and D. Correct rules and counterexamples can earn reasoning credit.

q_logic_reasoning_08.title: Validity when the premises cannot hold together
q_logic_reasoning_08.statement: Under the classical definition of semantic validity, is “p; ¬p; therefore q” valid? Explain whether this means that every particular q has already been proved in reality.
q_logic_reasoning_08.answer_text: It is formally valid: no assignment makes both p and ¬p true, so there is no counterexample with all premises true and q false. This does not mean that arbitrary real-world assertions have been proved from reliable facts; the premises themselves cannot both be true.
q_logic_reasoning_08.explanation: Semantic consequence is a conditional truth-preservation relation. Unsatisfiable premises make that condition vacuously true, but a practical argument must also check whether its premises can hold together.
q_logic_reasoning_08.grading_criteria: Judging it valid by definition: 35%; explaining the absence of any row with all premises true: 40%; distinguishing the reliability of real-world premises: 25%.

q_predicate_domain_05.title: A ternary predicate takes three objects
q_predicate_domain_05.statement: Let D={0,1}, and let T(x,y,z) mean the integer equality x+y=z. Evaluate T(1,0,1) and T(1,1,0), and explain whether specifying T(1,y,1) has eliminated all free variables.
q_predicate_domain_05.answer_text: The first two values are true and false, respectively. T(1,y,1) still has free variable y: it is true for y=0 and false for y=1, so it is not yet a closed assertion.
q_predicate_domain_05.explanation: The three arguments enter the equation in their respective positions. Restricting variables to 0 or 1 does not require the sum of any two domain elements to lie in D.
q_predicate_domain_05.grading_criteria: Each of the two truth values: 25%; free y and the two assignments: 50%.

q_predicate_domain_06.title: Existence depends on whether the domain contains zero
q_predicate_domain_06.statement: Compare the truth value of “There exists x such that x²+x=0” over the positive integers and over the nonnegative integers. Give a complete reason for each domain.
q_predicate_domain_06.answer_text: It is false over the positive integers: for x≥1, x(x+1)>0, so it cannot be zero. It is true over the nonnegative integers, with witness x=0, since 0²+0=0.
q_predicate_domain_06.explanation: Changing the domain can add or remove available witnesses. The nonnegative integer 0 cannot serve as a witness in the positive-integer domain.
q_predicate_domain_06.grading_criteria: Excluding every object in the positive-integer domain: 55%; a valid witness in the nonnegative-integer domain: 45%.

q_predicate_domain_07.title: Checking quantifiers from a finite relation extension
q_predicate_domain_07.statement: Let D={0,1}, and suppose the complete set of true tuples for binary predicate R is {(0,0),(0,1),(1,1)}. Evaluate R(1,0), ∀x∃yR(x,y), and ∃y∀xR(x,y), giving witnesses or counterexamples.
q_predicate_domain_07.answer_text: R(1,0) is false. ∀x∃yR is true: for x=0 choose y=0, and for x=1 choose y=1. ∃y∀xR is true: choose the common witness y=1, since both R(0,1) and R(1,1) are true.
q_predicate_domain_07.explanation: Only the listed tuples are true. Choosing witnesses row by row and finding one common witness in a single column are different checks; this relation satisfies both.
q_predicate_domain_07.grading_criteria: The individual instance: 20%; each quantified formula with valid witnesses: 40%.

q_predicate_domain_08.title: Comparing different predicate interpretations on the same domain
q_predicate_domain_08.statement: Fix D={0,1}. Model M interprets R(x,y) as x=y, while model N interprets it as x≠y. Evaluate ∀xR(x,x) and ∃x∃yR(x,y) in both models.
q_predicate_domain_08.answer_text: In model M, the universal formula is true and the existential formula is true, witnessed by x=y=0. In model N, the universal formula is false because no object satisfies x≠x; the existential formula is true, witnessed by x=0,y=1.
q_predicate_domain_08.explanation: The domain alone does not determine a formula’s truth value; predicate interpretations are also part of a model. The witnesses for an existential formula can also differ between interpretations.
q_predicate_domain_08.grading_criteria: Each of the four truth values: 15%; corresponding witnesses or counterexamples and the distinction between interpretations: 40%.

q_predicate_quantifier_05.title: Different uses of a counterexample and a witness
q_predicate_quantifier_05.statement: Let D={0,1,2}, and let P(x) mean x²=x. Which statement about ∀xP(x) and ∃xP(x) is correct?
q_predicate_quantifier_05.explanation: P(0) and P(1) are true, providing existential witnesses. P(2) is false, providing a counterexample to the universal statement. Thus the universal statement is false and the existential statement is true.
q_predicate_quantifier_05.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing only B.

options.text: The universal statement is false and the existential statement is true
The universal statement is true and the existential statement is false

q_predicate_quantifier_06.title: Restricted quantifiers when nobody enrolled
q_predicate_quantifier_06.statement: The domain D contains three students. Let S(x) mean enrolled and P(x) mean passed. No student enrolled. Evaluate ∀x(S(x)→P(x)) and ∃x(S(x)∧P(x)). Do you need to know the specific interpretation of P?
q_predicate_quantifier_06.answer_text: The restricted universal statement is true and the restricted existential statement is false; no knowledge of P is needed. S is false for every object, making each implication true and each conjunction S∧P false.
q_predicate_quantifier_06.explanation: A nonempty full domain can have an empty restricted subset. “All enrolled students passed” does not assert that at least one student enrolled.
q_predicate_quantifier_06.grading_criteria: The two truth values: 50%; an object-by-object explanation and why P is not needed: 50%.

q_predicate_quantifier_07.title: Each object has a related object, but no object relates to all
q_predicate_quantifier_07.statement: Using a binary predicate R on the same nonempty domain, express “Every object is R-related to at least one object, but no object is R-related to every object.” Give an interpretation of R on D={0,1} satisfying it. R(x,x) is allowed.
q_predicate_quantifier_07.answer_text: (∀x∃yR(x,y))∧¬∃x∀yR(x,y). Take R to be equality. For each x choose y=x, making the first conjunct true. No x equals both 0 and 1, so the second conjunct is also true.
q_predicate_quantifier_07.explanation: The first quantifier chain allows the witness to depend on x. The second conjunct denies that a single object relates to every object; it does not say that each object has no relations at all.
q_predicate_quantifier_07.grading_criteria: The two quantifier structures: 50%; an explicit finite relation and verification of each part: 50%.

q_predicate_quantifier_08.title: Exactly one object satisfies a property
q_predicate_quantifier_08.statement: Without introducing a new quantifier symbol, use only ∀, ∃, =, and connectives to express “Exactly one object in the nonempty domain D satisfies P.” Explain why ∃xP(x) alone is insufficient.
q_predicate_quantifier_08.answer_text: ∃x(P(x)∧∀y(P(y)→y=x)). The outer existential guarantees at least one object satisfying P; the inner universal says every object satisfying P equals that witness, giving at most one. ∃xP(x) alone allows two or more witnesses and does not ensure uniqueness.
q_predicate_quantifier_08.explanation: Existence and uniqueness are different requirements. In a model where two objects satisfy P, the ordinary existential formula is true but the uniqueness formula is false.
q_predicate_quantifier_08.grading_criteria: The existence part: 30%; a correct universal uniqueness condition: 45%; explaining why mere existence is insufficient: 25%.

q_predicate_variable_05.title: Legal renaming does not reverse argument positions
q_predicate_variable_05.statement: Which formulas can be obtained from ∀x∃yR(x,y) solely by legal renaming of bound variables? Here u and v are fresh names.

q_predicate_variable_07.title: A vacuous outer quantifier and variable shadowing

q_predicate_reasoning_06.title: Conjoining a quantified formula with an independent statement

q_predicate_reasoning_07.title: A specified constant does not justify universal generalization
q_predicate_reasoning_07.statement: A derivation has only the assumption P(c), where c is a specified constant, but directly concludes ∀xP(x). Is this step valid? Give a counterexample on D={0,1}, and state the condition on choosing an object needed for universal generalization.

q_predicate_reasoning_08.title: Reasoning by cases for an arbitrary object, then generalizing
q_predicate_reasoning_08.statement: Given ∀x(P(x)∨Q(x)), ∀x(P(x)→R(x)), and ∀x(Q(x)→R(x)), prove ∀xR(x). Show the arbitrary choice of object, instantiation, and case split.

Since no special condition was imposed on a, universal generalization validly yields ∀xR(x).

q_predicate_reasoning_08.grading_criteria: Arbitrary object and instantiation: 35%; deriving R(a) by cases: 40%; valid generalization: 25%.

q_predicate_prenex_05.title: Prenex formulas may retain free parameters
q_predicate_prenex_05.statement: Is ∀u∃v(R(u,v,z)∧¬S(v)) in prenex normal form? Give its quantifier prefix, matrix, and free-variable set.
q_predicate_prenex_05.answer_text: Yes. Its prefix is ∀u∃v, and its matrix is R(u,v,z)∧¬S(v), which contains no quantifiers. Its free-variable set is {z}. A formula in prenex normal form need not be closed.

q_predicate_prenex_06.title: Moving a quantifier fails without the free-variable condition
q_predicate_prenex_06.statement: Someone rewrites A=(∃xP(x))∨Q(x) directly as B=∃x(P(x)∨Q(x)). Let D={0,1}, let P be false everywhere, let Q be true only at 1, and assign free x the value 0. Compare A and B, and identify the violated condition for moving the quantifier.

q_predicate_prenex_07.title: Prenex conversion of a universal antecedent and existential consequent

q_predicate_prenex_08.title: Prenex conversion of a quantified biconditional

q_proof_direct_contradiction_05.title: Proving a parity conclusion by contraposition
q_proof_direct_contradiction_05.statement: Use proof by contraposition to prove that for any integer n, if 3n+1 is even, then n is odd.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_05.answer_text: The contrapositive is: if n is not odd, that is, if n is even, then 3n+1 is not even. Take any even integer n and write n=2k for an integer k. Then 3n+1=6k+1=2(3k)+1 is odd. The contrapositive holds, so the original implication holds.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_05.explanation: The odd-even dichotomy makes “not odd” equivalent to even for integers. A proof by contraposition must clearly negate the consequent and antecedent of the original implication; it does not prove the converse.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_05.grading_criteria: The contrapositive: 35%; an integer parameter and the algebra: 45%; returning to the original claim: 20%.

q_proof_direct_contradiction_06.title: Proving transitivity of divisibility from its definition
q_proof_direct_contradiction_06.statement: Let a, b, and c be nonzero integers with a dividing b and b dividing c. Use a direct proof to show that a divides c.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_06.answer_text: Since a|b, some integer r satisfies b=ar. Since b|c, some integer s satisfies c=bs. Substituting gives c=(ar)s=a(rs). As rs is an integer, the definition of divisibility gives a|c. The objects were arbitrary, so this holds for all a, b, and c satisfying the hypotheses.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_06.explanation: A divisibility conclusion requires an integer quotient as a witness, here rs. Merely stating that divisibility is transitive does not replace the required proof from the definition.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_06.grading_criteria: The two integer quotients: 35%; substitution and combination: 40%; integrality and the defining conclusion: 25%.

q_proof_direct_contradiction_07.title: An exclusive parity conclusion from an odd sum
q_proof_direct_contradiction_07.statement: Use proof by contradiction to show that for integers a and b, if a+b is odd, exactly one of a and b is odd.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_07.answer_text: Keep the assumption that a+b is odd, and suppose a and b do not contain exactly one odd integer. By the odd-even dichotomy, there are only two cases. If both are even, write a=2r,b=2s, giving sum 2(r+s). If both are odd, write a=2r+1,b=2s+1, giving sum 2(r+s+1). In both cases the sum is even, contradicting the hypothesis that it is odd. Hence exactly one is odd.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_07.explanation: Negating “exactly one” must cover both zero and two odd integers; excluding only the both-even case is insufficient.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_07.grading_criteria: Correct negation and exhaustive cases: 35%; calculation in both cases: 45%; contradiction and conclusion: 20%.

q_proof_direct_contradiction_08.title: Classifying by odd parts to prove a pair exists
q_proof_direct_contradiction_08.statement: Choose any 5 distinct integers from {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}. Prove that two of them have a ratio equal to a positive integer power of 2. You may use contradiction and need not specify the chosen numbers.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_08.answer_text: Group every number by its odd part after removing all factors of 2: {1,2,4,8}, {3,6}, {5}, and {7}. Suppose no two chosen numbers have a ratio that is a positive integer power of 2. At most one can be chosen from each group: two distinct numbers in one group equal the same odd integer times different powers of 2, so the larger divided by the smaller is a positive integer power of 2. Four groups would then allow at most 4 choices, contradicting the selection of 5. Therefore the required pair exists.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_08.explanation: The groups must cover 1 through 8 and ensure that two numbers in the same group have the required ratio. Distinct integers have different exponents, so the ratio is not 2^0=1.
q_proof_direct_contradiction_08.grading_criteria: The complete four groups: 30%; the property within each group: 30%; the contradiction by counting and existence conclusion: 40%.

q_proof_induction_06.title: An incorrect auxiliary comparison in inequality induction
q_proof_induction_06.statement: Someone attempts to prove 2^n>n² for every n≥1. From 2^k>k², they obtain 2^(k+1)>2k², then claim 2k²≥(k+1)² for all k≥1. Identify the earliest counterexample to the original claim and the gap in the auxiliary comparison. Then use induction to prove the correct claim “It holds for every n≥5.”
q_proof_induction_06.answer_text: The original claim first fails at n=2, since 4 is not greater than 4. The auxiliary comparison already fails at k=1, since 2<4. Correct proof: for n=5, 32>25. Take any k≥5 and assume 2^k>k². Then 2^(k+1)>2k²>(k+1)², because 2k²−(k+1)²=(k−1)²−2≥14>0. Induction therefore gives the claim for every n≥5.
q_proof_induction_06.explanation: A true base case is not sufficient: every additional inequality in the inductive step must hold over the full permitted range. Changing the starting point requires checking the new base case and step again.
q_proof_induction_06.grading_criteria: The two earliest failures with verification: 35%; the new base case: 15%; the new inductive step: 40%; the conclusion for the stated range: 10%.

q_proof_induction_07.title: An induction proof of a finite geometric sum
q_proof_induction_07.statement: Use mathematical induction to prove that for every integer n≥1, 1+3+3²+⋯+3^(n−1)=(3^n−1)/2.
q_proof_induction_07.answer_text: For n=1, the left side is 1 and the right side is (3−1)/2=1. Take arbitrary k≥1 and assume the first k terms sum to (3^k−1)/2. The first k+1 terms then sum to (3^k−1)/2+3^k=(3·3^k−1)/2=(3^(k+1)−1)/2. Thus the result holds for k+1, and mathematical induction establishes it for every n≥1.
q_proof_induction_07.explanation: The new term is 3^k, rather than 3^(k+1). The final exponent must agree with the number of terms.
q_proof_induction_07.grading_criteria: Base case: 20%; induction hypothesis: 20%; new term and simplification: 45%; conclusion for the full range: 15%.

q_proof_induction_08.title: Using the parity of consecutive integers in a divisibility induction
q_proof_induction_08.statement: Use mathematical induction to prove that n³−n is divisible by 6 for every integer n≥0.
q_proof_induction_08.answer_text: For n=0, the value 0 is divisible by 6. Take arbitrary k≥0 and assume k³−k=6t for an integer t. Then (k+1)³−(k+1)=(k³−k)+3k(k+1). One of the consecutive integers k,k+1 is even, so k(k+1)=2s for an integer s. The new expression is 6t+6s=6(t+s), divisible by 6. Induction proves the result for every n≥0.
q_proof_induction_08.explanation: Besides using the induction hypothesis, show that the new term 3k(k+1) is a multiple of 6; the factor 3 alone is insufficient.
q_proof_induction_08.grading_criteria: Base case and hypothesis: 30%; difference identity: 25%; even product of consecutive integers and divisibility: 35%; conclusion: 10%.

q_proof_strong_induction_05.title: Organizing strong induction as ordinary induction
q_proof_strong_induction_05.statement: Suppose P(n) starts at n₀, and define Q(k) to mean ‘P(n₀),P(n₀+1),…,P(k) all hold’. Explain how ordinary induction on Q implements strong induction, stating the base case and successor target.
q_proof_strong_induction_05.answer_text: Q(n₀) is simply P(n₀). Assuming Q(k) provides all statements P from n₀ through k. Use the successor argument of strong induction to derive P(k+1), then combine it with Q(k) to obtain Q(k+1). Ordinary induction on Q establishes every Q(k), hence every P(n).
q_proof_strong_induction_05.explanation: The strong induction hypothesis can be packaged as a stronger conjunction. It allows no use of future indices and is not a stronger proof axiom than ordinary induction.
q_proof_strong_induction_05.grading_criteria: The base case for Q: 25%; deriving Q(k+1) from Q(k): 50%; conclusion for all P: 25%.

q_proof_strong_induction_06.title: Constructing a binary power sum using a smaller quotient
q_proof_strong_induction_06.statement: Use strong induction to prove that every positive integer n is a sum of distinct nonnegative integer powers of 2. Uniqueness is not required.
q_proof_strong_induction_06.answer_text: For n=1, use 2^0. Let n≥2 and assume the result holds for every 1≤j<n. Write n=2m+r with r∈{0,1}; then 1≤m<n. By the hypothesis, m is a sum of distinct powers 2^e. Multiplying every term by 2 represents 2m as a sum of distinct powers 2^(e+1), all with exponent at least 1. If r=0, this represents n. If r=1, add 2^0, whose exponent differs from all existing ones. Thus n has the required representation, and strong induction proves the result for every positive integer.
q_proof_strong_induction_06.explanation: The key conditions are that m is smaller than n and nonzero, and that adding 2^0 does not repeat an existing higher power. The construction proves existence only and does not automatically prove uniqueness.
q_proof_strong_induction_06.grading_criteria: Base case and bounds on the smaller quotient: 30%; applying induction and shifting exponents: 35%; both remainders and distinctness: 25%; conclusion: 10%.

q_proof_strong_induction_07.title: An upper bound for a recursive sequence with two initial values
q_proof_strong_induction_07.statement: Let T₀=0, T₁=1, and Tₙ=Tₙ₋₁+Tₙ₋₂ for n≥2. Use strong induction to prove Tₙ≤2^(n−1) for every n≥1.
q_proof_strong_induction_07.answer_text: For n=1, T₁=1≤1; for n=2, T₂=1≤2. Let n≥3 and assume the result holds for every 1≤j<n. Then Tₙ≤2^(n−2)+2^(n−3)=3·2^(n−3)≤4·2^(n−3)=2^(n−1). Strong induction establishes the result for every n≥1.
q_proof_strong_induction_07.explanation: The claimed inequality covers only n≥1, so n=0 cannot be substituted directly into the induction hypothesis. Handle n=2 first, then for n≥3 both previous indices are at least 1.
q_proof_strong_induction_07.grading_criteria: Both base cases: 30%; valid hypothesis range and recurrence: 25%; inequality comparison: 35%; conclusion: 10%.

q_proof_strong_induction_08.title: Recursively classifying wins and losses when taking one or two
q_proof_strong_induction_08.statement: Two players alternate removing 1 or 2 counters from a pile of n counters and cannot remove more than remain. Whoever takes the last counter wins; a player with no counters at the start of their turn loses. Both play optimally. Use strong induction to prove that the first player wins if and only if n is not a multiple of 3, allowing n=0.
q_proof_strong_induction_08.answer_text: At n=0 the first player has no move and loses; at n=1 or 2 the first player takes the whole pile and wins. Let n≥3 and assume the classification holds for smaller piles. If n is a multiple of 3, removing 1 or 2 leaves remainders 2 or 1 modulo 3 respectively. Both are winning positions for the next player by the hypothesis, so the current player has no winning move. If n has remainder 1 modulo 3, remove 1 to leave a multiple of 3. If its remainder is 2, remove 2 to leave a multiple of 3. Both remaining piles are smaller and losing for the opponent by the hypothesis, so the current player can force a win. The three cases cover every n, completing strong induction.
q_proof_strong_induction_08.explanation: A losing position requires every legal move to give the opponent a winning position. A winning position requires just one move that gives the opponent a losing position. Do not reverse these quantifiers.
q_proof_strong_induction_08.grading_criteria: Base cases 0,1,2: 20%; all moves from multiples of 3: 30%; strategies for remainders 1 and 2: 20% each; strong induction and conclusion: 10%.

q_logic_equivalence_09.title: Applying absorption to an entire compound formula
q_logic_equivalence_09.statement: Use equivalence laws to simplify F=(p∨q)∧((p∨q)∨r), and explain the role of the common subformula.
q_logic_equivalence_09.answer_text: Let A=p∨q. Then F=A∧(A∨r)≡A≡p∨q by absorption.

q_set_operation_01.title: Differences and symmetric difference of finite sets
q_set_operation_01.explanation: The common elements of A and B are 2 and 6. Removing them from each set gives the two differences, whose union is the symmetric difference. The union is {1,2,3,4,6}, missing only 5 from the given universe.
q_set_operation_01.grading_criteria: Both differences must exclude the common elements; the symmetric difference must not contain 2 or 6; the complement must be taken relative to the given U.

q_set_operation_02.statement: Let A={1,2}. Which statements are correct?
q_set_operation_02.explanation: The empty set is a subset of every set, so A is correct. A has only elements 1 and 2, not the empty set, so B is false. The element 1 of {1} belongs to A, so C is correct. The elements of P(A) are all subsets of A, including A itself, so D is correct.

q_set_operation_03.title: Registration counts for two activities
q_set_operation_03.statement: A class has 40 students. Of these, 24 register for programming, 18 for mathematics, and 10 for both. Find how many register for at least one activity, exactly one activity, and neither activity.
q_set_operation_03.answer_text: At least one: 32 students; exactly one: 22 students; neither: 8 students.
q_set_operation_03.explanation: Let A and B be the two registration sets. |A∪B|=24+18−10=32. Exactly one has size (24−10)+(18−10)=22, or 32−10=22. Neither has size 40−32=8.
q_set_operation_03.grading_criteria: Use the union, symmetric difference, and complement in the universe for the three counts respectively. Do not use 24+18−10 for exactly one.

q_set_operation_04.title: An identity for power sets and intersection
q_set_operation_04.statement: For arbitrary sets A and B, prove P(A∩B)=P(A)∩P(B).
q_set_operation_04.answer_text: For any set X, X∈P(A∩B) ⇔ X⊆A∩B ⇔ X⊆A and X⊆B ⇔ X∈P(A) and X∈P(B) ⇔ X∈P(A)∩P(B). Therefore the two sets are equal.
q_set_operation_04.explanation: Elements of a power set are themselves sets. Take an arbitrary set X and expand the definitions of power set, subset, and intersection in turn. The proof applies whether A and B are finite or empty.
q_set_operation_04.grading_criteria: The argument must concern a set X; give both inclusions or an equivalence chain, clearly distinguishing ∈ from ⊆.

q_relation_cartesian_01.title: Listing a Cartesian product
q_relation_cartesian_01.statement: Let A={0,1} and B={a,b,c}. List A×B and find its number of elements.
q_relation_cartesian_01.explanation: Each element of A pairs with all three elements of B. The left component comes from A and the right from B, giving 2×3=6 ordered pairs.
q_relation_cartesian_01.grading_criteria: List all six pairs in the correct component order; do not include pairs such as (a,0) in A×B.

q_relation_cartesian_02.title: Counting relations from Cartesian-product size
q_relation_cartesian_02.statement: Finite set A has 2 elements and B has 3. There are ____ binary relations from A to B, of which ____ is/are the empty relation.
q_relation_cartesian_02.explanation: A×B has 6 elements. A relation is any subset of this set of 6 ordered pairs. Each pair may be selected or omitted, so there are 2^6=64 relations. Omitting every pair yields exactly one empty relation.
q_relation_cartesian_02.grading_criteria: The first blank requires the power-set size, rather than 2×3; the second must identify exactly one empty relation.

q_relation_cartesian_03.title: Identifying valid binary relations
q_relation_cartesian_03.statement: Let A={0,1} and B={a,b}. Which sets are binary relations from A to B?
q_relation_cartesian_03.explanation: Every pair in A and D has its left component in A and its right component in B. The empty set C is a subset of A×B. In B, the component types in (a,0) are reversed, so it does not belong to A×B. D is not single-valued, but this does not prevent it from being a relation.
q_relation_cartesian_03.grading_criteria: Select all of A, C, D and explain that a relation need not be a function.

q_relation_cartesian_04.title: Distributing a Cartesian product over intersection
q_relation_cartesian_04.statement: Prove that A×(B∩C)=(A×B)∩(A×C) for arbitrary sets A,B,C.
q_relation_cartesian_04.answer_text: Take any ordered pair (x,y). It belongs to the left side if and only if x∈A and y∈B∩C, meaning x∈A, y∈B, and y∈C. This is equivalent to (x,y) belonging to both A×B and A×C, hence to the right side. Therefore the equality holds.
q_relation_cartesian_04.explanation: The elements on both sides are ordered pairs. Fix a pair and expand the definitions of Cartesian product and intersection. Empty-set cases are included in the same proof.
q_relation_cartesian_04.grading_criteria: Prove both directions or give a full equivalence chain; comparing element counts only in the finite case is insufficient.

q_relation_operation_01.title: The order of relation composition
q_relation_operation_01.statement: On A={1,2,3}, let R={(1,2),(2,3)} and S={(2,1),(3,2)}. Use the convention that S∘R means first R, then S. Find S∘R and R∘S.
q_relation_operation_01.explanation: First R then S gives 1→2→1 and 2→3→2, yielding the first two pairs. First S then R gives 2→1→2 and 3→2→3, yielding the other two pairs. The different results show that relation composition is generally not commutative.
q_relation_operation_01.grading_criteria: Both compositions must use a shared intermediate element. List each result rather than merely saying they differ.

q_relation_operation_02.title: An inverse relation differs from a complement relation
q_relation_operation_02.statement: Let A={1,2,3} and R={(1,2),(1,3),(3,3)}. Find the inverse R⁻¹ and the complement R^c relative to A×A.
q_relation_operation_02.explanation: The inverse swaps the two components of each pair and thus has three elements. The complement removes the three pairs in R from the nine pairs in A×A and thus has six elements. Their definitions and sizes generally differ.
q_relation_operation_02.grading_criteria: Retain (3,3) in the inverse. The complement must exclude all three original pairs of R and specify its universe as A×A.

q_relation_operation_03.title: Relation powers express reachability of exactly a given length
q_relation_operation_03.statement: Let A={a,b,c} and R={(a,b),(b,c),(c,a),(a,c)}, with R²=R∘R and R³=R∘R². Find R² and |R³|. Relation chains may repeat vertices.
q_relation_operation_03.explanation: Two-step chains give a→a, a→c, b→a, c→b, c→c. Appending another R edge gives R³={(a,a),(a,b),(a,c),(b,b),(b,c),(c,a),(c,c)}, with 7 ordered pairs. A pair of endpoints is counted only once even if multiple chains realize it.
q_relation_operation_03.grading_criteria: List all five pairs of R². Justify the seven pairs of R³ or equivalent row-by-row reachability; the number of chains is not the size of the relation.

q_relation_operation_04.title: Reversing order when taking the inverse of a composition
q_relation_operation_04.statement: Let R⊆A×B and S⊆B×C, where S∘R means first R, then S. Prove (S∘R)⁻¹=R⁻¹∘S⁻¹.
q_relation_operation_04.answer_text: Take any c∈C and a∈A. (c,a)∈(S∘R)⁻¹ ⇔ (a,c)∈S∘R ⇔ there exists b∈B with (a,b)∈R and (b,c)∈S ⇔ there exists b∈B with (c,b)∈S⁻¹ and (b,a)∈R⁻¹ ⇔ (c,a)∈R⁻¹∘S⁻¹. Therefore the relations are equal.
q_relation_operation_04.explanation: Taking inverses reverses a chain a→b→c to c→b→a, so the composition order reverses. Both sides are relations from C to A, with matching types.
q_relation_operation_04.grading_criteria: State that the intermediate element still belongs to B. Prove both inclusions and keep the composition order correct.

q_relation_property_01.title: Partial self-loops versus reflexivity
q_relation_property_01.statement: On A={1,2,3}, let R={(1,1),(2,2),(1,2)}. Determine whether R is reflexive and whether it is irreflexive. If only adding pairs is allowed, what is the smallest set of pairs to add to make it reflexive?
q_relation_property_01.answer_text: R is neither reflexive nor irreflexive. Adding only (3,3) makes it reflexive.
q_relation_property_01.explanation: Reflexivity requires all three diagonal pairs, but (3,3) is absent. Irreflexivity requires no diagonal pairs, whereas (1,1) and (2,2) are present. Adding the only missing diagonal pair, (3,3), establishes reflexivity, and every reflexive superrelation must contain it.
q_relation_property_01.grading_criteria: Give a witness for the failure of each property and identify the unique diagonal pair whose addition is minimally required.

q_relation_property_02.title: Vacuous truth in the empty relation
q_relation_property_02.statement: On the nonempty set A={x,y}, let R=∅. Which properties hold?
q_relation_property_02.explanation: The empty relation lacks (x,x) and (y,y), so it is not reflexive. The antecedents of symmetry, antisymmetry, and transitivity require ordered pairs in R. Since there are none, no instance violates these implications.
q_relation_property_02.grading_criteria: Select exactly B,C,D. Explain that nonempty A causes reflexivity to fail, while the other three hold because there are no counterexamples.

q_relation_property_03.title: Failure of symmetry does not imply antisymmetry
q_relation_property_03.statement: Someone claims: 'Every relation that is not symmetric must be antisymmetric.' Give a counterexample on A={1,2,3}, and identify explicit witnesses for both failures.
q_relation_property_03.answer_text: Take R={(1,2),(2,1),(2,3)}. Symmetry fails because (2,3) is present but (3,2) is absent. Antisymmetry also fails because 1≠2 and both (1,2),(2,1) belong to R.
q_relation_property_03.explanation: Failure of symmetry needs an edge missing its reverse; failure of antisymmetry needs a bidirectional pair of distinct elements. Both kinds of witness can occur in one relation. The different technical term 'asymmetric relation' is not introduced here.
q_relation_property_03.grading_criteria: Give an explicit relation and separate witnesses for failure of symmetry and antisymmetry; property names alone are insufficient.

q_relation_property_04.title: Is a union of transitive relations transitive?
q_relation_property_04.statement: Must R∪S be transitive when R and S are transitive relations on the same set? Give a proof or a minimal explicit counterexample, and check R and S individually for transitivity.
q_relation_property_04.answer_text: No. On A={1,2,3}, take R={(1,2)}, S={(2,3)}. Each has no composable pair of edges and is transitive. Their union contains (1,2),(2,3) but not (1,3), so it is not transitive.
q_relation_property_04.explanation: The two antecedent edges of transitivity may come from different relations. Separate transitivity does not constrain such mixed two-step chains, so union does not preserve transitivity.
q_relation_property_04.grading_criteria: Verify that both relations in the counterexample are themselves transitive and identify the missing pair (1,3) in their union.

q_relation_equivalence_01.title: Equivalence classes modulo three
q_relation_equivalence_01.statement: On A={0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}, define aRb if and only if 3 divides a−b. List all distinct equivalence classes and find |R|.
q_relation_equivalence_01.explanation: Classes are determined by remainders modulo 3. Each contains 3 elements and contributes all 3² within-class ordered pairs. No pairs join different classes, so |R|=3×9=27.
q_relation_equivalence_01.grading_criteria: List three distinct classes covering A. Count pairs by summing squared class sizes and include diagonal pairs.

q_relation_equivalence_02.title: Recognizing partitions
q_relation_equivalence_02.statement: Let A={1,2,3,4}. Which families are partitions of A?
q_relation_equivalence_02.explanation: In A and C, blocks are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, and cover A. The first two blocks of B overlap at 2. D omits 4 from its union.
q_relation_equivalence_02.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,C and identify B's overlapping element and D's omitted element.

q_relation_equivalence_03.title: Classifying binary strings by weight
q_relation_equivalence_03.statement: Let A be all binary strings of length 4. Two strings are equivalent when they contain the same number of 1s. Find the number of classes, each class size, and the total number of ordered pairs in the equivalence relation.
q_relation_equivalence_03.answer_text: There are 5 classes, indexed by 0,1,2,3,4 ones, with sizes 1,4,6,4,1. The total number of ordered pairs is 70.
q_relation_equivalence_03.explanation: A string with k ones chooses k of four positions, giving C(4,0),C(4,1),C(4,2),C(4,3),C(4,4) strings. Only strings of equal weight are related, so the relation size is 1²+4²+6²+4²+1²=70.
q_relation_equivalence_03.grading_criteria: Give all 5 classes and their sizes, then count ordered pairs within classes; simply adding the 16 strings is insufficient.

q_relation_equivalence_04.title: Relation inclusion and partition refinement
q_relation_equivalence_04.statement: Let R,S be equivalence relations on A. Prove that R⊆S if and only if every R-class is contained in some S-class.
q_relation_equivalence_04.answer_text: If R⊆S, then for every a, x∈[a]_R implies xRa, hence xSa, so [a]_R⊆[a]_S. Conversely, suppose every R-class lies in an S-class. If aRb, then a,b are in the same R-class and thus the same S-class, so aSb. Therefore R⊆S.
q_relation_equivalence_04.explanation: Fewer allowed links generally give a finer partition. The converse must use that all elements of one R-class lie in one S-class, rather than choosing separate classes for each element.
q_relation_equivalence_04.grading_criteria: Prove both directions and explain why containment of an R-class makes any two of its elements S-related. The statement also holds when A is empty.

q_relation_order_01.title: Covers in a divisibility poset
q_relation_order_01.statement: Order A={1,2,3,6,12} by divisibility. List every covering pair (a,b), where b covers a, and give the least and greatest elements.
q_relation_order_01.answer_text: The covering pairs are (1,2),(1,3),(2,6),(3,6),(6,12). The least element is 1 and the greatest is 12.
q_relation_order_01.explanation: For example, 2|12, but 6 is an intermediate element with 2|6|12, so (2,12) is not a cover. The number 1 divides every element, and every element divides 12.
q_relation_order_01.grading_criteria: Remove all comparisons obtainable through intermediate elements when listing covers. State least and greatest relative to the given set and divisibility relation.

q_relation_order_02.title: Bounds in a power-set poset
q_relation_order_02.statement: Let U={a,b,c} and order P(U) by inclusion. For S={{a},{b}}, find all upper bounds, all lower bounds, the least upper bound, and the greatest lower bound.
q_relation_order_02.answer_text: Upper bounds: {a,b}, {a,b,c}. The only lower bound is ∅. The least upper bound is {a,b}; the greatest lower bound is ∅.
q_relation_order_02.explanation: An upper bound must contain both a and b, giving {a,b} or {a,b,c}. A lower bound must lie in both {a} and {b}, so it can only be empty. Union gives the least upper bound and intersection the greatest lower bound.
q_relation_order_02.grading_criteria: Distinguish bounds, which are elements of P(U), from the family S. List all bounds rather than only the two optimal ones.

q_relation_order_03.title: Minimal and maximal need not mean least and greatest
q_relation_order_03.statement: Order A={2,3,6,10} by divisibility. Which statements are correct?
q_relation_order_03.explanation: Both 2 and 3 have no strictly smaller divisor in A and are minimal. Both 6 and 10 have no strictly greater multiple in A and are maximal. Since 3 divides neither 2 nor 10, it is not least. Since 10 does not divide 6, 6 is not greatest. In fact there is neither a least nor a greatest element.
q_relation_order_03.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,C and use incomparable elements to explain why B,D fail.

q_relation_order_04.title: A unique minimal element and finiteness
q_relation_order_04.statement: Prove that a nonempty finite poset with exactly one minimal element m has m as its least element. Then show that the conclusion can fail without finiteness.
q_relation_order_04.answer_text: Take any x. If x is not minimal, choose a strictly smaller element. Finiteness makes this descent terminate at a minimal element, necessarily m, so m≤x. As x was arbitrary, m is least. For an infinite counterexample, take A=Z∪{a}, with the usual order on integers and a comparable only to itself. The integer chain has no minimal element, so a is the unique minimal element. It is incomparable with every integer and is not least.
q_relation_order_04.explanation: A finite poset has no infinite strictly descending chain, so a minimal element lies below every element. In an infinite poset, some branches may descend forever with no minimal element, and the unique existing minimal element need not lie below them.
q_relation_order_04.grading_criteria: Explain why descent terminates and how uniqueness is used. Check that the infinite example is a poset, has exactly one minimal element, and has no least element.

q_relation_closure_01.title: Two closures of a chain relation
q_relation_closure_01.statement: On A={1,2,3}, let R={(1,2),(2,3)}. Find R⁺ and R* and their cardinalities, where R⁺ is the transitive closure and R* the reflexive transitive closure.
q_relation_closure_01.explanation: The only two-step chain adds (1,3); there are no further new positive-length reachable pairs. Since R has no cycle, R⁺ contains no diagonal pairs. R* unconditionally includes all three diagonals.
q_relation_closure_01.grading_criteria: Distinguish positive-length reachability from reachability allowing length zero. Give both closures and both cardinalities correctly.

q_relation_closure_02.title: Closures of the empty relation
q_relation_closure_02.statement: On A={a,b}, let R=∅. Which statement about its closures is correct?
q_relation_closure_02.explanation: The empty relation is already symmetric and transitive, so these closures remain empty. Reflexive closure must add both diagonal pairs, and reflexive transitive closure is also exactly I_A.
q_relation_closure_02.grading_criteria: Select B and explain that transitivity does not unconditionally require adding diagonal pairs.

options.text: The symmetric closure of R is I_A
The reflexive closure of R is empty

q_relation_closure_03.title: Generating an equivalence relation from required links
q_relation_closure_03.statement: Let A={a,b,c,d,e}, R={(a,b),(b,c),(d,e)}. Find the classes of the least equivalence relation containing R and its size.
q_relation_closure_03.answer_text: The classes are {a,b,c} and {d,e}; the equivalence relation has size 3²+2²=13.
q_relation_closure_03.explanation: Symmetry adds reverse edges; transitivity relates all of a,b,c and all of d,e; reflexivity supplies every diagonal. No requirement connects the two groups, so leastness excludes cross-group pairs.
q_relation_closure_03.grading_criteria: Explain why every pair within a group is related and no link between groups is required. Include each group's diagonals in the count.

q_relation_closure_04.title: Proving the equivalence-closure construction
q_relation_closure_04.statement: Let R be any relation on A and S=R∪R⁻¹. Prove that E=S*=I_A∪S∪S²∪… is the least equivalence relation containing R. Composition here is right to left.
q_relation_closure_04.answer_text: E contains R and I_A, so it is reflexive. Since S is symmetric, every S-chain can be reversed, so E is symmetric. Finite S-chains can be concatenated, including zero-length chains, so E is transitive. For any equivalence relation T containing R, symmetry gives S⊆T, reflexivity gives I_A⊆T, and repeated transitivity gives S^k⊆T. Thus E⊆T, proving leastness.
q_relation_closure_04.explanation: Prove both the three equivalence properties and leastness. Including I_A is necessary: an element completely isolated in S cannot be related to itself by a positive-length chain.
q_relation_closure_04.grading_criteria: Verify reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, and containment in every equivalence superrelation. Do not omit leastness or isolated elements.

q_function_mapping_01.title: Functions require totality and single-valuedness
q_function_mapping_01.statement: Let A={1,2}, B={a,b}. Which relations are functions from A to B?
q_function_mapping_01.explanation: A and D assign exactly one output to each input 1,2. B assigns two distinct outputs to 1 and fails single-valuedness. C gives no value for 2 and fails totality. D remains a valid function despite equal outputs for two inputs.
q_function_mapping_01.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,D; identify failure of single-valuedness in B and totality in C.

q_function_mapping_02.title: Counting functions and empty-set cases
q_function_mapping_02.statement: There are ____ functions from a 3-element set to a 2-element set, ____ functions from the empty set to that 2-element set, and ____ functions from a nonempty set to the empty set.
q_function_mapping_02.explanation: Each of three inputs independently chooses either of two outputs, giving 2³=8. An empty domain has no inputs requiring assignments, so the unique empty relation is a function. A nonempty domain has an input, but an empty codomain offers no value, so no function exists.
q_function_mapping_02.grading_criteria: All three blanks must be correct. Do not count zero functions for an empty domain or one function from a nonempty domain to the empty set.

q_function_mapping_03.title: Images and set preimages
q_function_mapping_03.statement: Let A={1,2,3,4}, B={0,1,2}. A function f:A→B sends odd inputs to 0 and even inputs to 1. Find f(A), f({1,4}), and f⁻¹[{1,2}].
q_function_mapping_03.explanation: Inputs 1,3 map to 0 and 2,4 to 1. The codomain element 2 has no preimage, but f is still valid. The preimage collects inputs actually mapping to 1 or 2, hence {2,4}.
q_function_mapping_03.grading_criteria: Write images as output sets and preimages as input sets. The codomain B is not the image.

q_function_mapping_04.title: Preimages preserve intersections; images need not
q_function_mapping_04.statement: Let f:A→B and S,T⊆B. Prove f⁻¹[S∩T]=f⁻¹[S]∩f⁻¹[T]. Then give a function and subsets U,V of A for which f(U∩V)=f(U)∩f(V) fails.
q_function_mapping_04.answer_text: For any x∈A, f(x)∈S∩T ⇔ f(x)∈S and f(x)∈T, equivalent to x belonging to both preimages. This proves the preimage equality. For a counterexample, let A={1,2}, B={a}, f(1)=f(2)=a, U={1}, V={2}. Then f(U∩V)=∅, but f(U)∩f(V)={a}.
q_function_mapping_04.explanation: Preimage membership keeps the same input x, so the intersection conditions match directly. In an intersection of images, the same output may come from different inputs in U and V, with none in U∩V.
q_function_mapping_04.grading_criteria: Give a bidirectional elementwise proof of the preimage equality. Specify the counterexample function and subsets and compute both unequal sides.

q_function_injection_01.title: Properties of an affine integer map
q_function_injection_01.statement: Define f:Z→Z by f(n)=2n+1. Is it injective, surjective, or bijective? Give reasons.
q_function_injection_01.answer_text: f is injective but not surjective, hence not bijective.
q_function_injection_01.explanation: If 2m+1=2n+1, then m=n, proving injectivity. All outputs are odd, so, for example, codomain element 0 is unattained. Thus f is not surjective and therefore not bijective.
q_function_injection_01.grading_criteria: Prove injectivity algebraically. Disprove surjectivity using a specific unattained integer and explain why it is unattained.

q_function_injection_02.title: Surjections from four elements to three
q_function_injection_02.statement: Let |A|=4 and |B|=3. How many surjections A→B are there? Explain your counting method.
q_function_injection_02.explanation: All three outputs must occur, so their preimage sizes must be 2,1,1. Choose the output used twice in 3 ways, its two inputs in C(4,2)=6 ways, and assign the remaining inputs to the other outputs in 2 ways. Total: 3×6×2=36.
q_function_injection_02.grading_criteria: Ensure every output occurs and avoid double-counting. Giving 3^4=81 without removing nonsurjections is incorrect.

q_function_injection_03.title: Existence constraints for finite sets
q_function_injection_03.statement: Let A={1,2,3}, B={a,b}. Which statements are correct?
q_function_injection_03.explanation: Three inputs into two outputs force a collision, ruling out injectivity. The assignment f(1)=a,f(2)=b,f(3)=b is surjective. The identity on A is bijective. Since A,B have different sizes, no bijection connects them.
q_function_injection_03.grading_criteria: Select exactly B,C. Justify nonexistence of an injection and give a reason or explicit construction for a surjection.

q_function_injection_04.title: Injectivity and surjectivity on finite sets of equal size
q_function_injection_04.statement: Let A,B each have n elements, with n finite, and let f:A→B. Prove f is injective if and only if surjective. Give an infinite-set example showing finiteness is necessary.
q_function_injection_04.answer_text: If f is injective, its n inputs give n distinct outputs. Since B has only n elements, all are attained, so f is surjective. If f were surjective but not injective, two inputs would coincide in value and its image would have at most n−1 elements, unable to cover B, a contradiction. For an infinite example, on N₀={0,1,2,…}, f(n)=n+1 is injective but misses 0 and is not surjective.
q_function_injection_04.explanation: Finite output counting is essential. For n=0 the unique empty function is both injective and surjective. Infinite sets can be bijective with proper subsets, so the finite 'one fewer output' argument does not apply.
q_function_injection_04.grading_criteria: Prove both directions, explicitly using finite equal cardinality. Give the domain, codomain, and an omitted element in the infinite example.

q_function_composition_01.title: Computing composition from tables
q_function_composition_01.statement: Let f:{1,2,3}→{a,b} have f(1)=a,f(2)=b,f(3)=a; let g:{a,b}→{0,1} have g(a)=1,g(b)=0. Find the table for g∘f.
q_function_composition_01.explanation: Looking up f first gives a,b,a; looking up those values in g gives 1,0,1. The composite has domain {1,2,3} and codomain {0,1}.
q_function_composition_01.grading_criteria: Give all three correct values and apply f before g. The letters a,b are intermediate, not final outputs.

q_function_composition_02.title: Composition is not commutative
q_function_composition_02.statement: On Z define f(n)=n+2 and g(n)=3n. Find (g∘f)(n) and (f∘g)(n), and decide whether the functions are equal.
q_function_composition_02.explanation: Adding 2 then multiplying by 3 gives 3(n+2)=3n+6. Multiplying by 3 then adding 2 gives 3n+2. Their outputs differ by 4 for every integer input.
q_function_composition_02.grading_criteria: Calculate both orders explicitly. Justify inequality using the expressions or a specific input.

q_function_composition_03.title: Types and identity functions
q_function_composition_03.statement: Given f:A→B, g:B→C, h:C→D, which statements hold for all such functions?
q_function_composition_03.explanation: Pointwise, either grouping gives h(g(f(a))), proving A. The two identities act on f's outputs and inputs without changing them, proving B,C. In f∘g, an output of g lies in C and need not belong to A, so D need not be defined.
q_function_composition_03.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,B,C. Explain that D can fail because the types do not match.

q_function_composition_04.title: Executing a modulo-five process twice
q_function_composition_04.statement: Reduce all numbers to representatives {0,1,2,3,4} modulo 5. Define f(x)=x+1 (mod5), g(x)=2x (mod5), and T=g∘f. Find T²(x) and all x satisfying T²(x)=x, where T²=T∘T.
q_function_composition_04.answer_text: T²(x)=4x+1 (mod5). The only solution is x=3.
q_function_composition_04.explanation: T(x)=2(x+1)=2x+2 (mod5). Applying it again gives 2(2x+2)+2=4x+6≡4x+1. Equating this to x gives 3x≡4(mod5). Since 3×2≡1, x≡8≡3. Indeed T(3)=3 and hence T²(3)=3; the other four representatives fail.
q_function_composition_04.grading_criteria: Treat T² as composition, not the numerical square of T(x). Solve modulo 5 and give representatives in the specified set.

q_function_inverse_01.title: The inverse table of a finite bijection
q_function_inverse_01.statement: Let A={a,b,c,d} and f:A→A satisfy f(a)=c,f(b)=a,f(c)=d,f(d)=b. Write the table of f⁻¹.
q_function_inverse_01.explanation: The four outputs cover A without repetition, so f is bijective. Find each output's unique source by reversing the four correspondences.
q_function_inverse_01.grading_criteria: Give all four inverse values and explain bijectivity. Do not interpret an inverse function as taking numerical reciprocals.

q_function_inverse_02.title: Codomains and existence of inverses
q_function_inverse_02.statement: Let f:Z→Z, f(n)=2n, and use f⁻¹[T] for the preimage of T. Which statements are correct?
q_function_inverse_02.explanation: The original f misses odd integers and is neither surjective nor bijective, so A fails. With codomain 2Z every output has exactly one preimage, proving B. The sources of 2,6 are 1,3, proving C. Preimages are defined for every function and do not imply a two-sided inverse, so D fails.
q_function_inverse_02.grading_criteria: Select exactly B,C and distinguish preimage notation f⁻¹[T] from a two-sided inverse function.

options.text: Changing the codomain to the even integers 2Z makes the rule bijective
If f⁻¹[{2,6}] is defined, the original f has a two-sided inverse

q_function_inverse_03.title: Inverse order for composite bijections
q_function_inverse_03.statement: Work modulo 7 on Z₇={0,1,2,3,4,5,6}. For f(x)=x+2, g(x)=3x, find a formula for (g∘f)⁻¹(y) and compute (g∘f)⁻¹(1).
q_function_inverse_03.explanation: The composite sends x to 3x+6. Since 3 has inverse 5 modulo 7, solving y≡3x+6 gives x≡5(y−6)≡5y+5. Alternatively apply g⁻¹(y)=5y then f⁻¹(z)=z−2, giving 5y−2≡5y+5. At y=1 this is 10≡3.
q_function_inverse_03.grading_criteria: Execute g⁻¹ before f⁻¹. Use modular arithmetic rather than ordinary division, and reduce the final value to a specified representative.

q_function_inverse_04.title: Left and right inverses must agree when both exist
q_function_inverse_04.statement: Let f:A→B, l:B→A, r:B→A satisfy l∘f=id_A and f∘r=id_B. Prove l=r and that f is bijective.
q_function_inverse_04.answer_text: By associativity, l=l∘id_B=l∘(f∘r)=(l∘f)∘r=id_A∘r=r. If f(a)=f(a′), applying l yields a=a′, so f is injective. For any b∈B, f(r(b))=b supplies a preimage, so f is surjective. Thus f is bijective and l=r=f⁻¹.
q_function_inverse_04.explanation: A left inverse guarantees injectivity; a right inverse guarantees surjectivity. Associativity joins them when both exist. The proof also covers empty sets whenever all the given functions exist.
q_function_inverse_04.grading_criteria: Prove equality of the inverses and separately establish injectivity and surjectivity. Keep the domains and codomains of all composites consistent.

q_set_operation_05.title: Set elements can themselves be sets
q_set_operation_05.statement: Let A={∅,{1}}. Which statements are correct?
q_set_operation_05.explanation: A has exactly the elements ∅ and {1}, proving A,B. The only element of {∅} belongs to A, proving C. The integer 1 itself is not an element of A, so D fails.
q_set_operation_05.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,B,C and distinguish set elements from integers nested inside them.

q_set_operation_06.title: Recovering subset counts from a power-set size
q_set_operation_06.statement: A finite set X satisfies |P(X)|=16. Then |X|=____, X has ____ nonempty subsets, and ____ nonempty proper subsets.
q_set_operation_06.explanation: 2^|X|=16=2⁴ gives |X|=4. Excluding ∅ from the 16 subsets leaves 15; excluding X as well leaves 14 nonempty proper subsets.
q_set_operation_06.grading_criteria: Identify the excluded objects. Nonempty and proper exclude two different subsets.

q_set_operation_07.title: An elementwise proof of De Morgan's law
q_set_operation_07.statement: Let A,B⊆U, with complements relative to the fixed universe U. Prove (A∩B)^c=A^c∪B^c.
q_set_operation_07.answer_text: For any x∈U, x∈(A∩B)^c means x does not belong to both A and B, equivalently x∉A or x∉B, equivalently x∈A^c∪B^c. Thus the sets are equal.
q_set_operation_07.explanation: The proof uses the equivalence of 'not both' with 'at least one not'. Restricting x to U matters because complements contain only elements of the universe.
q_set_operation_07.grading_criteria: Give the full bidirectional chain of equivalences and use the same U for all complements.

q_set_operation_08.title: Counting overlapping registrations for three activities
q_set_operation_08.statement: A class has 60 students. Activities A,B,C have 32,28,20 registrants, respectively. |A∩B|=15, |A∩C|=10, |B∩C|=8, and 5 register for all three. Find the numbers registering for at least one, exactly two, and none.
q_set_operation_08.answer_text: At least one: 52; exactly two: 18; none: 8.
q_set_operation_08.explanation: Inclusion-exclusion gives |A∪B∪C|=32+28+20−15−10−8+5=52. Each of the three pairwise intersections counts each triple registrant once, so exactly two gives 15+10+8−3×5=18. None gives 60−52=8.
q_set_operation_08.grading_criteria: Pairwise intersections include the triple intersection. For exactly two, subtract the triple intersection three times, not once.

q_relation_cartesian_05.title: Reading a relation matrix in row and column order
q_relation_cartesian_05.statement: A relation from A={u,v} to B={0,1,2} has rows u,v and columns 0,1,2, with rows (1,0,1),(0,1,0). List R and state the matrix dimensions of R⁻¹.
q_relation_cartesian_05.answer_text: R={(u,0),(u,2),(v,1)}. The matrix of R⁻¹ has 3 rows and 2 columns, the transpose of the original 2-by-3 matrix.
q_relation_cartesian_05.explanation: Each 1 corresponds to the ordered pair (row element,column element). Inverting makes B the source and A the target, exchanging row and column sets and changing 2×3 to 3×2.
q_relation_cartesian_05.grading_criteria: Match all three pairs to the specified ordering. Explain that inverse-matrix rows belong to B and columns to A.

q_relation_cartesian_06.title: Counting relations with required and forbidden edges
