q_number_linear_congruence_03.statement: Each batch produces 12 parts. Packing all parts into boxes of 20 leaves exactly 8 parts. What is the minimum number of batches? The batch count must be a positive integer.
q_number_linear_congruence_03.explanation: Let x be the batch count. Then 12x≡8(mod 20). As gcd(12,20)=4, reduce to 3x≡2(mod 5). The inverse of 3 modulo 5 is 2, so x≡4(mod 5), with minimum positive solution 4. The 48 parts fill 2 boxes and leave 8.
q_number_linear_congruence_03.grading_criteria: Set up the correct congruence, reduce to x≡4(mod 5), choose 4 using positivity, and check.

q_number_linear_congruence_04.title: Solvability and the number of residue classes
q_number_linear_congruence_04.statement: Let m>0 and g=gcd(a,m). Prove ax≡b(mod m) is solvable if and only if g∣b, and explain why there are exactly g solution classes modulo m when it is solvable.
q_number_linear_congruence_04.answer_text: Necessity follows from ax−my=b. If g∣b, a/g and m/g are coprime, giving a unique solution x₀ modulo m/g. The solutions modulo m are exactly x₀+k(m/g), k=0,…,g−1.
q_number_linear_congruence_04.explanation: If a solution exists, ax−my=b for some integer y. Since g divides both terms on the left, g∣b. Conversely, if g∣b, put a′=a/g,b′=b/g,m′=m/g. Since gcd(a′,m′)=1, Bézout gives an inverse of a′ modulo m′, so a′x≡b′(mod m′) has exactly one solution class x₀. All integer solutions are x=x₀+km′. Taking k=0,…,g−1 gives g distinct classes modulo m; other k repeat them.
q_number_linear_congruence_04.grading_criteria: All three parts are required: necessity, coprime reduction with existence and uniqueness, and lifting to exactly g classes.

q_number_linear_congruence_05.title: Which right sides permit a solution?
q_number_linear_congruence_05.statement: For 8x≡b(mod12), which listed values of b make the congruence solvable?
q_number_linear_congruence_05.explanation: gcd(8,12)=4, so solvability is equivalent to 4∣b. Among 1,4,6,8, only 4 and 8 satisfy it.
q_number_linear_congruence_05.grading_criteria: Choose B,D only; the gcd 4 determines the answer.

q_number_linear_congruence_06.title: Finding a modular inverse
q_number_linear_congruence_06.statement: Find the multiplicative inverse of 7 modulo 26, using a representative from 0 through 25, and check the product.
q_number_linear_congruence_06.grading_criteria: Include a correct extended Euclidean or equivalent calculation, standard representative 15, and product verification.

q_number_linear_congruence_07.title: Solving a congruence with a right side other than 1
q_number_linear_congruence_07.explanation: gcd(5,18)=1, so 5 is invertible. As 5·11=55≡1(mod18), multiplication by 11 gives x≡77≡5(mod18). Every solution lies in this class; check 5·5=25≡7.
q_number_linear_congruence_07.grading_criteria: Find the correct inverse, reduce to 5, and give all integer solutions with period 18.

q_number_linear_congruence_08.title: Combining congruences with a finite range
q_number_linear_congruence_08.statement: Find all integers x satisfying 6x≡9(mod15) and 1≤x≤20.
q_number_linear_congruence_08.explanation: gcd(6,15)=3 divides 9, so reduce to 2x≡3(mod5). The inverse of 2 modulo 5 is 3, giving x≡9≡4(mod5). Between 1 and 20 this progression gives exactly 4,9,14,19.
q_number_linear_congruence_08.grading_criteria: First obtain the complete congruence class, then accurately select the four values in range.

q_number_prime_01.title: Identifying a prime
q_number_prime_01.statement: Which positive integer below is prime?
q_number_prime_01.explanation: 49=7² and 91=7·13, while 1 is not prime by definition. For 53, test only the primes 2,3,5,7 up to √53. None divides 53, so it is prime.
q_number_prime_01.grading_criteria: Choose C; explaining the trial-division bound and rejecting the other choices may support process feedback.

q_number_prime_02.title: Prime factorization and counting positive divisors
q_number_prime_02.statement: Express 756 as a product of prime powers and find its number of positive divisors.
q_number_prime_02.explanation: Repeated division by 2 leaves 189, and 189=3³·7, so 756=2²·3³·7. Every positive divisor has form 2ᵃ3ᵇ7ᶜ with a∈{0,1,2}, b∈{0,1,2,3}, c∈{0,1}. Thus there are 3·4·2=24.
q_number_prime_02.grading_criteria: Half credit for correct prime factorization; half for the choices for each exponent and the result 24.

q_number_prime_03.title: Divisibility is closed under integer linear combinations
q_number_prime_03.statement: Let a,b,c be integers with a≠0, a∣b, and a∣c. Prove a∣(4b−3c).
q_number_prime_03.answer_text: Take integers u,v with b=au,c=av. Then 4b−3c=a(4u−3v), so a∣(4b−3c).
q_number_prime_03.explanation: There are integers u,v with b=au,c=av. Then 4b−3c=4au−3av=a(4u−3v). Since 4u−3v is an integer, the definition of divisibility gives the conclusion.
q_number_prime_03.grading_criteria: Full credit requires integer-multiple representations, correct substitution, and noting that the remaining factor is an integer.

q_number_prime_04.title: Why primes cannot be exhausted by a finite list
q_number_prime_04.statement: Prove there are infinitely many primes. Explain why the integer constructed has a prime factor absent from the assumed finite list.
q_number_prime_04.answer_text: Suppose all primes are p₁,…,pₖ and take N=p₁⋯pₖ+1. Since N>1 it has a prime factor q, but no pᵢ divides N. Thus q is absent from the list, a contradiction.
q_number_prime_04.explanation: Suppose the only primes are p₁,…,pₖ. Set N=p₁⋯pₖ+1>1. Prime factorization gives at least one prime divisor q of N. For every i, N has remainder 1 modulo pᵢ, so pᵢ does not divide N. Thus q is none of the listed primes, contradicting completeness of the list. There is no need, and no justification, to claim N itself must be prime.
q_number_prime_04.grading_criteria: Explain every step: the finite-list assumption, construction of N, existence of a prime factor, exclusion of that factor from the list, and contradiction.

q_number_prime_05.title: Proving transitivity from the divisibility definition
q_number_prime_05.statement: Let a,b,c be nonzero integers with a∣b and b∣c. Prove a∣c.
q_number_prime_05.answer_text: From b=au and c=bv, obtain c=a(uv), where uv is an integer.
q_number_prime_05.explanation: There are integers u,v such that b=au and c=bv. Substitution gives c=(au)v=a(uv). Since uv∈ℤ, the definition gives a∣c.
q_number_prime_05.grading_criteria: Give both integer-multiple representations and complete the substitution; arrows merely repeating the hypotheses are insufficient.

q_number_prime_06.title: Square-root trial division identifies a composite
q_number_prime_06.statement: Determine whether 221 is prime or composite and give a prime factor no greater than √221.
q_number_prime_06.answer_text: 221 is composite; 13≤√221 is a prime factor, and 221=13·17.
q_number_prime_06.explanation: 14²=196<221<225=15², so √221 lies between 14 and 15. Testing 2,3,5,7,11,13 finds that 13 divides 221 with quotient 17. Thus 221 is composite and 13 is in the required trial range.
q_number_prime_06.grading_criteria: Correct classification, a nontrivial factorization, and verification of the square-root bound are all required.

q_number_prime_07.title: Counting perfect-square divisors
q_number_prime_07.statement: Given 756=2²·3³·7, find all its positive perfect-square divisors.
q_number_prime_07.explanation: Every prime exponent in a perfect square must be even. The exponent of 2 can be 0 or 2, that of 3 can be 0 or 2, and that of 7 must be 0. The four choices give 1,2²=4,3²=9,2²·3²=36, with no others.
q_number_prime_07.grading_criteria: State that exponents must be even and list all four divisors without repetition or omission.

q_number_prime_08.title: Refuting an assertion that always produces primes
q_number_prime_08.statement: After checking several small nonnegative integers n, someone claims n²+n+41 is prime for every nonnegative integer n. Give a specific counterexample and explain why finitely many successful checks cannot prove the assertion.
q_number_prime_08.answer_text: Take n=40: 40²+40+41=1681=41² is composite. Finite checks do not cover all nonnegative integers.
q_number_prime_08.explanation: For n=40, the expression is 1600+40+41=1681=41·41, which has nontrivial factor 41 and disproves the universal assertion. Calculations at small n verify only those cases and cannot rule out composite values at unchecked n.
q_number_prime_08.grading_criteria: Give a valid n, correct arithmetic and composite factorization, and explain that a universal conclusion requires a general proof.

q_number_rsa_01.title: Choosing a public exponent for toy RSA
q_number_rsa_01.statement: For classroom demonstration only, toy RSA uses p=5,q=11. Which e satisfies the public-exponent requirement gcd(e,φ(n))=1? These parameters must not be used for real encryption.
q_number_rsa_01.explanation: n=55 and φ(n)=4·10=40. The gcds with 40 are 2 for e=2, 5 for e=5, 1 for e=7, and 10 for e=10. Thus only e=7 satisfies the condition.
q_number_rsa_01.grading_criteria: Choose C and check against φ(n)=40, not n=55.

q_number_rsa_02.title: One encryption and decryption with toy RSA
q_number_rsa_02.statement: Toy RSA uses p=5,q=11,e=3 and message m=7. Find the private exponent d with 0<d<40, the ciphertext c, and verify decryption. This is only a modular-arithmetic lesson, not secure encryption parameters.
q_number_rsa_02.explanation: φ(55)=40. From 3d≡1(mod 40), d=27 since 3·27=81. The ciphertext is 7³=343≡13(mod 55). Square-and-multiply gives 13²≡4,13⁴≡16,13⁸≡36,13¹⁶≡31(mod 55). Since 27=16+8+2+1, 13²⁷≡31·36·4·13≡7(mod 55), recovering the message.
q_number_rsa_02.grading_criteria: One third each for inverse d, encryption c, and modular-power verification of decryption; results must be in the appropriate modulus ranges.

q_number_rsa_03.title: Toy RSA when the message is not coprime
q_number_rsa_03.statement: Toy RSA uses p=3,q=11,n=33,e=3,d=7 and message m=3, which is not coprime to n. Compute encryption and decryption, and explain why Euler’s theorem modulo 33 cannot be applied directly to m. This is for teaching only.
q_number_rsa_03.answer_text: c=27 and 27⁷≡3(mod 33). Euler’s theorem cannot be used directly since gcd(3,33)=3.
q_number_rsa_03.explanation: The ciphertext is 3³=27. Since 27²≡3 and 27⁴≡9(mod 33), 27⁷≡9·3·27=729≡3(mod 33). Recovery still works for this noncoprime message. For a proof, both sides are 0 modulo 3; use Fermat’s little theorem modulo 11 and then CRT. Euler’s theorem a^φ(n)≡1 requires gcd(a,n)=1, which fails here.
q_number_rsa_03.grading_criteria: Include the ciphertext, square-and-multiply decryption, the failed coprimality condition, and an explanation using CRT.

q_number_rsa_04.title: Correctness of classroom RSA for all messages
q_number_rsa_04.statement: Let p,q be distinct primes, n=pq, and e,d positive integers with ed≡1(mod (p−1)(q−1)). Prove m^(ed)≡m(mod n) for every integer m, including messages not coprime to n. This concerns algebraic correctness of a teaching algorithm and is not a security argument for a real system.
q_number_rsa_04.answer_text: Work modulo p and q separately, distinguishing whether each divides m. In the nondivisible cases, ed−1 is a multiple of the prime minus 1, so apply Fermat’s little theorem. CRT then gives the result modulo pq.
q_number_rsa_04.explanation: Write ed=1+k(p−1)(q−1) for a nonnegative integer k. Modulo p, if p∣m then both m^(ed) and m are 0. Otherwise Fermat gives m^(p−1)≡1, so m^(ed)=m·(m^(p−1))^(k(q−1))≡m. Similarly modulo q, both sides are 0 if q∣m, and otherwise use m^(q−1)≡1. Since p,q are coprime, divisibility of m^(ed)−m by both implies divisibility by pq.
q_number_rsa_04.grading_criteria: For each prime modulus cover both divisibility cases, then combine by coprimality or CRT; citing Euler’s theorem modulo n alone is insufficient.

q_number_rsa_05.title: Another set of classroom key parameters
q_number_rsa_05.statement: Toy RSA uses distinct primes p=7,q=11 and public exponent e=7. Find n,φ(n), and the private exponent with 0<d<60. This is a classroom example and must not be used for real encryption.
q_number_rsa_05.grading_criteria: Give the modulus, Euler totient, and correct modular inverse.

q_number_rsa_06.title: A message divisible by a prime factor in classroom RSA
q_number_rsa_06.statement: Toy RSA uses n=55,e=3,d=27,m=5. Compute the ciphertext and check modulo 5 and modulo 11 that decryption recovers 5. This illustrates the teaching algorithm only, without addressing real security.
q_number_rsa_06.answer_text: The ciphertext is 15 and the decrypted residue is 5.
q_number_rsa_06.explanation: 5³=125≡15(mod55). Modulo 5, 15²⁷≡0, matching 5. Modulo 11, 15≡4 and 4¹⁰≡1, so 4²⁷≡4⁷. Since 4²≡5 and 4⁴≡3, 4⁷≡3·5·4=60≡5. The unique solution modulo 55 with residue 0 modulo 5 and 5 modulo 11 is 5, so decryption recovers 5.
q_number_rsa_06.grading_criteria: Correctly give ciphertext 15, checks modulo 5 and 11, and CRT combination to 5.

q_number_rsa_07.title: Algebraic demonstrations versus real encryption security
q_number_rsa_07.statement: Which statement correctly describes a classroom textbook-RSA example using small primes and no randomized padding?
q_number_rsa_07.explanation: The example verifies algebraic relations involving modular powers, inverses, and CRT, but small parameters are easily factored. The deterministic unpadded process also lacks the full security properties required in real systems. Classroom correctness calculations therefore cannot directly serve as a secure encryption scheme.
q_number_rsa_07.grading_criteria: Choose B; distinguish correctness, meaning recovery of messages, from security, meaning resistance to attacks.

options.text: Successful recovery on decryption proves suitability for real encryption.
It illustrates algebraic correctness but cannot directly be used as real secure encryption.
Small primes guarantee security as long as the private exponent is not written down.
Existence of a modular inverse itself makes factorization absolutely impossible.

q_number_rsa_08.title: Determinism of the classroom unpadded procedure
q_number_rsa_08.statement: Using the same toy public key n=55,e=3, will two direct calculations of mᵉ modn for integer message m=7 give the same ciphertext? Compute it and explain why this does not guarantee real cryptographic security.
q_number_rsa_08.answer_text: Both give 13. Direct textbook modular exponentiation is deterministic; correct decryption does not imply real encryption security.
q_number_rsa_08.explanation: For fixed m,e,n, exponentiation and remainder give a unique result: 7³=343≡13(mod55), so both ciphertexts are equal. There is no random step. This illustrates a teaching transform; invertibility alone does not establish resistance to attacks. Real systems additionally require standard encoding, randomization, and secure implementation; these toy parameters cannot be used directly.
q_number_rsa_08.grading_criteria: Include ciphertext 13 both times, the reason for determinism, and the distinction between correctness and real security.

q_count_basic_01.title: Mutually exclusive resource choices
q_count_basic_01.statement: A shelf has 4 distinct popular-science booklets and 3 distinct history booklets, with no overlap between the categories. How many ways are there to borrow exactly 1?
q_count_basic_01.explanation: Borrowing science and borrowing history are disjoint exhaustive alternatives. The sum rule gives 4+3=7; the task does not ask for one of each.
q_count_basic_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for B; 0 for any other choice.

q_count_basic_02.title: A passcode with nonrepeating digits
q_count_basic_02.statement: A passcode consists of 1 letter followed by 2 digits. Choose the letter from A,B,C and digits from 0,1,2,3,4. The two digits must differ, and the digit part may start with 0. Count the passcodes.
q_count_basic_02.explanation: There are 3 letter choices, 5 first-digit choices, and exactly 4 second-digit choices after excluding the chosen first digit. Each triple uniquely determines a code, so the product rule gives 3×5×4=60. Do not exclude leading 0 or identify different digit orders.
q_count_basic_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the 3 letters and 5 first digits, 4 for the 4 second digits and order, and 3 for 60.

q_count_basic_03.title: Conditions for counting principles
q_count_basic_03.statement: Let A,B be arbitrary finite sets. Which assertions always hold?
q_count_basic_03.explanation: The Cartesian product consists of ordered pairs, so A is correct even if A and B intersect. B ignores overlap. C describes a true partition, disjoint and exhaustive, permitting the sum rule. D is false: positions of successive choices are usually part of the result, so exchanging order need not give the same object.
q_count_basic_03.grading_criteria: 10 points for exactly A,C; 5 for omissions without wrong selections; 0 if any incorrect option is selected.

options.text: If objects are divided into pairwise disjoint exhaustive classes, their class sizes can be added.
The order of results from two steps can always be ignored.

q_count_basic_04.title: Pairing even- and odd-parity binary strings
q_count_basic_04.statement: Let n≥1 be an integer. Prove that exactly $2^{n-1}$ binary strings of length n have an even number of ones. Explain why the correspondence used omits and repeats nothing.
q_count_basic_04.answer_text: Flipping the first bit bijects strings with even and odd numbers of ones; each class has $2^{n-1}$ elements.
q_count_basic_04.explanation: Partition the 2^n length-n strings into E and O by even or odd number of ones. They are disjoint and exhaustive. Define f by flipping the first bit and keeping all other bits. This adds or removes one 1, so f maps E to O. Flipping again restores the original string, giving an inverse and hence a bijection. Thus |E|=|O|; the sum rule gives 2|E|=2^n, so |E|=2^(n−1). The assumption n≥1 ensures a first bit exists.
q_count_basic_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for the partition and total, 3 for the flip and parity change, 3 for invertibility, and 2 for the count and n≥1.

q_count_perm_comb_01.title: A review group without roles
q_count_perm_comb_01.statement: How many groups of 3 can be selected from 7 distinct volunteers if no roles are assigned?
q_count_perm_comb_01.explanation: The member set alone determines the group, without internal order. Compute C(7,3)=7×6×5/(3×2×1)=35. The count 7×6×5=210 counts the 6 orderings of each group separately.
q_count_perm_comb_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for A; 0 for other choices.

q_count_perm_comb_02.title: Both member categories must be represented
q_count_perm_comb_02.statement: A project has 5 engineers and 4 designers, all distinct. Select a group of 3 with no roles, including at least 1 person from each category. Count the groups.
q_count_perm_comb_02.explanation: Classify by engineer count: 1 engineer and 2 designers gives C(5,1)C(4,2)=5×6=30 groups; 2 engineers and 1 designer gives C(5,2)C(4,1)=10×4=40. These disjoint cases exhaust the valid groups, giving 30+40=70. With no roles, do not multiply by 3!.
q_count_perm_comb_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for complete case division, 3 for each combination product, and 2 for total 70.

q_count_perm_comb_03.title: Distinct arrangements of repeated labels
q_count_perm_comb_03.statement: Six labels read A,A,B,B,B,C. Equal letters are indistinguishable. How many distinct strings result from arranging them in a row?
q_count_perm_comb_03.explanation: Temporarily number equal labels. The 6 distinct labels have 6! arrangements. Removing numbers, every string has exactly 2!3! representations from the permutations of the two As and three Bs. Thus there are 720/(2×6)=60 strings. The denominator’s 1! for the single C can be omitted.
q_count_perm_comb_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for 6! labeled arrangements, 5 for explaining multiplicity 2!3!, and 3 for division and result 60.

q_count_perm_comb_04.title: A group-with-convener identity
q_count_perm_comb_04.statement: For 1≤k≤n, prove $k\binom nk=n\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ by counting. Specify the common objects counted by both sides.
q_count_perm_comb_04.answer_text: Both sides count selecting k of n people and designating one selected person as convener.
q_count_perm_comb_04.explanation: Let the people form an n-element set. Count pairs (S,c), where S is a k-element subset and c∈S. Choosing S first and c within S gives C(n,k)k. Choosing c from all n people first, then k−1 of the remaining n−1 to join S, gives nC(n−1,k−1). Both constructions biject to the same objects, so the counts agree. The range 1≤k≤n makes the choices meaningful.
q_count_perm_comb_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for specifying common objects, 3 for group then person, 3 for person then other members, and 1 for the conclusion and range.

q_count_binomial_01.title: Extracting a coefficient in a simple expansion
q_count_binomial_01.explanation: Producing x² requires exactly 2 of the 5 factors to contribute x and the others 1, so the coefficient is C(5,2)=10.
q_count_binomial_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for 10; identifying C(5,2) suffices, without a full expansion.

q_count_binomial_02.title: A specified term with a negative constant
q_count_binomial_02.explanation: Choose 4 of the 6 factors to contribute 2x and the remaining 2 to contribute −3. The coefficient is C(6,4)·2⁴·(−3)²=15×16×9=2160. The negative sign occurs an even number of times, giving a positive result.
q_count_binomial_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the combination count, 4 for the two power factors and sign, and 3 for 2160.

q_count_binomial_03.title: Sums of binomial coefficients
q_count_binomial_03.statement: Let n be a positive integer. Which identities hold for every such n?
q_count_binomial_03.explanation: A follows from (1+1)^n. B follows from (1−1)^n=0 for n≥1. For C, sum kC(n,k)=nC(n−1,k−1) over k to get n·2^(n−1), or differentiate (1+x)^n and set x=1. D fails at n=2: the left side is 1+4+1=6 but the right side is 4. The correct square sum is C(2n,n).
q_count_binomial_03.grading_criteria: 10 points for exactly A,B,C; 5 for omissions without wrong selections; 0 if any incorrect option is selected.

q_count_binomial_04.title: A two-group selection proof of the square sum
q_count_binomial_04.statement: For a nonnegative integer n, prove $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk^2=\binom{2n}{n}$. Give a complete combinatorial or coefficient-comparison argument.
q_count_binomial_04.answer_text: Choose n elements from the union of two disjoint n-element sets and classify by the number k chosen from the first.
q_count_binomial_04.explanation: Let A,B be disjoint sets of size n. Directly choosing an n-element subset of A∪B gives C(2n,n). Classify by the number k chosen from A; then n−k come from B, giving C(n,k)C(n,n−k)=C(n,k)². The cases k=0,…,n are disjoint and exhaustive, so their sum equals the total. For n=0, both sides equal 1, representing the unique empty selection.
q_count_binomial_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for the objects chosen from 2n elements, 3 for complete classification by k, 3 for each product and symmetry, and 2 for summation and the n=0 boundary.

q_count_pigeonhole_01.title: A guaranteed lower bound on label repetitions
q_count_pigeonhole_01.statement: Each of 15 cards has one of 7 labels. Regardless of the assignment, some label must occur at least how many times? Find the largest guaranteed integer.
q_count_pigeonhole_01.explanation: Divide cards into 7 label classes. If every class had at most 2 cards, there would be at most 14, so some class has at least 3. The distribution 3,2,2,2,2,2,2 has 15 cards and no class of size 4, so the largest guarantee is exactly 3.
q_count_pigeonhole_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for B; 0 for other choices.

q_count_pigeonhole_02.title: Divisibility of a difference of measurements
q_count_pigeonhole_02.statement: Eight devices each produce an integer measurement, possibly equal or negative. Prove that two distinct devices have measurements whose difference is divisible by 7.
q_count_pigeonhole_02.answer_text: Classify the devices by the 7 remainders modulo 7; two of the 8 must share a class.
q_count_pigeonhole_02.explanation: Every integer has a unique remainder 0,1,…,6 modulo 7; negative integers use the same congruence classes. Place the 8 devices in 7 boxes by measurement remainder. Two distinct devices must share a box, with measurements u,v satisfying u−v=7t for some integer t. Equal measurements give difference 0, also divisible by 7, so repetitions cause no problem.
q_count_pigeonhole_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the 7 residue classes, 3 for assigning 8 devices and applying the principle, and 4 for divisibility and handling repeated or negative values.

q_count_pigeonhole_03.title: A guaranteed sum from complementary pairs
q_count_pigeonhole_03.statement: Choose any 13 distinct integers from {1,2,…,24}. Prove that two sum to 25, and explain why choosing 12 need not suffice.
q_count_pigeonhole_03.answer_text: Use pairs {1,24},{2,23},…,{12,13}. Thirteen numbers fill some pair. The set {1,…,12} shows 12 do not guarantee it.
q_count_pigeonhole_03.explanation: Partition the 24 integers into 12 disjoint boxes {i,25−i}, 1≤i≤12. Each box contains two numbers summing to 25. With 13 distinct selected numbers, some box contains both of its numbers, giving the pair. Choosing only 1 through 12 gives no pair summing to 25, so 13 is the minimum guaranteed quantity.
q_count_pigeonhole_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for a complete 12-pair partition, 4 for distinctness and the pigeonhole argument, and 2 for a 12-number counterexample.

q_count_pigeonhole_04.title: Integer points and an integer midpoint
q_count_pigeonhole_04.statement: Five distinct points in the plane have integer coordinates. Prove that two have a segment midpoint whose two coordinates are also integers.
q_count_pigeonhole_04.answer_text: Classify points into 4 coordinate-parity types. Two of the same type have even sums in each coordinate.
q_count_pigeonhole_04.explanation: There are four coordinate-parity types: (even,even),(even,odd),(odd,even),(odd,odd). Of 5 distinct points, two distinct points P=(x1,y1),Q=(x2,y2) share a type. Thus x1+x2 and y1+y2 are both even, making ((x1+x2)/2,(y1+y2)/2) integral. Each coordinate must have matching parity across the points; the horizontal and vertical coordinates of one point need not match each other.
q_count_pigeonhole_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the 4 types, 3 for finding distinct points of one type, and 4 for proving both midpoint coordinates integral.

q_count_inclusion_01.title: Overlap of two conditions
q_count_inclusion_01.statement: Among some records, 12 have label A, 9 have label B, and 4 have both. How many have at least one label?
q_count_inclusion_01.explanation: Adding gives 21, counting the 4 double-labeled records twice. Subtract their intersection once: 12+9−4=17.
q_count_inclusion_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for C; 0 for other choices.

q_count_inclusion_02.title: Accounting for three properties
q_count_inclusion_02.statement: Among 100 devices, 40 have A,35 have B,30 have C; 12 have A and B,10 have A and C,9 have B and C, and 4 have all three. Pairwise counts include devices with all three. Find the numbers with at least one property, exactly one, and none.
q_count_inclusion_02.answer_text: At least one:78; exactly one:55; none:22.
q_count_inclusion_02.explanation: The union has 40+35+30−12−10−9+4=78 devices, so 100−78=22 have none. Only A: 40−12−10+4=22; only B:35−12−9+4=18; only C:30−10−9+4=15. Exactly one totals 22+18+15=55. As a check, exactly two is (12−4)+(10−4)+(9−4)=19, and 55+19+4=78.
q_count_inclusion_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for union 78 and its formula, 5 for the individual only counts 22,18,15 and total 55, and 2 for complement 22.

q_count_inclusion_03.title: Surjective assignment to three locations
q_count_inclusion_03.statement: Assign 5 distinct exhibits to 3 exhibition areas labeled A,B,C, each exhibit in exactly one area and every area nonempty. Count the assignments and explain the need for intersection corrections.
q_count_inclusion_03.explanation: There are 3⁵=243 unrestricted assignments. Let A_A denote that area A is empty, with analogous events for the others. A specified empty area leaves 2⁵ assignments, totaling 3·2⁵. If two specified areas are empty, all exhibits go to the remaining one, giving 1 assignment for each of C(3,2)=3 pairs. All three cannot be empty because there are 5 exhibits. Inclusion–exclusion gives 243−96+3=150. Subtracting only 3·2⁵ removes assignments using one area twice, so intersections must be added back.
q_count_inclusion_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for universe 3⁵, 3 for empty-area events and 3·2⁵, 3 for pairwise and triple intersections, and 2 for 150.

q_count_inclusion_04.title: An inclusion–exclusion proof of misplaced letters
q_count_inclusion_04.statement: Four letters and four envelopes are each numbered 1 through 4, with one letter per envelope. Prove that exactly 9 assignments put no letter in its matching envelope. Explain every inclusion–exclusion term.
q_count_inclusion_04.explanation: All assignments are bijections between distinct letters and envelopes, totaling 4!. Let A_i mean letter i enters its matching envelope. Fixing k correct letters fixes their destinations, leaving (4−k)! arrangements of the rest. The k letters can be chosen in C(4,k) ways. Thus the count with no correct letter is Σ(k=0 to 4)(−1)^k C(4,k)(4−k)!=24−24+12−4+1=9. The last term 1 is the all-correct assignment, with 0!=1.
q_count_inclusion_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for the universe and bad events, 4 for intersections (4−k)! and choices C(4,k), 2 for alternating summation, and 2 for result 9 and the final term.

q_count_generating_01.title: Formal encoding of a geometric sequence
q_count_generating_01.statement: Let $a_n=2^n$ (n≥0). As a formal power series, its ordinary generating function $A(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ is ____.
q_count_generating_01.explanation: The formal expansion 1/(1−2x)=1+2x+4x²+8x³+… has coefficient 2^n at x^n. Multiplying this series by 1−2x gives constant coefficient 1 and cancellation at every other degree, so it is the formal inverse of 1−2x.
q_count_generating_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for 1/(1−2x); no numerical convergence condition is needed.

q_count_generating_02.title: Coefficients for two package sizes
q_count_generating_02.statement: A product comes in packages of 2 units and 3 units. Any nonnegative number of each may be used; packages of the same size are indistinguishable and selection order is ignored. How many ways give exactly 12 units? Give the generating function and coefficient.
q_count_generating_02.answer_text: The generating function is $1/((1-x^2)(1-x^3))$, and the required coefficient is 3.
q_count_generating_02.explanation: Choosing 0,1,2,… two-unit packages gives 1+x²+x⁴+…=1/(1−x²), and three-unit packages give 1/(1−x³). The x¹² coefficient of their product counts nonnegative solutions of 2u+3v=12. Parity makes v even, and 0≤v≤4, so v=0,2,4 with u=6,3,0 respectively: 3 ways. Indistinguishability and ignored order mean no extra permutation factor.
q_count_generating_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for each factor, 2 for 2u+3v=12, and 4 for all three solutions and count 3.

q_count_generating_03.title: Initial terms in recurrence shifts
q_count_generating_03.statement: The sequence satisfies $a_0=1$ and $a_n=a_{n-1}+n$ (n≥1). Use formal power series to find A(x) and an expression for a_n. You may use $\sum_{n\ge1}nx^n=x/(1-x)^2$.
q_count_generating_03.explanation: Multiply by x^n and sum over n≥1. The left side is A(x)−1, the lagged-term sum is xA(x), and the final sum is x/(1−x)². Hence (1−x)A(x)=1+x/(1−x)², giving A(x)=1/(1−x)+x/(1−x)³=(1−x+x²)/(1−x)³. Iterating the recurrence also gives a_n=1+1+2+…+n=1+n(n+1)/2, including n=0.
q_count_generating_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for shifts A−1 and xA, 3 for the generating function, and 3 for the general term and n=0 check.

q_count_generating_04.title: Do formal identities require convergence after substitution?
q_count_generating_04.statement: Someone says: “$\sum_{n\ge0}x^n=1/(1-x)$ cannot be a generating-function identity because the left side diverges at x=2.” Explain the flaw and verify the identity using formal multiplication.
q_count_generating_04.answer_text: Formal series identities compare coefficients and do not require summation at x=2; (1−x)(1+x+x²+…)=1 holds coefficientwise.
q_count_generating_04.explanation: In formal power series, x is a symbol; substituting any number to form an infinite numerical sum is not automatic. Set S=Σ(n≥0)x^n. The constant coefficient of (1−x)S is 1, while every x^n coefficient for n≥1 is 1−1=0. Thus the product is 1. Since 1−x has constant coefficient 1, it has a unique formal inverse, giving S=1/(1−x). Under a separate analytic interpretation the geometric series converges only for |x|<1; divergence at x=2 does not invalidate the formal identity.
q_count_generating_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for formal versus analytic interpretation, 4 for coefficientwise multiplication, 2 for inverse reasoning or equivalent, and 1 for analytic condition |x|<1.

q_recurrence_model_01.title: Boundary values for a strip-tiling recurrence
q_recurrence_model_01.statement: Let a_n count tilings of a length-n strip using indistinguishable tiles of lengths 1 and 2, with one empty tiling. Which recurrence and initial values are correct?
q_recurrence_model_01.explanation: For n≥2, a first tile of length 1 corresponds to any tiling of length n−1, and a first tile of length 2 to any tiling of length n−2. The cases are disjoint and exhaustive. Since a_0=1 and a_1=1, A is correct; a_0 cannot be 0.
q_recurrence_model_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for A; 0 for other choices.

q_recurrence_model_02.title: Codes with no adjacent ones
q_recurrence_model_02.statement: Let b_n count binary strings of length n with no adjacent ones, including one empty string. Give a recurrence with sufficient initial conditions and find b_6.
q_recurrence_model_02.explanation: For n≥2, classify by ending. Removing a final 0 leaves any valid length-(n−1) string, giving b_(n−1). A final 1 must be preceded by 0; removing the final 01 leaves any valid length-(n−2) string, giving b_(n−2), with unique reconstruction. The disjoint cases add. b_0=1 and b_1=2 (0,1), giving b_2=3,b_3=5,b_4=8,b_5=13,b_6=21.
q_recurrence_model_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for the ending cases and reversible correspondences, 3 for range and two initial values, and 3 for 21.

q_recurrence_model_03.title: Divide-and-conquer at odd sizes
q_recurrence_model_03.statement: An algorithm costs 1 unit for 1 element. For n≥2, it splits into subproblems of sizes ⌊n/2⌋ and ⌈n/2⌉, processes both, then spends n additional units. Let T_n be total cost. Give its recurrence and find T_5.
q_recurrence_model_03.explanation: Both subproblems execute, so add their costs rather than taking a maximum or product, and include the extra n. For odd n the subproblem sizes differ and cannot both be n/2. T_2=1+1+2=4, T_3=T_1+T_2+3=8, and T_5=T_2+T_3+5=4+8+5=17. No T_0 is needed, since both subproblem sizes are at least 1 for n≥2.
q_recurrence_model_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for integer subproblem sizes, 3 for summing both costs, adding n, and the base value, and 4 for T_2,T_3,T_5=17.

q_recurrence_model_04.title: Stairs with no consecutive two-step moves
q_recurrence_model_04.statement: Climb to height n using moves of 1 or 2 steps, never using two 2-step moves consecutively. Let a_n count valid move sequences, with one empty sequence. Prove $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-3}$ for n≥3 and give sufficient initial conditions.
q_recurrence_model_04.explanation: Classify by the last move. If it is 1, deletion bijects to all valid sequences of height n−1. If it is 2 and n≥3, a preceding move exists and cannot be 2, so the ending is 1,2. Deleting both moves leaves any valid height-(n−3) sequence; appending 1,2 never creates consecutive 2s, so this is also a bijection. The cases are disjoint and exhaustive. Initial values are a_0=1 (empty),a_1=1 (1),a_2=2 (1,1 or 2), sufficient to compute from n=3.
q_recurrence_model_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for classification, 2 for each deletion/reconstruction bijection, 2 for the role of n≥3, and 2 for all three initial values.

q_recurrence_homogeneous_01.title: Identifying a linear homogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients
q_recurrence_homogeneous_01.statement: All relations below are considered for n≥2. Which is a linear homogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients?
q_recurrence_homogeneous_01.explanation: A has constant coefficients 3,−2, sequence terms only to the first power, and no forcing term. B has nonzero forcing n and is nonhomogeneous. C squares a sequence term and is nonlinear. D has coefficient n varying with index and therefore not constant.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for A; 0 for other choices.

q_recurrence_homogeneous_02.title: Two distinct characteristic roots
q_recurrence_homogeneous_02.explanation: The characteristic equation r²−5r+6=0 factors as (r−2)(r−3)=0. Distinct roots give a_n=C·2^n+D·3^n. Initial conditions give C+D=2 and 2C+3D=5, so C=D=1. Each exponential satisfies the recurrence, so their sum does too; at n=0,1 it gives 2,5, identifying the sequence.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the characteristic equation and roots, 2 for the general form, 3 for constants, and 2 for the formula and initial-value/recurrence checks.

q_recurrence_homogeneous_03.title: A double root requires the extra term
q_recurrence_homogeneous_03.statement: Find a closed form for $a_n=4a_{n-1}-4a_{n-2}$ (n≥2), $a_0=1,a_1=4$, and explain why $C2^n$ alone is insufficient.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_03.answer_text: $a_n=(n+1)2^n$ (n≥0). A double root requires the second independent solution n times the exponential.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_03.explanation: The characteristic equation is r²−4r+4=(r−2)²=0. Root 2 has multiplicity 2, giving (C+Dn)2^n. From a_0=1, C=1; from a_1=4, 2(1+D)=4, so D=1. With only C2^n, a_0=1 would force a_1=2, contradicting 4, so the n2^n term is essential.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the double root, 3 for the complete form including n, 2 for constants and formula, and 2 for the single-exponential contradiction.

q_recurrence_homogeneous_04.title: A real sequence of period four
q_recurrence_homogeneous_04.statement: The sequence satisfies $a_0=1,a_1=0$ and $a_n=-a_{n-2}$ (n≥2). Prove its least positive period is 4 and give a real-valued closed form.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_04.explanation: Applying the recurrence twice gives a_(n+4)=−a_(n+2)=a_n, so 4 is a period. The first four terms are 1,0,−1,0. A period 1,2,or 3 would require a_0 to equal a_1,a_2,or a_3, namely 0,−1,or 0, none equal to 1. Thus the least positive period is 4. The expression cos(nπ/2) has the same initial values and satisfies cos(nπ/2)=−cos((n−2)π/2). Uniqueness from the two initial values gives the formula.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for repetition after four steps, 3 for excluding smaller positive periods, 3 for the cosine formula and check, and 1 for initial-value uniqueness.

q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_01.title: A homogeneous solution plus a particular solution
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_01.statement: Suppose $h_n=2h_{n-1}$ and $p_n=2p_{n-1}+3$, both for n≥1. Which sequence necessarily satisfies $a_n=2a_{n-1}+3$?
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_01.explanation: For a_n=h_n+p_n, a_n−2a_(n−1)=(h_n−2h_(n−1))+(p_n−2p_(n−1))=0+3. The sequence h_n alone has no forcing term, 2p_n gives forcing 6, and h_n−p_n gives forcing −3.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for B; 0 for other choices.

q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_02.title: Shifting a constant forcing term
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_02.explanation: Set b_n=a_n+3. Then b_n=2a_(n−1)+6=2b_(n−1), with b_0=4. Thus b_n=4·2^n and a_n=4·2^n−3. At n=0 this is 1; substitution gives 2(4·2^(n−1)−3)+3=4·2^n−3. The shift −3 can also be viewed as a constant particular solution.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for a correct shift or constant particular solution, 3 for the homogeneous part and initial value, 2 for the formula, and 2 for checking.

q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_03.title: Exponential forcing coinciding with a characteristic root
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_03.statement: Find a closed form for $a_n=2a_{n-1}+2^n$ (n≥1), $a_0=0$. Explain why $C2^n$ cannot be a particular solution.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_03.explanation: Divide by 2^n and set b_n=a_n/2^n. Then b_n=b_(n−1)+1 with b_0=0, so b_n=n and a_n=n2^n. A trial p_n=C2^n gives p_n−2p_(n−1)=0, which cannot equal 2^n. This is resonance between characteristic root 2 and the forcing base, requiring an n factor. Substitution gives n2^n−2(n−1)2^(n−1)=2^n, and the initial value is also 0.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for normalization and its initial value, 3 for the formula, 3 for resonance and failure of the original trial, and 1 for checking.

q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_04.title: Constant forcing and a double root
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_04.statement: Find a closed form for $a_n-2a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}=2$ (n≥2), $a_0=0,a_1=1$, and explain why a quadratic particular solution must be considered.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_04.explanation: The homogeneous characteristic equation is (r−1)²=0, giving C+Dn. Constant forcing 2·1^n has base 1, a double root. Constants and linear polynomials have zero second difference, so try An². Since n²−2(n−1)²+(n−2)²=2, A=1 gives a particular solution. The complete solution is n²+C+Dn. Initial values give C=0 and D=0, so a_n=n².
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the double root and homogeneous form, 3 for the second-difference or resonance explanation, 2 for the particular coefficient, and 2 for both initial values and the final formula.

q_recurrence_initial_01.title: Number of standard initial values for order three
q_recurrence_initial_01.statement: For $a_n=a_{n-1}+2a_{n-2}+a_{n-3}$ (n≥3), standard initial conditions are consecutive terms starting at a_0. What is the minimum number needed to determine the sequence uniquely forward for arbitrary initial values?
q_recurrence_initial_01.explanation: Computing a_3 requires a_2,a_1,a_0, so these three are the standard initial values. They determine a_3, then a_4, and so on uniquely. Fewer leave at least one starting parameter free. Extra values may be given, but are unnecessary for minimality and must be checked for compatibility.
q_recurrence_initial_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for C; 0 for other choices.

q_recurrence_initial_02.title: Recovering a sequence from a later value
q_recurrence_initial_02.statement: A real sequence satisfies $a_n=3a_{n-1}$ (n≥1) and a_2=18. Find a_0 and a closed form, explaining why backward recovery from a_2 is possible.
q_recurrence_initial_02.explanation: Since the coefficient 3 is nonzero, a_2=3a_1 gives a_1=6, and a_1=3a_0 gives a_0=2. Forward geometric recursion then gives a_n=2·3^n. With coefficient 0 the division would fail; here the nonzero coefficient makes the earlier two terms uniquely recoverable.
q_recurrence_initial_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for recovering a_1 and a_0, 3 for the formula, and 3 for the nonzero-coefficient and uniqueness explanation.

q_recurrence_initial_03.title: An early term omitted by the recurrence range
q_recurrence_initial_03.statement: Given $a_0=0,a_1=1$, suppose $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$ holds only for n≥3. Do these data uniquely determine a_4? If not, give two valid sequences with different a_4 and explain how to add sufficient information.
q_recurrence_initial_03.answer_text: No; a_2 is unspecified. Taking a_2=1 or 2 gives a_4=3 or 5. Specify a_2, or explicitly change the valid range to n≥2.
q_recurrence_initial_03.explanation: The formula cannot be used at n=2, so a_2 may be any real t. Thereafter a_3=t+1 and a_4=2t+1. Taking t=1 gives 0,1,1,2,3,…; t=2 gives 0,1,2,3,5,…. Both satisfy the original initial values and recurrence for n≥3 but have different a_4. Giving a_2 determines the rest uniquely; alternatively, extending the valid range to n≥2 forces a_2=a_1+a_0=1 and also gives uniqueness.
q_recurrence_initial_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for noting n=2 is outside the range and a_2 is free, 4 for two valid examples with different a_4, and 3 for a sufficient addition.

q_recurrence_initial_04.title: Redundant and contradictory conditions
q_recurrence_initial_04.statement: For real sequences satisfying $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$ (n≥2), classify each set of additional conditions as having a unique solution, multiple solutions, or no solution, and prove it: (A) $a_0=1$ and $a_2-a_1=1$; (B) $a_0=1$ and $a_2-a_1=2$.
q_recurrence_initial_04.answer_text: (A) has infinitely many solutions, with arbitrary real a_1; (B) has no solution.
q_recurrence_initial_04.explanation: At n=2 the recurrence gives a_2−a_1=a_0. In (A), the second condition already follows from a_0=1 and places no restriction on a_1. Any real t as a_1, followed by forward recursion from a_0=1, satisfies (A), giving infinitely many solutions. In (B), the recurrence and a_0=1 force a_2−a_1=1 but also require 2, a contradiction, so no solution exists. Two written conditions are not automatically independent and compatible.
q_recurrence_initial_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for a_2−a_1=a_0, 4 for redundancy in (A) and the arbitrary-t family, and 3 for proving the contradiction in (B).

q_count_basic_05.title: Different numbers of later branches
q_count_basic_05.statement: A visit reservation chooses a route and then a session. Category A has 2 distinct routes, each with 3 sessions; category B has 3 distinct routes, each with 4 sessions. Select one route and one session for that route. Count reservations and explain why “5 routes times the session count of any route” is invalid.
q_count_basic_05.answer_text: 2×3+3×4=18 choices; different routes have different session counts.
q_count_basic_05.explanation: Category A gives 2×3=6 choices and B gives 3×4=12. The routes are distinct and one category is chosen, so the total is 6+12=18. Multiplying all 5 routes by 3 omits B sessions, while multiplying by 4 invents A sessions.
q_count_basic_05.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for correct counts in A and B, 3 for total 18, and 3 for the differing branch-count explanation.

q_count_basic_06.title: Removing order labels from ordered choices
q_count_basic_06.statement: Choose 2 of 12 distinct volunteers as partners, without order or different duties. First count by “first person, second person,” then remove repetitions and find the number of pairs.
q_count_basic_06.explanation: There are 12 choices for the first and 11 different choices for the second, giving 132 ordered pairs. Each unordered pair {u,v} corresponds exactly to (u,v) and (v,u). Since u=v is excluded, the multiplicity is always 2. Equal-multiplicity counting gives 132/2=66.
q_count_basic_06.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for 132 ordered pairs, 5 for exactly two preimages of each unordered result, and 2 for 66.

q_count_basic_07.title: Complement counting for strings that are not all zero
q_count_basic_07.statement: For nonnegative integer n, count binary strings of length n containing at least one 1, and explain the subtraction using disjoint classes. The empty string contains no 1.
q_count_basic_07.answer_text: There are $2^n-1$ strings; for n=0 this is 0.
q_count_basic_07.explanation: There are 2^n strings in total. Divide into those containing at least one 1 and those entirely zero; these are disjoint and exhaustive. The latter class contains one string, including the unique empty string when n=0. The sum rule gives target count+1=2^n, hence 2^n−1. At n=0 no strings qualify and the formula gives 0.
q_count_basic_07.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for universe 2^n, 3 for the disjoint exhaustive split, 3 for one all-zero string and subtraction, and 2 for the empty-string boundary.

q_count_basic_08.title: When the division rule applies
q_count_basic_08.statement: A program outputs 6 numbered records. Removing numbers gives three distinct results U,V,W, appearing 1,2,3 times respectively. Someone says, “There are 3 numbers, so the number of distinct results is 6÷3=2.” Identify the error and give a sufficient condition for valid use of the division rule.
q_count_basic_08.answer_text: The fiber sizes are 1,2,3, not equal, so division by 3 is invalid. A sufficient condition is that every result has exactly the same positive number r of numbered representations and none is omitted; then divide the record total by r.
q_count_basic_08.explanation: The division rule requires every result to be counted the same number of times, not merely three numbers or a maximum of three appearances. Here U,V,W are already three results and their multiplicities sum to 6, but the fibers are not constant, so 6/3 is unjustified. If another output process covers all results with exactly r records per result, the records partition into equal disjoint classes. The sum rule gives total records=r×number of results, allowing division.
q_count_basic_08.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for unequal multiplicities and the actual three results, 4 for coverage and equal multiplicity, and 3 for explaining division through grouped counting.

q_count_perm_comb_05.title: Three named roles
q_count_perm_comb_05.statement: Assign coordinator, recorder, and inspector to 3 of 7 distinct members, one person per role with no person holding two roles. Count the assignments.
q_count_perm_comb_05.explanation: The three roles are distinct, so this is ordered selection: 7 choices for coordinator, 6 remaining for recorder, and 5 for inspector, giving P(7,3)=210. Dividing by 3! would merge valid assignments having the same people in different roles.
q_count_perm_comb_05.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for recognizing order, 4 for the factors 7,6,5, and 3 for 210 and why not to divide by 3!.

q_count_perm_comb_06.title: Combining adjacent objects into a block
q_count_perm_comb_06.statement: Arrange 7 distinct manuals in a row. Two named A and B must be adjacent, with either internal order. Count the arrangements.
q_count_perm_comb_06.explanation: Combine A,B into a block. Together with the other 5 manuals this gives 6 distinct objects, arranged in 6! ways. The block can be AB or BA, giving 2 internal orders. Expanding the block uniquely recovers a valid arrangement, so the total is 2·6!=1440. Do not divide by 2 because those internal orders are different results.
q_count_perm_comb_06.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for 6 objects after blocking, 2 each for 6! and the two internal orders, and 3 for reversibility and 1440.

q_count_perm_comb_07.title: A first-position restriction in multiset permutations
q_count_perm_comb_07.statement: Use digits 0,0,1,1,2 once each to form five-digit decimal integers. The first digit cannot be 0. Count the distinct integers.
q_count_perm_comb_07.explanation: All five-character arrangements, including leading zero, total 5!/(2!2!)=30. Fixing a leading 0 leaves 0,1,1,2, with 4!/(1!2!1!)=12 arrangements. Subtract to get 30−12=18. Equal digits are indistinguishable, so neither 5! nor retaining multiplicity 2 for zero after fixing the first digit is correct.
q_count_perm_comb_07.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for total 30, 4 for updated multiplicities and 12 leading-zero arrangements, and 3 for difference 18.

q_count_perm_comb_08.title: Two named teams with unordered membership
q_count_perm_comb_08.statement: From 8 distinct people, choose disjoint team A of 2 and team B of 3; everyone else is unassigned. Teams are named but have no internal roles. Count the selections.
q_count_perm_comb_08.explanation: Choose team A in C(8,2)=28 ways, then team B from the remaining 6 in C(6,3)=20, giving 560. Team names distinguish assignments, so swapping teams cannot identify results. Internal order is irrelevant, so do not multiply by 2! or 3!. Equivalently use 8!/(2!3!3!), with the last 3! for the unassigned people.
q_count_perm_comb_08.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for choosing from remaining people without overlap, 3 for named teams and unordered interiors, and 3 for 560 or the equivalent multinomial coefficient.

q_count_binomial_05.title: Summing even-index terms
q_count_binomial_05.statement: Compute $\binom80+\binom82+\binom84+\binom86+\binom88$ using the binomial theorem rather than adding terms individually.
q_count_binomial_05.explanation: Let E,O be the even- and odd-index sums. From (1+1)^8, E+O=256; from (1−1)^8, E−O=0. Thus E=128. Equivalently add the two expansions and divide by 2 so odd terms cancel.
q_count_binomial_05.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for each substitution equation and 4 for cancellation and 128.

q_count_binomial_06.title: Convolution with groups of different sizes
q_count_binomial_06.statement: Compute $\sum_{k=0}^{3}\binom3k\binom6{5-k}$ and explain its combinatorial meaning.
q_count_binomial_06.explanation: Take disjoint groups A,B of sizes 3,6 and select 5 of the 9 people. If k are from A, then 5−k are from B, giving C(3,k)C(6,5−k) choices for k=0,1,2,3. These disjoint exhaustive cases sum to C(9,5)=126. Directly, the terms are 6,45,60,15, totaling 126.
q_count_binomial_06.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for disjoint groups and common selection objects, 4 for classifying by k and the product, and 3 for 126.

q_count_binomial_07.title: A set proof of Pascal’s identity
q_count_binomial_07.statement: For integers n≥2 and 1≤k≤n−1, prove $\binom nk=\binom{n-1}k+\binom{n-1}{k-1}$.
q_count_binomial_07.answer_text: Partition the k-subsets of an n-element set by whether they contain one fixed element.
q_count_binomial_07.explanation: Fix an element u of the universe. A k-subset excluding u must be chosen from the remaining n−1 elements, giving C(n−1,k). A subset including u needs k−1 more from the others, giving C(n−1,k−1). The classes are disjoint and exhaustive, so the sum rule gives the identity. The specified range makes all binomial coefficients defined with the usual nonnegative indices.
q_count_binomial_07.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for fixing an element and classifying, 3 for each class count, and 1 for the summed conclusion.

q_count_binomial_08.title: A signed product coefficient
q_count_binomial_08.statement: Find the coefficient of $x^5$ in $(1+x)^3(1-x)^4$. Explain the degrees contributed by each factor or give an equivalent simplification.
q_count_binomial_08.explanation: Rewrite as (1−x²)³(1−x). The first factor has only even powers, so x⁵ can only come from its x⁴ term and the second factor’s −x. The x⁴ coefficient in the first factor is C(3,2)(−1)²=3, giving −3. Direct convolution gives the contributions 3−12+6=−3; signs vary with the degree from the second factor.
q_count_binomial_08.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for correct factor combination or convolution, 3 for identifying terms producing x⁵, and 4 for the binomial coefficient, sign, and result −3.

q_count_pigeonhole_05.title: Exceeding different capacities at the threshold
q_count_pigeonhole_05.statement: Three buffers allow at most 2,4,5 records respectively. Records may be assigned arbitrarily. What is the minimum total that guarantees some buffer exceeds its own limit? Prove minimality.
q_count_pigeonhole_05.answer_text: 12 records; 11 can be distributed as 2,4,5 without exceeding limits.
q_count_pigeonhole_05.explanation: If no buffer exceeds its limit, there are at most 2+4+5=11 records, so 12 force an excess. Conversely, 11 records can be assigned 2,4,5 without exceeding any limit, so fewer than 12 do not guarantee it. With unequal box capacities, sum the individual limits.
q_count_pigeonhole_05.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for total capacity 11, 3 for proving 12 sufficient, and 4 for the threshold distribution proving minimality.

q_count_pigeonhole_06.title: Prefix sums guarantee a consecutive block
q_count_pigeonhole_06.statement: Given any 7 integers x_1,…,x_7, prove that some nonempty consecutive block has sum divisible by 7. Negative numbers and 0 are allowed.
q_count_pigeonhole_06.answer_text: Classify the 8 prefix sums S_0=0,S_j=x_1+…+x_j modulo 7, then subtract two congruent sums.
q_count_pigeonhole_06.explanation: Define S_0=0 and S_j=Σ(i=1 to j)x_i for 1≤j≤7. These 8 indexed objects have only 7 remainders modulo 7, so some 0≤i<j≤7 satisfy S_i≡S_j(mod 7). Their difference S_j−S_i=x_(i+1)+…+x_j is a consecutive-block sum; j>i makes it nonempty. It is a multiple of 7, including if it is 0.
q_count_pigeonhole_06.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for 8 prefix sums including S_0, 3 for a congruence collision, and 4 for the nonempty block difference and divisibility.

q_count_pigeonhole_07.title: A short distance inside a square
q_count_pigeonhole_07.statement: Place any 5 distinct points in a closed unit square. Prove two have Euclidean distance at most √2/2, explaining points on partition lines.
q_count_pigeonhole_07.answer_text: Divide into 4 squares of side 1/2 and uniquely assign boundary points. Two in the same square have distance at most its diagonal √2/2.
q_count_pigeonhole_07.explanation: Divide by the midlines into four boxes. Classify each coordinate using [0,1/2) and [1/2,1], assigning every point to exactly one box. Of 5 points, two share a box. Their horizontal and vertical differences have absolute values at most 1/2, so distance squared is at most 1/4+1/4=1/2 and distance at most √2/2. Assign boundary endpoints to the designated right or upper box; the bound remains valid.
q_count_pigeonhole_07.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for four parts and unique boundary assignment, 2 for the 5-to-4 pigeonhole argument, and 4 for the squared-distance estimate and nonstrict bound.

q_count_pigeonhole_08.title: Why acquaintance counts have one fewer possible class
q_count_pigeonhole_08.statement: Nine people attend an event. Acquaintance is symmetric and nobody counts themselves. Prove two know the same number of people.
q_count_pigeonhole_08.answer_text: Counts lie between 0 and 8, but 0 and 8 cannot both occur. At most 8 counts are present, so two of 9 people share one.
q_count_pigeonhole_08.explanation: Possible counts are 0,1,…,8. If someone knows 8, they know everyone else; symmetry means everyone else knows them, excluding count 0. Thus if 0 occurs, 8 does not; if 0 does not occur, only 1 through 8 remain. Either way there are at most 8 classes. Placing 9 people in them gives a repeated count. Excluding simultaneous 0 and 8 is essential; 9 people in 9 classes alone would not suffice.
q_count_pigeonhole_08.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for the candidate range, 4 for symmetry excluding simultaneous 0 and 8, 3 for at most 8 classes and the principle, and 1 for the conclusion.

q_count_inclusion_05.title: The complement of two divisibility conditions
q_count_inclusion_05.statement: How many integers from 1 through 90 inclusive are divisible by neither 6 nor 10?
q_count_inclusion_05.explanation: There are ⌊90/6⌋=15 multiples of 6 and 9 multiples of 10. Their intersection consists of multiples of 30, giving 3. The union has 15+9−3=21, leaving 90−21=69. The product 6×10=60 is not the least common multiple needed for the intersection.
q_count_inclusion_05.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the two multiple counts, 3 for lcm 30 and intersection 3, and 4 for inclusion–exclusion and complement 69.

q_count_inclusion_06.title: Exact property counts from intersection sums
q_count_inclusion_06.statement: For finite sets A,B,C, write S1=|A|+|B|+|C|, S2=|A∩B|+|A∩C|+|B∩C|, and S3=|A∩B∩C|. Prove the count belonging to exactly one set is S1−2S2+3S3, and the count belonging to exactly two is S2−3S3.
q_count_inclusion_06.answer_text: Let N_j count elements in exactly j sets. Then S1=N1+2N2+3N3, S2=N2+3N3, S3=N3; solving gives both formulas.
q_count_inclusion_06.explanation: An element in exactly one set appears once in S1 and never in S2,S3. One in exactly two appears twice in S1 and once in S2. One in all three contributes 3,3,1 to S1,S2,S3 respectively. Hence S1=N1+2N2+3N3, S2=N2+3N3, S3=N3. Thus N3=S3, N2=S2−3S3, and N1=S1−2N2−3N3=S1−2S2+3S3. Elements in none of the sets contribute 0 to every sum.
q_count_inclusion_06.grading_criteria: 10 points: 5 for classification and the three equations, 2 for N2, 2 for N1, and 1 for zero contribution outside the union.

q_count_inclusion_07.title: Excluding missing characters after fixing the first position
q_count_inclusion_07.statement: Count length-5 strings using only A,B,C, with first character A and each character appearing at least once.
q_count_inclusion_07.explanation: The first A is fixed, already satisfying the A requirement. The other 4 positions have 3⁴=81 choices. Subtract 2⁴ strings missing B and 2⁴ missing C. Missing both means all four are A, giving 1 string subtracted twice that must be restored. Thus 81−16−16+1=50. Missing A cannot be a nonempty bad event because A is fixed first.
q_count_inclusion_07.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for universe 81 after fixing the first character, 4 for the two missing-character counts of 16, and 4 for intersection 1 and total 50.

q_count_inclusion_08.title: Why inclusion–exclusion gives weight one
q_count_inclusion_08.statement: For finite sets A_1,…,A_m, take an element belonging to exactly r sets, 1≤r≤m. Prove that its total contribution to the union inclusion–exclusion formula is 1, and explain why this establishes the general formula.
q_count_inclusion_08.explanation: The element appears C(r,k) times among k-fold intersections, because k sets must be chosen from the r containing it. Its weight is C(r,1)−C(r,2)+…+(−1)^(r+1)C(r,r). Since 0=(1−1)^r=1+Σ(k=1 to r)(−1)^k C(r,k), rearrangement gives weight 1. An element belonging to no set appears in no intersection sum and has weight 0. Thus, element by element, the right side counts each union element once and equals the union size.
q_count_inclusion_08.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for k-fold multiplicity, 3 for the binomial weight calculation, and 3 for zero-property elements and the elementwise conclusion.

q_count_generating_05.title: Convolution of two geometric series
q_count_generating_05.statement: As formal power series, prove $[x^n](1-x)^{-2}=n+1$ for every n≥0 without analytic differentiation.
q_count_generating_05.answer_text: Write (1−x)^(−2) as a product of two geometric series; its degree-n coefficient is Σ(k=0 to n)1=n+1.
q_count_generating_05.explanation: The formal identity (1−x)^(−1)=Σ(j≥0)x^j holds. The x^n coefficient of its square counts nonnegative pairs i+j=n. For i=0,1,…,n, exactly one j=n−i corresponds, giving n+1 pairs. Every degree in the product uses only finitely many terms, so no numerical x or convergence discussion is needed. At n=0 the coefficient 1 is included.
q_count_generating_05.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for two formal geometric series, 5 for convolution or pair counting, and 2 for the boundary and independence from convergence.

q_count_generating_06.title: Combining bounded and unbounded choices
q_count_generating_06.statement: Count nonnegative integer solutions of u+v+w=4 with u≤2, v≤3, and no additional upper bound on w. Give an ordinary generating function and compute the target coefficient.
q_count_generating_06.answer_text: The generating function is $(1+x+x^2)(1+x+x^2+x^3)/(1-x)$; its $x^4$ coefficient is 11.
q_count_generating_06.explanation: The u factor permits 0,1,2, the v factor 0 through 3, and the w factor is 1/(1−x). The x⁴ coefficient of their product counts the solutions. By u: for u=0, v=0,…,3 gives 4 choices; for u=1, v=0,…,3 gives 4; for u=2, v=0,…,2 gives 3. Each (u,v) uniquely fixes nonnegative w=4−u−v, so 4+4+3=11.
q_count_generating_06.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for three factors and their size interpretation, 5 for a complete calculation by u or convolution, and 1 for 11.

q_count_generating_07.title: The correct numerator for a second-order recurrence
q_count_generating_07.statement: Given $f_0=0,f_1=1$ and $f_n=f_{n-1}+f_{n-2}$ (n≥2), find F(x) and check its numerator using the first few terms.
q_count_generating_07.explanation: Multiply by x^n and sum for n≥2: F−f_0−f_1x=x(F−f_0)+x²F. Substituting gives F−x=xF+x²F, hence F=x/(1−x−x²). The denominator has constant term 1 and is formally invertible. The recurrence begins 0,1,1,2,3, so F has constant coefficient 0 and linear coefficient 1, matching numerator x. Numerator 1 would contradict the initial values.
q_count_generating_07.grading_criteria: 10 points: 5 for all three sums and initial corrections, 3 for F, and 2 for checking the numerator with early terms.

q_count_generating_08.title: Generating-function decomposition from integer division
q_count_generating_08.statement: For positive integer m, prove formally that $\frac{1+x+\cdots+x^{m-1}}{1-x^m}=\frac1{1-x}$, and use integer division to explain why every nonnegative-degree coefficient is exactly 1.
q_count_generating_08.answer_text: Every nonnegative n has a unique representation n=qm+r with q≥0 and 0≤r<m, so the left side contributes exactly once to each x^n.
q_count_generating_08.explanation: Write the left side as (Σ(r=0 to m−1)x^r)(Σ(q≥0)x^(qm)). A contribution to x^n corresponds to n=qm+r with nonnegative integers. Division with remainder gives exactly one such representation with 0≤r<m. Thus every coefficient is 1, and the series is Σ(n≥0)x^n=1/(1−x). Alternatively use (1−x)(1+x+…+x^(m−1))=1−x^m and formal division; both denominators have constant term 1.
q_count_generating_08.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for expanding the two choices, 4 for existence and uniqueness of quotient/remainder, and 3 for coefficientwise equality and valid formal denominators.

q_recurrence_model_05.title: Region increments from lines
q_recurrence_model_05.statement: Draw n infinite lines in a plane successively, with no pair parallel and no three concurrent. Let R_n be the number of regions and R_0=1. Explain why the nth line adds n regions, give a recurrence, and find R_4.
q_recurrence_model_05.explanation: The nth line meets the previous n−1 lines at n−1 distinct points, splitting it into n pieces including the two end rays. Every old region is an intersection of half-planes and hence convex, so its intersection with a line is connected. Thus the n pieces pass through distinct old regions, each splitting one region in two and adding one. Therefore R_n=R_(n−1)+n, with R_0=1, yielding R_1=2,R_2=4,R_3=7,R_4=11.
q_recurrence_model_05.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for n−1 distinct intersections from the assumptions, 3 for each of n pieces adding one region, and 4 for recurrence, initial value, and 11.

q_recurrence_model_06.title: Ternary strings need two ending states
q_recurrence_model_06.statement: Strings use only 0,1,2 and forbid adjacent 22. Let u_n count valid length-n strings ending in 2, and v_n those ending in something other than 2. Assign the empty string to v_0: u_0=0,v_0=1. Give both state recurrences and count length-4 strings.
q_recurrence_model_06.explanation: A 2 can follow only a string not ending in 2, so u_n=v_(n−1). Either 0 or 1 can follow any valid string, giving two choices per prefix and v_n=2(u_(n−1)+v_(n−1)). Starting at (0,1), the states are (1,2),(2,6),(6,16),(16,44), with totals 3,8,22,60. Assigning the empty string to v_0 makes the n=1 transition correct.
q_recurrence_model_06.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for each transition, 2 for the initial state and empty-string convention, and 2 for the four-step total 60.

q_recurrence_model_07.title: A recursion tree with constant merge cost
q_recurrence_model_07.statement: Consider only n=2^k with k≥0. An algorithm costs T_1=0 at n=1. For n≥2 it runs two size-n/2 subproblems and spends 1 additional unit. Find T_n using induction or a recursion tree.
q_recurrence_model_07.answer_text: T_n=n−1 for n a nonnegative integer power of 2.
q_recurrence_model_07.explanation: The model is T_n=2T_(n/2)+1. Induct on k: for k=0,n=1, T_1=0=1−1. If T_(2^(k−1))=2^(k−1)−1, then T_(2^k)=2(2^(k−1)−1)+1=2^k−1. Thus the formula holds for every power-of-two size. In a recursion tree, n zero-cost leaves correspond to n−1 internal nodes each costing 1.
q_recurrence_model_07.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for the recurrence, 2 for the base case, 4 for induction, and 2 for the formula and valid range.

q_recurrence_model_08.title: An invalid model that never reaches its base case
q_recurrence_model_08.statement: Someone models a terminating algorithm by $T_0=0$ and $T_n=T_{\lceil n/2\rceil}+1$ for n≥1. Identify the problem. If the base case is changed to T_1=0 and the same recurrence used only for n≥2, find T_5.
q_recurrence_model_08.answer_text: Originally n=1 gives T_1=T_1+1, a contradiction, and size cannot decrease from 1 to 0. After correction, T_5=3.
q_recurrence_model_08.explanation: For n=1, ceil(1/2)=1, so the call returns to the same size and cannot reach base 0. Finite real costs would also give the contradiction 0=1. This is not a valid terminating model. With T_1=0 and recursion only for n≥2, ceil(n/2)<n, so sizes decrease. The chain 5→3→2→1 incurs three additional units, giving T_5=3.
q_recurrence_model_08.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for the n=1 self-loop and contradiction, 3 for strict decrease after correction, and 3 for the chain and T_5=3.

q_recurrence_homogeneous_05.title: Signs from a negative characteristic root
q_recurrence_homogeneous_05.statement: Find a closed form for $a_n=-a_{n-1}+2a_{n-2}$ (n≥2), $a_0=0,a_1=3$, using correct parentheses for the negative root.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_05.explanation: The characteristic polynomial r²+r−2=(r−1)(r+2) has roots 1,−2, giving C+D(−2)^n. The initial values give C+D=0 and C−2D=3, so C=1,D=−1. Hence a_n=1−(−2)^n. The negative sign belongs to the base; 1+2^n and 1−2^n are incorrect.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_05.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the equation and roots, 2 for the complete form, 3 for both initial-value equations and constants, and 2 for the formula’s signs.

q_recurrence_homogeneous_06.title: A triple root gives a quadratic sequence
q_recurrence_homogeneous_06.explanation: The characteristic polynomial r³−3r²+3r−1=(r−1)³ gives C+Dn+En². The initial values give C=1,D+E=1,2D+4E=4, yielding D=0,E=1. Thus a_n=n²+1. Its zero third difference also verifies the recurrence. A triple root requires retaining the n² term.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_06.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the triple root, 3 for three free constants in the complete form, 3 for solving constants and the formula, and 1 for verification or the multiplicity explanation.

q_recurrence_homogeneous_07.title: Oscillation does not imply a periodic full sequence
q_recurrence_homogeneous_07.statement: A real sequence satisfies $a_n=-4a_{n-2}$ (n≥2), $a_0=1,a_1=0$. Find a closed form and decide whether a_n and $b_n=a_n/2^n$ are periodic.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_07.answer_text: $a_n=2^n\cos(n\pi/2)$; a_n is not periodic, while b_n has least positive period 4.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_07.explanation: Roots ±2i give the real formula 2^n cos(nπ/2) matching the initial values. Equivalently, a_(2m)=(−4)^m and a_(2m+1)=0. The even terms have unbounded absolute values 4^m, while a finite-valued periodic sequence repeats only finitely many values and is bounded. Thus a_n is not periodic. After normalization, b_n repeats 1,0,−1,0 with least period 4. Considering only the complex-root angles and ignoring amplitude 2^n would misclassify a_n.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_07.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for the formula or even/odd description, 3 for unboundedness excluding periodicity of a, and 3 for the period and minimality for b.

q_recurrence_homogeneous_08.title: Proving linear superposition for homogeneous recurrences
q_recurrence_homogeneous_08.statement: Suppose u_n,v_n satisfy the same linear homogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients and k lagged terms, valid for n≥k. Prove w_n=αu_n+βv_n also satisfies it for any real constants α,β. Explain how to obtain its initial values.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_08.answer_text: By linearity, w_n=Σ(c_jw_(n−j)); its initial values are w_i=αu_i+βv_i for 0≤i<k.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_08.explanation: Write u_n=Σ(j=1 to k)c_ju_(n−j), with the same relation for v. Then w_n=αΣc_ju_(n−j)+βΣc_jv_(n−j)=Σc_j(αu_(n−j)+βv_(n−j))=Σc_jw_(n−j) for each n≥k. Its first k values are combined directly by definition and usually differ from the original initial values of u or v. Superposition preserves the recurrence but does not automatically preserve specified nonzero initial conditions.
q_recurrence_homogeneous_08.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for the common recurrence, 5 for the termwise linear-combination proof, and 3 for the initial-value formula and its qualification.

q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_05.title: Differences of particular solutions and solution-set structure
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_05.statement: Suppose p_n,q_n satisfy the same linear nonhomogeneous recurrence L(a)=f with constant coefficients, where f is not identically zero. Prove p−q satisfies the homogeneous recurrence and explain why the original solution set is generally not a vector space.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_05.answer_text: L(p−q)=f−f=0. The zero sequence does not satisfy L(a)=f, so this nonhomogeneous solution set is not a vector space.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_05.explanation: Since L is a linear combination of lagged terms, L(p−q)=L(p)−L(q)=0. A vector space must contain the zero sequence, but L(0)=0 while f is not identically zero, so the zero sequence does not solve the equation. The nonhomogeneous solution set is therefore not a vector space. Once a particular solution p is fixed, all others are p plus homogeneous solutions, a translate of the homogeneous solution space.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_05.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for linearity and the homogeneous difference, 4 for excluding a vector space by the zero sequence, and 2 for the translate structure.

q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_06.title: A nonresonant exponential particular solution
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_06.explanation: The homogeneous solution is C3^n. Base 2 is not characteristic root 3, so try A2^n. Substitution gives A2^n−3A2^(n−1)=−A2^(n−1)=2^n, hence A=−2. The full solution is C3^n−2·2^n. From a_0=0, C−2=0, so C=2.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_06.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the homogeneous part and nonresonant trial, 3 for A=−2 by substitution, 2 for C=2 from the initial value, and 2 for the formula.

q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_07.title: Polynomial resonance raises the degree
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_07.statement: Find a closed form for $a_n-a_{n-1}=n^2$ (n≥1), $a_0=0$. You may use undetermined coefficients, but explain the degree of the particular solution.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_07.explanation: The homogeneous root 1 is simple, and forcing is a quadratic times 1^n, so try An³+Bn²+Cn. Its first difference is 3An²+(−3A+2B)n+(A−B+C). Comparing with n² gives A=1/3,B=1/2,C=1/6. Add the homogeneous constant D; a_0=0 gives D=0. Thus a_n=n³/3+n²/2+n/6=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, also the sum of squares from 1 to n.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_07.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for simple resonance requiring a cubic trial, 4 for differences and coefficient equations, 3 for coefficients and the initial constant, and 1 for the simplified formula.

q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_08.title: Superposition for mixed forcing terms
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_08.statement: Find a closed form for $a_n=2a_{n-1}+3+2^n$ (n≥1), $a_0=1$, explaining particular solutions for the constant and exponential forcing separately.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_08.explanation: The homogeneous solution is C2^n. For constant forcing 3, use −3 since −3−2(−3)=3. For forcing 2^n, resonance with root 2 gives particular solution n2^n, whose operator value is 2^n. Linearity makes their sum n2^n−3 a particular solution for 3+2^n. Thus the complete solution is (C+n)2^n−3. The initial value gives C−3=1, hence C=4. Apply the initial condition once to the full combined solution.
q_recurrence_nonhomogeneous_08.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for each particular solution, 2 for combination by linearity, and 2 for the initial constant and formula.

q_recurrence_initial_05.title: Why identical initial values cannot branch
q_recurrence_initial_05.statement: Let k≥1. Suppose real sequences u,v both satisfy a_n=c_1a_(n−1)+…+c_ka_(n−k)+f(n) for n≥k, with the same coefficients and f, and u_i=v_i for 0≤i<k. Prove u_n=v_n for all n≥0.
q_recurrence_initial_05.answer_text: Use strong induction on n: the common recurrence and equal earlier terms force equal current terms.
q_recurrence_initial_05.explanation: Equality at n=0,…,k−1 is given. Suppose n≥k and u_j=v_j for all j<n. Subtracting the recurrences gives u_n−v_n=Σ(i=1 to k)c_i(u_(n−i)−v_(n−i)); the common f(n) cancels. Every difference on the right is 0 by induction, so u_n=v_n. Strong induction completes the proof. This is forward uniqueness and requires no division by the last coefficient.
q_recurrence_initial_05.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for k base cases, 2 for a clear induction hypothesis, 5 for subtraction, cancellation of f, and zero differences, and 1 for the conclusion.

q_recurrence_initial_06.title: Redundant information on even terms
q_recurrence_initial_06.statement: A real sequence satisfies $a_n=a_{n-2}$ (n≥2). Do a_0=2,a_2=2 uniquely determine it? What is the formula after adding a_1=5? What if a_2=3 is given instead?
q_recurrence_initial_06.answer_text: No; odd-index terms remain free. Adding a_1=5 makes even terms 2 and odd terms 5. Giving a_0=2 and a_2=3 together gives no solution.
q_recurrence_initial_06.explanation: The recurrence makes all even-index terms equal a_0 and all odd-index terms equal a_1. Since a_2=2 already follows from a_0=2, it is redundant and leaves a_1 arbitrary. Adding a_1=5 uniquely gives a_(2m)=2,a_(2m+1)=5 for m≥0. If a_2=3, it contradicts a_2=a_0=2, so no solution exists.
q_recurrence_initial_06.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the two parity chains, 3 for redundancy and the free parameter, 2 for the piecewise formula after a_1, and 2 for the contradiction.

q_recurrence_initial_07.title: Backward recovery fails at a zero coefficient
q_recurrence_initial_07.statement: A real sequence satisfies a_n=0·a_(n−1) for n≥1, and only a_1=0 is known. Can a_0 be recovered? If a_0=7 is also given, is the sequence unique? Distinguish forward and backward uniqueness.
q_recurrence_initial_07.answer_text: a_0 cannot be recovered and may be any real number. Given a_0=7, the unique sequence is 7,0,0,….
q_recurrence_initial_07.explanation: Every a_0 gives a_1=0 and all subsequent terms 0, so a_1 provides no information about a_0. One cannot write a_0=a_1/0. Given a_0=7, the recurrence uniquely forces every later term to 0. A forward function can have a unique output without being injective, so its input need not be recoverable from the output.
q_recurrence_initial_07.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for arbitrary a_0, 2 for no division by zero, 3 for the unique sequence starting at 7, and 2 for distinguishing forward and backward recovery.

q_recurrence_initial_08.title: Carry initial values through sequence transformations
q_recurrence_initial_08.statement: Given $a_0=2$ and $a_n=\frac{n}{n+1}a_{n-1}+\frac1{n+1}$ for n≥1, set $b_n=(n+1)a_n$. Find the initial value and recurrence for b, then a_n.
q_recurrence_initial_08.explanation: Multiplying by n+1 gives (n+1)a_n=na_(n−1)+1. Since b_(n−1)=n a_(n−1), b_n=b_(n−1)+1. Transform the initial value too: b_0=(0+1)a_0=2, not 0 or 1. Hence b_n=n+2; dividing by nonzero n+1 gives a_n=(n+2)/(n+1). At n=0 this is 2, as required.
